messages.body_plain:
Including parens solved the issue - then it is perhaps error in the manual. Anyway thanks!
I've included the faulty example at the bottom of the previous post. Now the example look like this:

simulate_gp = "
data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  real x[N];
}
transformed data {
  vector[N] mu;
  cov_matrix[N] Sigma;
  for (i in 1:N)
    mu[i] = 0;
  for (i in 1:N)
    for (j in 1:N)
      Sigma[i,j] = exp(-pow(x[i] - x[j],2))

                  + (i==j ? 0.1 : 0.0);

}
parameters {
  vector[N] y;
}
model {
  y ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);
}
"

Best,
Wiktor

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multilevel Ordered Logistic Regression
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Multilevel Ordered Logistic Regression
messages.body_plain:
The details are all in the manual chapter on constraint
transformations near the end.  Basically, the first
element is unconstrained and the others are exp(base) + previous
element.

I don't think your more explicit model will do that.

Yes, that'll put a hierarchical prior on them, but I think
you need the truncations, so I'm not sure it's well formed.
You are following our recommendations here:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations

but I'm pretty sure those need to be revised to indicate
that we need the truncation points.  I will make a fresh post
to try to get an answer.  I have very little time over the next
week or two, so I don't have time to dig deeper on my own, but
I'm sure someone else will know.

- Bob

>   for (i in 1:Ntests) {

>      Cutpoints[i][3] ~ normal(CutpointsMean[3] , CutpointsSigma[3]);
>   }
>
>
>
> Efficiency aside, is the above a correct way of modelling a hierarchical ordinal response in Stan? I'm new to Stan and I'm not quite sure on how the internals of the ordered vector work. Said that, the results I get seem sensible.
>
> In order to enforce the ordering constraints more explicitly, I have also created another model
> where the first cutpoint is modelled as a normal distribution while the other two cutpoints are modelled as two half normal distributions that represent a relative positive offset respect to the previous cutpoint.
> The final cutpoints are computed by adding the first cutpoint and the other two cutpoints offsets as appropriate:
>
>  parameters {
>     real          Cutpoints1[Ntests]; // cutpoint 1 group i
>     real<lower=0> Cutpoints2[Ntests]; // offset cutpoint 2 group i
>     real<lower=0> Cutpoints3[Ntests]; // offset cutpoint 3 group i
>
>
>     real          CutpointsMean1;     // global cutpoint 1
>     real<lower=0> CutpointsDMean2;    // global cutpoint 2 offset
>     real<lower=0> CutpointsDMean3;    // global cutpoint 3 offset
>
>     real<lower=0> CutpointsSigma[3];  // global cutponts sigma values
>
>
>     ...
>  }
>
>
>  model {
>
>
>      CutpointsSigma   ~ exponential(1);

>     CutpointsMean1   ~ normal(1, 1);   // these prior are problem specific

>     CutpointsDMean2  ~ normal(1.5, 1.5);
>     CutpointsDMean3  ~ normal(2, 2);
>
>     for (i in 1:Ntests) {
>       Cutpoints1[i] ~ normal(CutpointsMean1 , CutpointsSigma[1]); // cutpoint 1 group i
>       Cutpoints2[i] ~ normal(CutpointsDMean2, CutpointsSigma[2]); // delta cutpoint 2            Cutpoints3[i] ~ normal(CutpointsDMean3, CutpointsSigma[3]); // delta cutpoint 3
>     }
>
>
>   for (i in 1:N) {
>
>       vector[3]  cuts;
>       vector[3]  ocuts;
>
>       cuts[1]    <-  Cutpoints1[tests[i]]; // from normal
>       cuts[2]    <-  Cutpoints2[tests[i]]; // from normal > 0 (half normal)
>       cuts[3]    <-  Cutpoints3[tests[i]]; // from normal > 0 (half normal)
>
>       // recover cutpoints from offsets
>       ocuts[1] <- cuts[1];                            // can take any value
>       ocuts[2] <- cuts[1] + cuts[2];                  // ocuts[2] > ocuts[1]
>       ocuts[3] <- cuts[1] + cuts[2] + cuts[3];        // ocuts[3] > ocuts[2] > ocuts[1]
>
>       y[i] ~ ordered_logistic("predictors go here", ocuts);
>
>   }
>
>
> Both the above models  produce very similar and sensible looking results, however as I'm new to Stan I may have missed something?
>
> Thanks,
> Antonio

messages.subject: ordered cut points --- need to truncate hierarchical prior?
messages.subject_clean: ordered cut points --- need to truncate hierarchical prior?
messages.body_plain:
If we have a parameter

  ordered[K] c[J];

with J different cutpoints, then our recommendations suggest
partial pooling with a hierarchical model:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations

But if we do that, won't we need to include the truncations
because of the ordering constraints?  I don't think they'll
drop out.  I'm afraid I don't have time to work out what we
need, but if someone could add a note to the wiki above,
that'd be super helpful.

This came up in a query from Antonio Martini in post
titled "Multilevel Ordered Logistic Regression", but I thought
I'd highlight my question.

Thanks,

- Bob

Some cool ML approaches were tried by various teams with some success, but they require years and years of data to train, and aren't applicable to new locations or changing conditions, so there is limited policy relevance. (And the sponsors basically said they weren't hopeful that Dengue modeling could be advanced all that much.)
> > >
> > > I have asked before about time varying inputs, and it's (appropriately) not high on the list of priorities for the core team. I'll be trying gamma priors - my first trial seems to have gotten fairly good convergence, without much fiddling, but that may be luck.

> > > > On Tuesday, July 12, 2016 at 4:28:31 PM UTC-4, David Manheim wrote:
> > > > > Hi Krzysztof,
> > > > >
> > > > > These are really good points. I do have the model converging, and I'm not finding stability problems anymore - though it took a fair amount of playing with my priors for that to occur consistently across multiple years of data.
> > > > >
> > > > > Re: Small numbers and stability, because it is a country level model that represents a single year, with a single implied strain, I am assuming a (low) level of constant baseline infected individuals. This is a kludgy way to account for instability near low numbers, but is effective, and not dissimilar to having an initial infection level. Stochasticity in transmission is a big deal for high fidelity, but for country level models, standard, basic compartmental modeling rarely accounts for it - a known limitation. This is a reason that microsimulation and agent based models are used much more widely now. See my new publication for details! http://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RR1576.html (Sorry, I'm really excited about that.)
> > > >
> > > > Thanks for mentioning the report, were you involved in the dengue modeling exercise?
> > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > The residuals for the model are comparable to residuals for other ODE models - not great. In this case, the big thing that reduced the systematic discrepancies was accounting for school closures - which I have rarely seen other models do, strangely. (This makes the transmission somewhat time-varying, though in a very specific way.)
> > > >
> > > > Thanks for sharing your experience with this.  The systematic patterns in residuals is another feature likely to cause computational problems so it may be a place where introducing time-varying parameters would improve algorithm efficiency enough to offset the extra computational cost.  It would be great to have a plug-in component like the birthday data model for this! Seems like everyone has to re-invent the wheel for dealing with big shocks from holidays.
> > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Re: lognormal priors, that's a great point. I can change them, and from what I understand, it will probably help. I need a non-negative distribution, so I need to consider which of the several options that Stan now supports I want to use - any suggestions? There are now so many options in the recent versions of Stan!
> > > >
> > > > I tend to use gamma priors (and generally spend a lot of time simulating to get the right parameters) or just do more or less standard normal priors and use a scaled logit to get them to cover the right range nicely.  Then you just need to check posterior results to make sure you're not bumping up against the upper end of the range.  There are divergent opinions on this around here so hopefully others will chime in with alternatives but in terms of taking care of computational problems the scaled logit trick works really well as long as you don't have strong background knowledge indicating that values extremely close to zero are likely.
> > > >
> > > > Krzysztof
> > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Thanks for the suggestions,
> > > > > David
> > > > >
> > > > > On Tuesday, July 12, 2016 at 2:07:53 PM UTC-4, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
> > > > > > Hi David,
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I'm excited to see some of these ODE models for disease in common practice but I've approached it much more
> > > > > > cautiously.  A colleague at UMass did some basic simulated data for the model Michael (Betancourt) coded up and
> > > > > > as far as we could tell the numerical performance of that simple model really depends on the parameters used
> > > > > > to simulate the data.  In general that's sort of a no-brainer but in this case reasonable parameter values seemed
> > > > > > to make the model hang or fail to converge (this wasn't exhaustive, just trying to get a handle on what needed to
> > > > > > be done to just be able to throw data sets at these models).  Our other main concern with doing ODE's was that
> > > > > > in our data sets small counts will sometimes be important and the fact that ODE-based disease models gloss over
> > > > > > stochasticity in transmission makes me think that there will be serious fit issues (and therefore computational issues)
> > > > > > unless you introduce time-varying transmission parameters.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > So that's a long-winded way of asking whether you got simpler SEIR models working consistently with this type of data (or even simulated data)? Have you looked at residuals for the current fits (even if you don't feel like you have convergence it's useful to see the space the model is exploring and the in-sample predictions it generates).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I'd also be careful about the log-normal priors since they can imply a pretty big upper tail (for example, that lognormal(log(400),5) prior if you simulate a thousand draws will regularly generate values in the 10^8 range which is going to cause computational problems in an ODE model unless there is enough data to make the posterior much tighter.  In a model this complex I have no intuition so I would go with more conservative priors.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I'm sure there are ways to make the computation more efficient too but in my experience issues like lack of fit and priors allowing outlandish parameter values are the first issues to tackle.

That will work, but with the exp transform, the priors will
be on different scales.  You don't need the Jacobians
because you're using them on the right side of ~.

> parameters {
>   vector[K-1]   Cutpoints[Ntests]; // no longer ordered
>   vector[K-1]   CutpointsMean;
>   real<lower=0> CutpointsSigma[K-1];

You can use

  vector<lower=0>[K - 1] CutpointsSigma;

if you wnat to use vector for all of the variables (won't matter
for efficiency --- it just makes everything consistent).

> for (i in 1:Ntests) {
>     Cutpoints[i][1] ~ normal(CutpointsMean[1] , CutpointsSigma[1]);
>     Cutpoints[i][2] ~ normal(CutpointsMean[2] , CutpointsSigma[2]);
>     Cutpoints[i][3] ~ normal(CutpointsMean[3] , CutpointsSigma[3]);
>   }

You can vectorize this as:

  Cutpoints[ , 1] ~ normal(CutpointsMean[1], CutpointsSigma[1]);
  ...

and it will be much more efficient.

- Bob

> On Aug 1, 2016, at 1:20 PM, Antonio Martini <antonio...@hotmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
>
> Thanks a lot for the pointers, I have rewritten the model using the Ordered Inverse Transform as follows:
>
> parameters {
>   vector[K-1]   Cutpoints[Ntests]; // no longer ordered
>   vector[K-1]   CutpointsMean;
>   real<lower=0> CutpointsSigma[K-1];
>   ...
> }
>
> model {
>
>   CutpointsSigma ~ exponential(1);
>   CutpointsMean  ~ normal(0, 10);
>
>  // The vectorized version didn't work for some reason, I will double check later on .
>   for (i in 1:Ntests) {
>     Cutpoints[i][1] ~ normal(CutpointsMean[1] , CutpointsSigma[1]);
>     Cutpoints[i][2] ~ normal(CutpointsMean[2] , CutpointsSigma[2]);
>     Cutpoints[i][3] ~ normal(CutpointsMean[3] , CutpointsSigma[3]);
>   }
>
>   for (i in 1:N)
>   {
>     vector[3]  cuts;
>
>     // map to ordered sequence by Ordered Inverse Transform
>     cuts    <- Cutpoints[tests[i]];
>     cuts[2] <- cuts[1] + exp(cuts[2]);
>     cuts[3] <- cuts[2] + exp(cuts[3]);
>
>     y[i] ~ ordered_logistic("predictors go here", cuts);
>   }
> }
>
> '
>
>
> As you can see, the cutpoints are no longer declared as ordered variables.The distribution of the ordinal response is computed after the model fit by applying the ordered inverse transform to the posterior of the unordered cutpoints.
>
> Would this work or there is still something missing?:)
>
> Thanks,Antonio
>
> On Monday, 1 August 2016 14:02:51 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The details are all in the manual chapter on constraint
> transformations near the end.  Basically, the first
> element is unconstrained and the others are exp(base) + previous
> element.
>
> I don't think your more explicit model will do that.
>
> Yes, that'll put a hierarchical prior on them, but I think
> you need the truncations, so I'm not sure it's well formed.
> You are following our recommendations here:
>
> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations
>
> but I'm pretty sure those need to be revised to indicate
> that we need the truncation points.  I will make a fresh post
> to try to get an answer.  I have very little time over the next
> week or two, so I don't have time to dig deeper on my own, but
> I'm sure someone else will know.
>
> - Bob
>

> > On Aug 1, 2016, at 7:18 AM, Antonio Martini <antonio...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Bob,
> >
> > Thanks for looking into this, As I wrote: " I have removed the part relating to the covariates for clarity. ".This in order to focus on the part that is more difficult to model without polluting the view. In the final model  predictors are included.
> >
> > regarding to:
> >

> >   for (i in 1:Ntests) {
> >      Cutpoints[i][1] ~ normal(CutpointsMean[1] , CutpointsSigma[1]);
> >      Cutpoints[i][2] ~ normal(CutpointsMean[2] , CutpointsSigma[2]);
> >      Cutpoints[i][3] ~ normal(CutpointsMean[3] , CutpointsSigma[3]);
> >   }
> >
> >
> >

> > Efficiency aside, is the above a correct way of modelling a hierarchical ordinal response in Stan? I'm new to Stan and I'm not quite sure on how the internals of the ordered vector work. Said that, the results I get seem sensible.
> >
> > In order to enforce the ordering constraints more explicitly, I have also created another model
> > where the first cutpoint is modelled as a normal distribution while the other two cutpoints are modelled as two half normal distributions that represent a relative positive offset respect to the previous cutpoint.
> > The final cutpoints are computed by adding the first cutpoint and the other two cutpoints offsets as appropriate:
> >
> >  parameters {
> >     real          Cutpoints1[Ntests]; // cutpoint 1 group i
> >     real<lower=0> Cutpoints2[Ntests]; // offset cutpoint 2 group i
> >     real<lower=0> Cutpoints3[Ntests]; // offset cutpoint 3 group i
> >
> >
> >     real          CutpointsMean1;     // global cutpoint 1
> >     real<lower=0> CutpointsDMean2;    // global cutpoint 2 offset
> >     real<lower=0> CutpointsDMean3;    // global cutpoint 3 offset
> >
> >     real<lower=0> CutpointsSigma[3];  // global cutponts sigma values
> >
> >

> >     ...
> >  }
> >
> >
> >  model {
> >
> >
> >      CutpointsSigma   ~ exponential(1);

> >     CutpointsMean1   ~ normal(1, 1);   // these prior are problem specific
> >     CutpointsDMean2  ~ normal(1.5, 1.5);
> >     CutpointsDMean3  ~ normal(2, 2);
> >

> >     for (i in 1:Ntests) {

> >       Cutpoints1[i] ~ normal(CutpointsMean1 , CutpointsSigma[1]); // cutpoint 1 group i
> >       Cutpoints2[i] ~ normal(CutpointsDMean2, CutpointsSigma[2]); // delta cutpoint 2            Cutpoints3[i] ~ normal(CutpointsDMean3, CutpointsSigma[3]); // delta cutpoint 3
> >     }
> >
> >

> >   for (i in 1:N) {
> >
> >       vector[3]  cuts;

> >       vector[3]  ocuts;
> >
> >       cuts[1]    <-  Cutpoints1[tests[i]]; // from normal
> >       cuts[2]    <-  Cutpoints2[tests[i]]; // from normal > 0 (half normal)
> >       cuts[3]    <-  Cutpoints3[tests[i]]; // from normal > 0 (half normal)
> >
> >       // recover cutpoints from offsets
> >       ocuts[1] <- cuts[1];                            // can take any value
> >       ocuts[2] <- cuts[1] + cuts[2];                  // ocuts[2] > ocuts[1]
> >       ocuts[3] <- cuts[1] + cuts[2] + cuts[3];        // ocuts[3] > ocuts[2] > ocuts[1]
> >
> >       y[i] ~ ordered_logistic("predictors go here", ocuts);
> >
> >   }
> >
> >
> > Both the above models  produce very similar and sensible looking results, however as I'm new to Stan I may have missed something?
> >
> > Thanks,
> > Antonio

We aren't going to allow (a + b) for variables declared as:

  matrix[M, N] a;
  real b[M, N];

  a + b;  // ***NO!!!***

There's no way to figure out what the result type would
be.  We also don't want to mix arrays and matrix operations.
If you want arithmetic, everything should be a matrix or
vector;  the arrays are just containers for iterating over.

We will be vectorizing binary functions.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

I'm with Bob. Not sure I understand you right.
What I get is that you want to constraint a matrix containing counts.
This is what you mentioned with simplex. The simplex construct in
STAN represents a special vector of probabilities that sum to 1.

And now as I hope understand right - you have a constraint not
necessarily 1 and its entries are real values.

For clarity, the following is not highly optimized STAN code
This could be done by STANs softmax function plus
vectorization.

Lets create a parameter theta which creates a multinomial
'simplex' pr.theta, each 0 <= pr.theta[i] <= 1
and sum(pr.theta) == 1.

sigma.theta ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

theta[1] ~ normal(0, sigma.theta)
theta[2] ~ normal(0, sigma.theta)
theta[3] ~ normal(0, sigma.theta)

pr.theta[1] <- 1/(1+exp(theta[1])+exp(theta[2])+exp(theta[3]))
pr.theta[2] <- exp(theta[1]) * pr.theta[1]
pr.theta[3] <- exp(theta[2]) * pr.theta[1]
pr.theta[4] <- exp(theta[3]) * pr.theta[1]

If you now want to change the upper limit to something else,
just change
 pr.theta[1] <- 1/(1+exp(theta[1])+exp(theta[2])+exp(theta[3]))
by
 pr.theta[1] <- my_fancy_upper_limit /(1+exp(theta[1])+exp(theta[2])+exp(theta[3]))

Take a look here to:
http://www.mathworks.com/help/stats/multinomial-models-for-nominal-responses.html

Another option you have is to specify a Dirichlet distribution upon a simplex in STAN and
scale it.

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/24349692/dirichlet-multinomial-winbugs-code

Andre

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Help parameterizing a constrained simplex?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Help parameterizing a constrained simplex?
messages.body_plain:
Think of the multinomial distribution — you have a collection of counts
in bins, n_{i}, with the constraint that \sum_{i = 1}^{I} n_{i} = N.  In the
limit of each n_{i} being large, then this can be reasonably approximated
by taking a simplex and scaling each value by N (which was originally
suggested and is equivalent to the softmax construction in the previous
email).  If _any_ of the n_{i} are small, however, then this approximation
falls apart and bad things happen.

Ultimately, however, this is a common mistake of not thinking generatively.
Counts are _data_, and we don’t fit data.  We fit a generative model of
how the data were produced.  So the relevant “contact” matrix isn’t over
counts, it’s over probabilities that could induce said counts.  And those
probabilities can often be easily modeled with simplices.

For example, each column could be a simplex with the corresponding
likelihood a mutlinomial distribution over the counts corresponding to
that column.  Same could be true for the rows.  These are known as
left and right stochastic matrices.

Things become more difficult if you have a double stochastic matrix,
where the rows _and_ columns have to sum to one.  There the matrix
doesn’t decouple into a collection of simplices and you’d have to be
more careful in the implementation (not sure how to do it off the top
of my head).

OK, so I am trying something like the suggested approaches, and it seems to keep the constrain, but seemingly samples much faster. (I'm running a larger sample now to see if that is really true, but so far, it's much better.)

I think it's essentially a left stochastic matrix, from what Michael described. Instead of having a matrix, I have a simplex of the percentage of total contacts per group, and a simplex of contacts in each group to each other group (i.e. the percentage of that group's total). I multiply these together, and multiply the product by the sum of the number of contacts.

This enforces only the total constraint. For the contact matrix constraint, I don't use some of those entries - I only use the upper triangular matrix entries, and replace the ones corresponding with the remainder with the values implied by the constraint. Now, I have a bunch of free variables as parameters, which seems non-ideal, but it works. (I checked the resulting matrix, and it follows my constraints.)

(Of course, I'd love to do something closer to what Michael suggested, thinking generatively, about how the contact matrix is a function of some underlying process. This kind-of does that, but I'm unsure how I would decompose my prior about relative propensity to interact, instead of simply providing the prior.)

Thanks,
David

With Stan, you don't need to build an MCMC sampler, it's
already built in.

> Only after noticing that stan does not allow int parameter sampling, I am confused on how to solve the problem.
> I saw on the reference and other threads that general solution is to marginalize out the discrete parameter by specifying full posterior. My question is do I have to decompose full posterior to marginalize out the parameter or working with conditional posterior is sufficient.

If you have posterior p(alpha, beta) where beta are the
integer parameters, you need to code up the marginalization

 p(alpha) = SUM_beta p(alpha, beta)

Usually algebra lets you move that summation inside to make
it tractable.  Often this would be of the form

  PROD_k p(alpha[k] | beta[k]) * p(beta[k]).

if that's what you mean.

Hi Bob,
Sure.

Disease transmission happens when an infected person and a noninfected person come in contact with one another, with some probability p that transmission occurs during that contact. (That probability is a key parameter in infectious disease modeling, which I need to estimate.)

In simple compartmental Epi models, we have a set of groups, or compartments, and we assume that these groups are homogenous. We also assume that the rate at which people contact one another is independent of disease status, so we find the underlying contact rate for different groups. The number of infected individuals in group A at t+1 is the sum over all groups of: ( Percentage of individuals in group i who are sick at time t, multiplied by percentage of individuals in group A that are susceptible at time t, multiplied by the number of contacts between group i and group A per time period, multiplied by the probability p that transmission occurs per contact.)

The contact rate in basic Epi models is frequently assumed or given, but is uncertain. I am attempting to estimate it, based on a prior about what these rates are. The contact rate between each pair of groups is summarized as a matrix - that's what I'm trying to find right now.

2 Constraints exist;

OK.  I was just thrown off by the form of your regression, which is
just a hardcoded slope of 1 and intercept of i (we like to use Greek
letters for parameters and reserve variables like i, j, k, and m, n for
integers).  And it doesn't roll the mean into the (alpha, beta) terms (or
does it?) in

  target += gamma_lpdf(y - (x[1] - i) | alpha,beta);

as you usually see in a standard GLM.

In order to have a positive variate for the gamma distribution, you
need

  y - x[1] + i > 0,

or equivalently

  i > x[1] - y,

which means you need a lower bound for i of

  max(x[1] - y) == max(x[1]) - y

I don't understand the rest of the regression, but that's
probably not important.

And forget what I said about priors on alpha and beta;
I hadn't kept in mind they are transformed parameters and you
do have priors on the components.

- Bob

P.S.  It's easier for us with just text for the models and GIF/JPG for
images.

messages.subject: Tips for reparameterizing / scaling a nonlinear model?
messages.subject_clean: Tips for reparameterizing / scaling a nonlinear model?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

   I have a fairly simple model relating temperature (T) to a log-linear rate of pathogen die-off (K) across a number of experimental data. The model essentially consists of a normal likelihood relating each mean natural log concentration (C) at time (t), and with sample standard devation (s) and sample size (n) to a linear function of K. K, in turn, is related to T through a normal distribution around an exponential function. K is not log transformed because a few experiments have negative values (i.e. there is population growth). For observation i in experiment j:

C[i] ~ Normal ( C_0[j] - K[j] * t[i] , s[i] / sqrt(n[i]) )

K[j] ~ Normal ( K_25 * exp( lambda * (T[j] - 25) , sigma_K )

There are currently 18 experiments with a total of 170 observations in the model.

If I scale t, C, and s, use noncentral parameterizations for K and C_0, and omit the temperature function, such that K is simply estimated separately for each experiment with a common prior distribution, I can run 5000 iterations within about 45 minutes.

On the other hand, if I include the temperature dependency function, A). I'm not sure how best to handle data / parameter scaling of K and T, due to the exponential function used to relate them, along with the fact that sometimes K <= 0, and B). The model takes up to 20 hours to run the same number of iterations, despite the fact that less parameters are actually estimated.

My guess is that the exponential term is really bogging things down. Is there a better way to parameterize or scale this model that might improve its speed?

Would rescaling temperature, then maybe reparameterizing the exponential term as ln (K[j] - sigma_K * Z_k[j]) / K25 = lambda * T be likely to help?

Apologies if this question is very basic or I'm missing something obvious.

messages.body_plain:
I thought about this some more and can't make things add up.

Shouldn't we be be modeling the chance that an uninfected
group member gets infected and the chance that an infected group
member gets over the infection?  Then you don't need to worry
about symmetry because only infected individuals contacting uninfected
individuals matters for creating new infections.

Shouldn't we adjust for possible double counting where an
individual has contact with more than one infected individual?
Is it just that these adjustments for coherence are so small
and the percentage of infections, infection rate, and transmission
rates are so low that it doesn't affect the answer much?

I don't see how making the sum of contacts constant helps you
identify transmission rate;  you just fix a point arbitrarily
for one parameter to identify the other.  Does this get corrected
in some kind of posterior summary?

Also, I'm still not sure what the data is that's being measured.

- Bob

> On Aug 2, 2016, at 1:57 PM, David Manheim <davidm...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
> Sure.
>
> Disease transmission happens when an infected person and a noninfected person come in contact with one another, with some probability p that transmission occurs during that contact. (That probability is a key parameter in infectious disease modeling, which I need to estimate.)
>
> In simple compartmental Epi models, we have a set of groups, or compartments, and we assume that these groups are homogenous. We also assume that the rate at which people contact one another is independent of disease status, so we find the underlying contact rate for different groups. The number of infected individuals in group A at t+1 is the sum over all groups of: ( Percentage of individuals in group i who are sick at time t, multiplied by percentage of individuals in group A that are susceptible at time t, multiplied by the number of contacts between group i and group A per time period, multiplied by the probability p that transmission occurs per contact.)
>
> The contact rate in basic Epi models is frequently assumed or given, but is uncertain. I am attempting to estimate it, based on a prior about what these rates are. The contact rate between each pair of groups is summarized as a matrix - that's what I'm trying to find right now.
>
> 2 Constraints exist;
> The matrix is governed by a simple constraint that contacts are symmetric; every contact in group 1 with someone in group 2 is also an contact between the person in group 2 with the person in group 1 - but because the groups are potentially different sizes, the two contact rates are not equal. Instead, you have the reciprical constraint; contact(i,j) = contact(j,i) * size(j)/size(i).
>
> The matrix also interacts with the probability of transmission, p, since, for example, doubling one and halving the other leaves the outcome the same. In order to control for that, I keep the sum of contacts constant in my model.
>
> I need to model the constraints in order to find a posterior estimate of both the contact matrix and the probability of transmission.
>
> Hope this is clearer,
> David Manheim
>
> On Tuesday, August 2, 2016 at 1:12:28 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I'm still not sure your decomposition makes sense in that
> if you have these symmetry constraints, it's not underlyingly
> independent simplexes per item.
>
> Could you take a step back and explain what this contact
> matrix is and what it represents?  Is it data?  If so, what
> is its shape and what do the entries represent?
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Aug 2, 2016, at 11:54 AM, David Manheim <davidm...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > OK, so I am trying something like the suggested approaches, and it seems to keep the constrain, but seemingly samples much faster. (I'm running a larger sample now to see if that is really true, but so far, it's much better.)
> >
> > I think it's essentially a left stochastic matrix, from what Michael described. Instead of having a matrix, I have a simplex of the percentage of total contacts per group, and a simplex of contacts in each group to each other group (i.e. the percentage of that group's total). I multiply these together, and multiply the product by the sum of the number of contacts.
> >
> > This enforces only the total constraint. For the contact matrix constraint, I don't use some of those entries - I only use the upper triangular matrix entries, and replace the ones corresponding with the remainder with the values implied by the constraint. Now, I have a bunch of free variables as parameters, which seems non-ideal, but it works. (I checked the resulting matrix, and it follows my constraints.)
> >
> > (Of course, I'd love to do something closer to what Michael suggested, thinking generatively, about how the contact matrix is a function of some underlying process. This kind-of does that, but I'm unsure how I would decompose my prior about relative propensity to interact, instead of simply providing the prior.)
> >
> > Thanks,
> > David
> >
> > On Tuesday, August 2, 2016 at 4:31:44 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > Think of the multinomial distribution — you have a collection of counts
> > in bins, n_{i}, with the constraint that \sum_{i = 1}^{I} n_{i} = N.  In the
> > limit of each n_{i} being large, then this can be reasonably approximated
> > by taking a simplex and scaling each value by N (which was originally
> > suggested and is equivalent to the softmax construction in the previous
> > email).  If _any_ of the n_{i} are small, however, then this approximation
> > falls apart and bad things happen.
> >
> > Ultimately, however, this is a common mistake of not thinking generatively.
> > Counts are _data_, and we don’t fit data.  We fit a generative model of
> > how the data were produced.  So the relevant “contact” matrix isn’t over
> > counts, it’s over probabilities that could induce said counts.  And those
> > probabilities can often be easily modeled with simplices.
> >
> > For example, each column could be a simplex with the corresponding
> > likelihood a mutlinomial distribution over the counts corresponding to
> > that column.  Same could be true for the rows.  These are known as
> > left and right stochastic matrices.
> >
> > Things become more difficult if you have a double stochastic matrix,
> > where the rows _and_ columns have to sum to one.  There the matrix
> > doesn’t decouple into a collection of simplices and you’d have to be
> > more careful in the implementation (not sure how to do it off the top
> > of my head).
> >
> > On Aug 2, 2016, at 2:20 AM, andre.pfeuffer via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> >
> >> Hi David,
> >>
> >> I'm with Bob. Not sure what  I understand you right.
> >> What I get is that you want to constraint a matrix containing counts.
> >> This is what you mentioned with simplex. The simplex construct in
> >> STAN represents a special vector of probabilities that sum to 1.
> >>
> >> And now as I hope understand right - you have a constraint not
> >> necessarily 1 and its entries are real values.
> >>
> >> For clarity, the following is not highly optimized STAN code
> >> This could be done by STANs softmax function plus
> >> vectorization.
> >>
> >> Lets create a parameter theta which creates a multinomial
> >> 'simplex' pr.theta, each 0 <= pr.theta[i] <= 1
> >> and sum(pr.theta) == 1.
> >>
> >> sigma.theta ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
> >>
> >> theta[1] ~ normal(0, sigma.theta)
> >> theta[2] ~ normal(0, sigma.theta)
> >> theta[3] ~ normal(0, sigma.theta)
> >>
> >> pr.theta[1] <- 1/(1+exp(theta[1])+exp(theta[2])+exp(theta[3]))
> >> pr.theta[2] <- exp(theta[1]) * pr.theta[1]
> >> pr.theta[3] <- exp(theta[2]) * pr.theta[1]
> >> pr.theta[4] <- exp(theta[3]) * pr.theta[1]
> >>
> >> If you now want to change the upper limit to something else,
> >> just change
> >>  pr.theta[1] <- 1/(1+exp(theta[1])+exp(theta[2])+exp(theta[3]))
> >> by
> >>  pr.theta[1] <- my_fancy_upper_limit /(1+exp(theta[1])+exp(theta[2])+exp(theta[3]))
> >>
> >> Take a look here to:
> >> http://www.mathworks.com/help/stats/multinomial-models-for-nominal-responses.html
> >>
> >> Another option you have is to specify a Dirichlet distribution upon a simplex in STAN and
> >> scale it.
> >>
> >> http://stackoverflow.com/questions/24349692/dirichlet-multinomial-winbugs-code
> >>
> >> Andre

messages.body_plain:
I didn't see a question in there.

For 3, categorical distributions only have a single parameter,
the simplex of possible outcomes.  But if there are only two,
it is a bit more efficient to use a beta-Bernoulli model than
a Dirichlet-categorical.

If you want to marginalize out the latent states in an HMM,
the manual shows how to use the forward algorithm to do that
in the HMM example in section 7.6.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
>From what I can see rstan does not save the mass matrix.

When you load the results from a cmdstan run in rstan,
the diagonal of the inverse of the mass matrix is in the
string adaptation_info in the stan_args list, which is part of
the stanfit object. As far as I can tell, the string adaptation_info
is not in stanfit@stan_args when you use rstan for sampling.

For example, you get mass matrix for the first chain with
stanfit@stan_args[[1]]$adaptation_info.

To extract the values out of the string:
adaptation_info = stanfit@stan_args[[1]]$adaptation_info
mass_matrix = eval(parse(text=paste0("c(",strsplit(adaptation_info,"\n#")[[1]][3],")")))

The tricky part is matching the right parameter name to the
right values, especially if one of your parameters is a
correlation matrix.

Guido

messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan experts,

I followed the relevant manual chapter (p149 on Stan Reference 2.11) to reorganize my data to a database-like structure to handle missing responses.

The model works pretty well with the data when ignoring those missing trials (non-responses were automatically replaced by our experimental program, so those generated data were treated as if they were recorded in this case). This model ran pretty smoothly and it was able to reach convergence (r_hat in the worst case was <=1.05).

However, when I was taking those missing trials seriously, and reconstructed my data into the database-like structure, the model runs nearly 10 times slower and the chains do not converge, with neff <= 10, out of 1000 samples after warm-up per chain (4000 total valid samples).

The .stan models are nearly the same except that one is used for the whole dataset (when ignoring the missing data), and the other is used for the ragged dataset. There is another rescaling in the ragged dataset but this is mostly identical to the whole dataset.

My QUESTION is: since the only difference between this two models is the data organization/structure, should I conclude that the database-like reconstruction causes this problem? Or did I make some mistake? Note that for the whole dataset, every subject has 100 trials, while in the ragged data structure, the trial number varies between 71 and 100, mean = 92.2, SD = 6.9. Is the variance in the trial numbers a potential problem for Stan sampling?

I attached the two models for the whole dataset and the ragged dataset, respectively. I am estimating these models on a Linux server with RStan 2.8.2. and R3.2.0.

Any suggestion is appreciated!

Thanks a lot,
Lei

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I’m new to rStan and Bayesian statistics, so I currently have limited knowledge of both, but require it for my research. I’m running a mixed-effects model on a dataset of 4000 observations (200 groups each with 20 cases). The model is quite extensive, 99 population-level effects (both binary and continuous) and 13 random-effects. Running this model on the cluster succeeds in 4 to 5 hours and gives me interpretable output.

In the analysis of this output I noticed the presence of heteroscedasticity looking at the plot of fitted values versus residual values. Experimentation on a smaller model (using the lme4 package) showed that taking the inverse of the response variable (1/Y) seems to solve this issue. I want to run the larger regression model using rStan and the inverse transformation of Y, but this requires an enormous amount of time to run. Running the model with 4000 iterations (1000 warmup) requires more than 8 days to finish and returns 2900 divergent transitions and many Rhats above 1.1. I do not want to run it with more iterations as it already takes so long to run.

Maybe it has something to do with the response values after the inverse transformation, which are very close to zero.

Y:            min=7183.004,                 max=88021.06,                 mean=35940.4

1/Y          min=1.136092e-5             max=0.0001392175           mean=3.741544e-05

i have been looking for a solution to the issue a long time, so if anybody has a helpful suggestion it would be most welcome. Thanks in advance.

Jeroen

(p.s. Before I found out about this mailing list, I posted a less detailed version of this question on Stackoverflow <http://stackoverflow.com/questions/38230768/how-to-fix-stan-sampling-getting-stuck-with-inverse-transformation-of-response-v> where I was suggested to use the 'QR=TRUE' argument to stan_lmer, but this did not resolve the issue unfortunately.)

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for taking a look.

The overall model can be separated into 3 tasks: fitting two logistic models and one log-linear model simultaneously. It's an epidemiology problem, dealing with time-dependent risk-factors for mortality. One dependent variable is a mortality outcome, and one is a discrete time-to-event outcome, where I am modeling a discrete hazard for switching from treatment to another. This second model is only fit to a subset of the data (i.e. you are "censored" when you switch treatments). The data structure is that one observation is equal to one year per person, so there are multiple records per person. The simulation i had posted was a simplified version of this where I did not model treatment switching.

I'm getting a treedepth that averages from 7 to 11, with stepsize that is approx 10^-3 for one model and approx 10^-6 for another that includes correction for measurement error (where I know there is non-identifiability). I understand the latter stepsize, at least, is quite poor.

The bivariate scatter plots that included model intercept for one of the causes of death looked good for the most part. I've included 2 from my actual example without measurement error- the one that looks like the parameters are fairly independent is what I would a typical scatter plot. The other plot that shows strong correlation is atypical, but occurs for one variable. The variable happens to be my main treatment of interest, so I can't just exclude it. The third plot is from the model in which I also try to correct for measurement error - obviously, this one is horrible, but I don't feel like I can really address this one until I get the simpler case working more efficiently.

I'm using a restricted, cubic spline with fixed knots to characterize my treatment (it's a standardized, continuous variable). I could move to something else like a cubic polynomial function, but I'm guessing I will have the same problem. I'm open to suggestions on how I could have a flexible, non-linear function on a continuous variable that won't suffer these problems.

I'm stumped re: reparameterization. A while ago, I found a list of things to try with slow logistic models in STAN, but I can't seem to find that again - I recall trying a number of things from that list, but nothing made this magically start working. I took a look at things like the "matt trick," but I didn't quite see how that would work here. Would I just use it with the variables that have the highest posterior correlation with the intercept terms? I'm happy for any suggestions.

On Wednesday, July 6, 2016 at 2:58:44 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I don't understand the model (my fault, not saying it's bad), but
> it does look like it's coded efficiently in Stan.  It looks like
> things are converging other than b0 and b[1:8] judging from the followup
> post, just slowly.
>
> That's usually a sign of non-identifiability.  b0 shows up here:
>
> > parameters{
> >   real b0;
> ...
> > b0 ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
>
> > d1  ~ bernoulli_logit(b0 + b[1]*tms + b[2]*tms2 + b[3]*tms3 +
> >                         b[4]*cx_cor2 + b[5]*cx_cor3 +
> >                         b[6]*cx_cor + b[7]*z + b[8]*cx_corz);
>
> Even though I haven't dug into the specifics, my guess is that you're
> getting strong correlations among b0 and b[1:8].  You can use pairs()
> to try to plot (just restrict to b0 and b).
>
> What is your treedepth like?  If it's high, it means there's a lot of
> nasty curvature and Stan's having to use a very small step size.
> Usually the only way around that is reparameterization.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Jun 18, 2016, at 12:35 AM, Alex Keil <alex...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I need help with a complex model that has some parts I can't seem to optimize.
> >
> > The goal of my code: I am trying to fit multiple longitudinal (time-pooled) logistic models to estimate a discrete hazard function for two mutually exclusive, terminal events (2 causes of death). The hazard functions are then used to calculate cumulative risk of each cause. This requires 3 or 4 models, depending on the problem. I model each cause of death, as well as one primary time-varying exposure (continuous) and a secondary  time-varying exposure (binary) that is correlated with the first one.
> >
> > My data: a data set with ~ 27,000 observations, each corresponding to one person-year, along with a binary indicator of death and the two exposures. There are ~90 events of type 1 and ~500 of type 2. All told, I have about 50 parameters (12 for each event model, 16 and 20 for the two risk factor models). In my field, the events are usually modeled as a function of cumulative exposure (among other things).
> >
> > Problem 1: getting the model to converge in a timely fashion
> > Problem 2: also correcting for measurement error
> >
> > I have had a stan model running on a server for two days.The following traceplot is the output of cumulative risk after a burnin of 1000 iterations. I expected slow, but I did not expect such poor MCMC. The traceplots for other parameters look equally abysmal. For reference, the posterior mean should be around 0.08.
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > I made a simulation that captures the important parts of the model without being too complex. This includes correcting for measurement error that is assumed to be Berkson error. The above trace plot is basically this model, but without correcting for measurement error. The simulation model seems to return much better looking trace plots, but is still slow. The real example includes two additional models, neither of which can be done without looping over observations.
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > // model implied by the data generating mechanism in the simulation
> > // standardizing all independent variables
> > data{
> >   int N;
> >   int d1[N];
> >   int d2[N];
> >   vector[N] mx;
> >   vector[N] z;
> >   vector[N] tms;
> >   vector[N] id;
> > }
> > transformed data{
> >   vector[N] tms2;
> >   vector[N] tms3;
> >   tms2 <- tms .* tms;
> >   tms3 <- tms .* tms2;
> >
> > }
> > parameters{

> >   vector[8] b;
> >   real c0;
> >   vector[8] c;
> >   vector<lower=0>[N] berk_err; // multiplicative measurement error
> > }
> > model{
> >   { // local environment
> >   vector[N] cx_cor;
> >   vector[N] cx_cor2;
> >   vector[N] cx_cor3;
> >   vector[N] cx_corz;
> >   // measurement model (assumed multiplicative berkson error):
> >   //   E(log(true_exposure) | measured_exposure) = log(measured_exposure)
> >     berk_err ~ lognormal(0, log(5./4.));
> >   //increment_log_prob(-(log(berk_err)));
> >   // cumulative exposure
> >   for(i in 1:N){
> >     if(i != 1 && id[i] == id[i-1]) cx_cor[i] <- cx_cor[i-1] + mx[i]*berk_err[i];
> >     else cx_cor[i] <- mx[i]*berk_err[i];}
> >   cx_cor2 <- cx_cor .* cx_cor;
> >   cx_cor3 <- cx_cor .* cx_cor2;
> >   cx_corz <- cx_cor .* z;
> >   b0 ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
> >   b  ~ normal(0, 3);
> >   c0 ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
> >   c  ~ normal(0, 3);
> >   // discrete, cause-specific hazard models
> >   d1  ~ bernoulli_logit(b0 + b[1]*tms + b[2]*tms2 + b[3]*tms3 +
> >                         b[4]*cx_cor2 + b[5]*cx_cor3 +
> >                         b[6]*cx_cor + b[7]*z + b[8]*cx_corz);
> >
> >   d2  ~ bernoulli_logit(c0 + c[1]*tms + c[2]*tms2 + c[3]*tms3 +
> >                         c[4]*cx_cor2 + c[5]*cx_cor3 +
> >                         c[6]*cx_cor + c[7]*z + c[8]*cx_corz);}
> >   // a model for E(log(x)|z,time, past x) and a model for logit(z| past x, time) go here
> > }
> > generated quantities{
> > // calculate cumulative risk here under different exposure scenarios
> > }
> >
> > One key part of this that I am fairly certain is slowing this down is that there is a loop due to my need to model death as a function of cumulative exposure. However, even under having things mostly vectorized, the model still a) runs too slow and b) is not converging. If I could solve problem (b) I would be happy. The component models all run quickly and without errors/warnings in the `glm` function in R.
> >
> >
> > For completeness, here is code to simulate the data in R.
> >
> > dgm <- function(N, maxT){
> >   set.seed(7826)
> >   data = matrix(NA, nrow=N*maxT, ncol=9)
> >   row = 0
> >   for(id in 1:N){

> >     mcx = 0
> >     hasdied = 0

> >       logit2 = -6 + 0.035*t10 - 0.0025*t10**2 + 0.00125*t10**3 + 0.05*cx  +
> >                 0.005*cx**2 + 0.00025*cx**3 + z - 0.025*z*cx
> >       # causes of death
> >       d1 = rbinom(1, 1, 1/(1+exp(-logit1)))
> >       d2 = ifelse(d1==1, 0, rbinom(1, 1, 1/(1+exp(-logit2))))
> >       data[row, ] = c(id, tm, mcx, mx, cx, z, d1, d2, hasdied)
> >       if(d1 | d2) hasdied = 1
> >     }}
> >  ret = data.frame(data[data[,9]==0, 1:8])
> >  names(ret) <- c('id', 'tm', 'mcx', 'mx', 'cx', 'z', 'd1', 'd2')
> >  ret
> > }
> >
> > dat = dgm(1000,60)
> >
> > I know the following problems are occurring:
> >  - the need to model time 'flexibly' by including polynomial or spline terms leads to some parameter correlation in the posterior (but not too bad, see figure below for the worst example I could find in the limited runs I have - most pairwise plots gave a nice circular cloud of points).
> >  - there is likely separation in at least one of the logistic models, though R gives no warnings
> >
> >
> >
> > I have tried the following things in an effort to speed this up:
> >  - standardizing/unstandardizing all variables on the RHS of the models
> >  - vectorizing/unvectorizing the probability models when possible

>           beta[n] = normal_rng(beta0, tau);
>       }
>       return beta;
>     }
> }

On Wednesday, August 3, 2016 at 3:02:37 PM UTC-4, londo...@googlemail.com wrote:
> I'm having problems generating reproducible results from stan's random number generator.

The expose_stan_functions() function only sets the seed the first time a user-defined function ending in _rng is called. You can't change its seed afterwards within the same R session because it is declared static. This behavior is documented in the Details section of ?expose_stan_functions.

Ben

IIRC, the reason it is currently this way is so that we didn't construct an unlimited number of Boost PRNGs that can only be destroyed by quitting the R session. That and you would have to update the state of the PRNG in R in order to get different numbers between consecutive calls to the user-defined _rng function. I am not seeing why someone would want to change the seed after setting it once since setting it once ensures reproducibility.

Our advice is always to start simple and build up so you
can see where things go wrong with minimal examples, but it's
not always easy to do this.

You should get the same answers and same convergence if you
have defined the same density in two different ways.  There
may be big speed differences, though.  But it sounds like you

What you have to be careful for is variables that are not

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampling very slow after inverse transformation of response variable
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Sampling very slow after inverse transformation of response variable
messages.body_plain:
I'd recommend not waiting four days for answers.  You usually won't
need 4000 iterations with Stan for well-behaved programs.

You might want to try RStanArm if you already have a working lme4
version.

In general, you want to rescale your variables so that the
parameters are roughly unit scale (0 mean, 1 std dev) in the posterior
wherever possible (on the unconstrained scale).  You
can deconvolve everything back to the original scales afterward.
That goes for both the Y and 1/Y cases.  Very small or large values cause
the adaptation to struggle in the same way that ill-conditioned matrices
(high ratio of largest to smallest eigenvalue) cause algebraic problems
in factoring them.

You'll also have problems if you have predictors that are highly
correlated.

Also, with this:

  vector[N] Z_1_1;
  vector[N] Z_1_2;
  vector[N] Z_1_3;
  vector[N] Z_1_4;
  vector[N] Z_1_5;
  vector[N] Z_1_6;
  vector[N] Z_1_7;
  vector[N] Z_1_8;
  vector[N] Z_1_9;
  vector[N] Z_1_10;
  vector[N] Z_1_11;
  vector[N] Z_1_12;
  vector[N] Z_1_13;

you can just define

  vector[N] Z_1[13];

and same for the r variables and then you can just do usual vector/matrix
operations on them.

You might also try adding tighter priors and including priors for all
the parameters (such as b).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Problems with reproducibility/setting seed for random number generator
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Problems with reproducibility/setting seed for random number generator
messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, August 3, 2016 at 5:58:07 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I have no idea how that interacts with R

Not at all, except for memory consumed

> or what users want for reproduciblity within an R session

I can't imagine anything other than it be reproducible, which it is currently.

The OP believes it is a bug that

foo_rng(seed = 42L) != foo_rng(seed = 42L)

which is because the first call to foo_rng constructs the Boost PRNG with the static keyword and seed 42 and then updates the state of the PRNG after generating some random number. Thus, the second call to foo_rng skips constructing the Boost PRNG and does not reset the seed to 42.

If the Boost PRNG were not declared with the static keyword, then

foo_rng() == foo_rng() # default seed in both cases is 0L

because it would be constructed with seed 0 by the first call to foo_rng and destroyed and then reconstructed with seed 0 by the second call to foo_rng and redestroyed. This behavior would be atypical for R users since

rnorm(n = 1) != rnorm(n = 1)

and, if not recognized, would lead to disastrous results because all the realizations of foo_rng() would be the same. To avoid this, the user would have to pass a seed explicitly each time foo_rng was called, so that

foo_rng(seed = 0L) != foo_rng(seed = 1L)

which is also atypical for R.

An alternative would be to introduce some additional functions like

construct_PRNG(seed = 0L)
destroy_PRNG()

that the user would have to call explicitly before / after calling foo_rng(). That seemed difficult for me (to pass the reference to the PRNG to all _rng functions) and for users (who do not have to do that before / after calling functions like rnorm).

The way it works now is the way it has always worked, it is reproducible, and no one has mentioned it until today. And I don't know why anyone would want to call a _rng function multiple times with the same PRNG state within the same R session.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Help parameterizing a constrained simplex?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Help parameterizing a constrained simplex?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

The model includes both the probability that an uninfected member gets infected, and the rate at which they recover. The reason symmetry is important is that infected people in group 1 infect susceptible people in group 2 at a rate proportional to their contacts - and infected people in group 2 infect susceptible people in group 1 at a rate proportional to the contact. These two processes are constrained, because contact is symmetric. Regarding double counting, this is a continuous diffeq model, so the issue is simplified away; fractional people are infected, and the overlap is incorporated.

Keeping the sum of contacts constant primarily helps with identifiability in the bayesian approximation model. The summary statistic we care about is the R0, the average number of newly infected individuals per infected individual, in a susceptible population - and this is a function of both the contact matrix and the rate.

The data I'm actually modeling isn't included here - but, in part, it is the number of infections observed in each group the subset of patients that show up at clinics that are part of the influenza disease surveillance network. This is an output of the differential equation model, which is based on Michael Betancourt's earlier model (which doesn't contain any subgroups, so it doesn't have these problems.)

Happy to answer any further questions - especially if they help me think about modeling this generatively, instead of my current approach. (But in the mean time, I'm still hoping for a more efficient way to model the contact matrix and its constraints.)

Cheers,
David

messages.body_plain:
Yes, that's a problem.  I'd thought we'd forced symmetry
on the inverse transform.

And yes, you want an alternative parameterization in
terms of Cholesky factors and to use multi_normal_cholesky.
You can use a scaled correlation matrix Cholesky factor
or just use the covariance matrix Cholesky factory
given that you don't have a prior (we don't have a
Cholesky-parameterized Wishart).

It's much much more efficient to vectorize the multi_normal
so that the matrix only has to be factored once (which is already
going to be more efficient using the Cholesky base type).  So that'd
look like this:

  vector<lower=-0.5, upper=0.5>[2] round_err[N];

  vector[2] z[N]
  for (n in 1:N) z[n] = y[n] - round_err[n];

  z ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, L_Sigma);

When we vectorize the binary operators like -, you won't need
to loop over n in the transformed parameters.

- Bob

near singular matrices (which end up singular
numerically) even with tons of data.  Asymptotics are
slooooooooow and even a little bit of prior information
to regularize those extreme matrices can make huge
improvements.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] confused about cov matrix
messages.body_plain:
If we have a covariance matrix type, I'd think Stan should be able to ensure that it's symmetric--that's a pretty trivial condition, no?

> On Aug 5, 2016, at 4:22 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Look at the traces — covariance matrices are tricky
> and you can get weird non-identifiabilities that admit
> near singular matrices (which end up singular
> numerically) even with tons of data.  Asymptotics are
> slooooooooow and even a little bit of prior information
> to regularize those extreme matrices can make huge
> improvements.
>
> On Aug 5, 2016, at 2:15 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
>> Michael:  There's no prior on Sigma here but we have tons of data.  So 14 warnings is kind of a problem.
>>
>> Also, Bob:  Is there an intuition as to why I'm supposed to do vector[2] z[N];, rather than the more natural (to me) matrix[N,2] z;?
>>
>>> On Aug 4, 2016, at 7:40 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> We can force symmetry but you can still get lose positive-definiteness
>>> with extreme correlations.  Given that there is no prior on Sigma, this
>>> isn’t necessarily surprising.
>>>
>>> On Aug 4, 2016, at 5:55 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>
>>>> Yes, that's a problem.  I'd thought we'd forced symmetry
>>>> on the inverse transform.
>>>>
>>>> And yes, you want an alternative parameterization in
>>>> terms of Cholesky factors and to use multi_normal_cholesky.
>>>> You can use a scaled correlation matrix Cholesky factor
>>>> or just use the covariance matrix Cholesky factory
>>>> given that you don't have a prior (we don't have a
>>>> Cholesky-parameterized Wishart).
>>>>
>>>> It's much much more efficient to vectorize the multi_normal
>>>> so that the matrix only has to be factored once (which is already
>>>> going to be more efficient using the Cholesky base type).  So that'd
>>>> look like this:
>>>>
>>>> vector<lower=-0.5, upper=0.5>[2] round_err[N];
>>>>
>>>> vector[2] z[N]
>>>> for (n in 1:N) z[n] = y[n] - round_err[n];
>>>>
>>>> z ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, L_Sigma);
>>>>
>>>> When we vectorize the binary operators like -, you won't need
>>>> to loop over n in the transformed parameters.
>>>>
>>>> - Bob
>>>>
>>>>> On Aug 4, 2016, at 12:42 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>>>>
>>>>> Hi all.  I fit the following model:
>>>>>
>>>>> data {
>>>>> int N;
>>>>> matrix[N,2] y;
>>>>> }
>>>>> parameters {
>>>>> vector[2] mu;
>>>>> cov_matrix[2] Sigma;
>>>>> matrix<lower=-0.5, upper=0.5>[N,2] round_err;
>>>>> }
>>>>> transformed parameters {
>>>>> matrix[N,2] z;
>>>>> z = y - round_err;
>>>>> }
>>>>> model {
>>>>> for (n in 1:N)
>>>>> z[n,] ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);
>>>>> }
>>>>>
>>>>> It was with a dataset with N=185 data points (i.e., y was a 185 x 2 matrix).
>>>>>
>>>>> Each chain gave a message kinda like this:
>>>>>
>>>>> The following numerical problems occured the indicated number of times after warmup on chain 4
>>>>>                                                                                                 count
>>>>> Exception thrown at line 16: multi_normal_log: Covariance matrix is not symmetric. Covariance matrix    14
>>>>> Exception thrown at line 16: multi_normal_log: LDLT_Factor of covariance parameter is not positive d     2
>>>>> When a numerical problem occurs, the Hamiltonian proposal gets rejected.
>>>>> If the number in the 'count' column is small, do not ask about this message on stan-users.
>>>>>
>>>>> --
>>>>>
>>>>> I'm not sure if 14 is a small number so I decided it was ok for me to ask about this message here!  The thing that's puzzling me here is that Sigma is declared as a cov_matrix so shouldn't it automatically be symmetric and positive definite?  Or should I be using another parameterization?  This seems like a problem.

messages.subject_clean: Discrepancy between glm and stan_glm for the Gamma family
messages.body_plain:
There are at least three factors that are combining to produce this discrepancy:

(1) There aren't very many observations
(2) The parameters are pretty large
(3) The identity link

What you're seeing is the combination of 1, 2, and 3 making the default rstanarm priors that are typically weakly informative actually quite strongly informative. This wouldn't be an issue with a log link (or if the data were rescaled) because that would make the parameter estimates much smaller.

I bet if you set the prior and prior_intercept arguments to NULL (which removes the priors) or set the scale parameters of the normal priors for prior and prior_intercept to a large value then you'll see more similar results to glm.

Hope that helps,

Jonah

messages.body_plain:
This model produces divergences after warmup, produces large R-hat values (particularly for beta[6] and sigma), and therefore shows no signs of having converged or even being a workable parameterization for this data set.  Why our HMC integrator is diverging I can only guess but probably something to do with (as Ben suggests) the exponential transform and little data.  On the beta[6] <0 side of the estimates for beta[6] there's not enough data to rule out very small values so in the unconstrained space the HMC sampler goes off towards very negative numbers.  If you look at the pairs plot for mu[26] (calculated as exp(beta[6]) in my run of your script) you can see that when mu is close to zero you get divergences.

It may be a legitimate model but it needs to be reparameterized to give HMC (or almost any other sampler) a fair chance of producing samples correctly.

Krzysztof

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] confused about cov matrix
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] confused about cov matrix
messages.body_plain:
Yes, as Michael says, it's easy to make symmetric.
I'll fix the constraining transform to ensure the result
is symmetric.

But we can't make it positive definite easily without
some kind of regularization.  Which is why I'm assuming
Michael's suggesting a prior.

- Bob

> On Aug 5, 2016, at 6:07 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> If we have a covariance matrix type, I'd think Stan should be able to ensure that it's symmetric--that's a pretty trivial condition, no?
>
>> On Aug 5, 2016, at 4:22 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> Look at the traces — covariance matrices are tricky
>> and you can get weird non-identifiabilities that admit
>> near singular matrices (which end up singular
>> numerically) even with tons of data.  Asymptotics are
>> slooooooooow and even a little bit of prior information
>> to regularize those extreme matrices can make huge
>> improvements.
>>
>> On Aug 5, 2016, at 2:15 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>
>>> Michael:  There's no prior on Sigma here but we have tons of data.  So 14 warnings is kind of a problem.
>>>
>>> Also, Bob:  Is there an intuition as to why I'm supposed to do vector[2] z[N];, rather than the more natural (to me) matrix[N,2] z;?
>>>
>>>> On Aug 4, 2016, at 7:40 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>> We can force symmetry but you can still get lose positive-definiteness
>>>> with extreme correlations.  Given that there is no prior on Sigma, this
>>>> isn’t necessarily surprising.
>>>>
>>>> On Aug 4, 2016, at 5:55 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>>> Yes, that's a problem.  I'd thought we'd forced symmetry
>>>>> on the inverse transform.
>>>>>
>>>>> And yes, you want an alternative parameterization in
>>>>> terms of Cholesky factors and to use multi_normal_cholesky.
>>>>> You can use a scaled correlation matrix Cholesky factor
>>>>> or just use the covariance matrix Cholesky factory
>>>>> given that you don't have a prior (we don't have a
>>>>> Cholesky-parameterized Wishart).
>>>>>
>>>>> It's much much more efficient to vectorize the multi_normal
>>>>> so that the matrix only has to be factored once (which is already
>>>>> going to be more efficient using the Cholesky base type).  So that'd
>>>>> look like this:
>>>>>
>>>>> vector<lower=-0.5, upper=0.5>[2] round_err[N];
>>>>>
>>>>> vector[2] z[N]
>>>>> for (n in 1:N) z[n] = y[n] - round_err[n];
>>>>>
>>>>> z ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, L_Sigma);
>>>>>
>>>>> When we vectorize the binary operators like -, you won't need
>>>>> to loop over n in the transformed parameters.
>>>>>
>>>>> - Bob
>>>>>
>>>>>> On Aug 4, 2016, at 12:42 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Hi all.  I fit the following model:
>>>>>>
>>>>>> data {
>>>>>> int N;
>>>>>> matrix[N,2] y;
>>>>>> }
>>>>>> parameters {
>>>>>> vector[2] mu;
>>>>>> cov_matrix[2] Sigma;
>>>>>> matrix<lower=-0.5, upper=0.5>[N,2] round_err;
>>>>>> }
>>>>>> transformed parameters {
>>>>>> matrix[N,2] z;
>>>>>> z = y - round_err;
>>>>>> }
>>>>>> model {
>>>>>> for (n in 1:N)
>>>>>> z[n,] ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);
>>>>>> }
>>>>>>
>>>>>> It was with a dataset with N=185 data points (i.e., y was a 185 x 2 matrix).
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Each chain gave a message kinda like this:
>>>>>>
>>>>>> The following numerical problems occured the indicated number of times after warmup on chain 4
>>>>>>                                                                                                count
>>>>>> Exception thrown at line 16: multi_normal_log: Covariance matrix is not symmetric. Covariance matrix    14
>>>>>> Exception thrown at line 16: multi_normal_log: LDLT_Factor of covariance parameter is not positive d     2
>>>>>> When a numerical problem occurs, the Hamiltonian proposal gets rejected.
>>>>>> If the number in the 'count' column is small, do not ask about this message on stan-users.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> --
>>>>>>
>>>>>> I'm not sure if 14 is a small number so I decided it was ok for me to ask about this message here!  The thing that's puzzling me here is that Sigma is declared as a cov_matrix so shouldn't it automatically be symmetric and positive definite?  Or should I be using another parameterization?  This seems like a problem.
>>>>>> A

>>>>>> P.S.  The model seemed to fit just fine.

messages.body_plain:

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Wrong results in regression with log link function
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Wrong results in regression with log link function
messages.body_plain:
This is not a problem with Stan.  The problem is in the posterior.
Bayesian posterior aren't just fuzzy maximum likelihood estimates.
They weigh the prior and the likelihood.  Your likelihood and
improper flat prior are the problem, and you can see that analytically
without any software.

beta[, 6] is zero everywhere other than n in 26:30:

beta[1:25, 6] = 0
beta[31: , 6] = 0

And when beta[, 6] is equal to 1, all other predictors are 0:

beta[26:31, 1:5] = 0
beta[26:31, 6] = 1

And the relevant outcomes are within two standard deviations (sigma = 0.5)
of zero:

> y[26:30]
[1] 0.8223102 0.7249307 0.4358804 0.7082023 0.3269365

Here's where you run into trouble:  the prior on beta is improper
and you have an exp() link function.  Therefore, you get a posterior
with a very flat likelihood for beta[6] < 0.  Because your prior
is improper, those combine to put most of your probability mass
on high negative values.

Stan can't sample effectively from very nearly improper posteriors,
and it shows its inability by providing divergence diagnostics and
R-hat values clearly indicating non-convergence.

Even if you add a normal(0, 5) prior for beta, it will pull the
posterior to the point where the true values are in the 95% posterior
intervals.  But because the likelihood is relatively flat, the prior will
have a very strong effect.

- Bob

> On Aug 5, 2016, at 8:45 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> This model produces divergences after warmup, produces large R-hat values (particularly for beta[6] and sigma), and therefore shows no signs of having converged or even being a workable parameterization for this data set.  Why our HMC integrator is diverging I can only guess but probably something to do with (as Ben suggests) the exponential transform and little data.  On the beta[6] <0 side of the estimates for beta[6] there's not enough data to rule out very small values so in the unconstrained space the HMC sampler goes off towards very negative numbers.  If you look at the pairs plot for mu[26] (calculated as exp(beta[6]) in my run of your script) you can see that when mu is close to zero you get divergences.
>
> It may be a legitimate model but it needs to be reparameterized to give HMC (or almost any other sampler) a fair chance of producing samples correctly.
>
> Krzysztof
>
>
> On Friday, August 5, 2016 at 7:26:52 PM UTC-4, Wayne Zhang wrote:
> Thank you for your reply. I could use lognormal, but that is not what I am after.
>
> The current regression with a log link is a legitimate model, and I would like to know why Stan does not yield reasonable estimates. Any ideas?
>
> On Fri, Aug 5, 2016 at 4:21 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> On Friday, August 5, 2016 at 7:15:43 PM UTC-4, Wayne Zhang wrote:
> I am running a simple regression model with a log link function: y ~ normal(exp(X*beta), sigma).

>
> Ben

models.  Is there some way to use loops to cut down on
the code size?  Or to summarize what you're trying to do?

parameterizations and the non-centered approach will fit
much better.

The divergent transitions are just places where Stan has
numerical problems simulating the Hamiltonian.  The low
n_eff is more worrying.

I didn't follow the missing data question.  Stan doesn't
allow NA data from R, so it all has to be modeled.  If
it's a parameter (being estimated), then it's not data.
R-hat will be NaN in cases where all of the draws have the
exact same value.

They can't be the same likelihood if they get
different answers.  You want to go through the
loops by hand to write down the likelihoods in each
case to make sure you're coding the same model.

- Bob

We have tested the simplest version and gradually built up to the current version, which we are satisfied with.
>
> I checked the model again, but I didn't find any unbounded parameters/variables without declaring priors. In fact, the only place I changed is the data section and the indexing approach. With the central part of the model being untouched, I am really confused with the dis-convergence. So, any other thoughts?

> Thanks again.
> Lei
>
>
>

> I'm afraid the programs were too complicated for me to follow.
> Our advice is always to start simple and build up so you
> can see where things go wrong with minimal examples, but it's
> not always easy to do this.
>
> You should get the same answers and same convergence if you
> have defined the same density in two different ways.  There

Jaslene,

The immediate answer is that the Rhat and ESS codes have trouble with constants, so
you shouldn’t worry about those results.  Ultimately this is because there is a very thin
line between a parameter not moving at all (constant) and a parameter moving very,
very slowly (large autocorrelations).

Note, however, that when you have missing data trying to simulate the missing values
doesn’t actually do much.  The problem is that you can never recover the missing
information, so simulating those values doesn’t improve the fit at all.  It is much more
preferable to marginalize the missing values out of the likelihood, for example

p(d_obs | theta) = \int d(d_missing) p(d_obs, d_missing | theta),

and then fit using the marginalized likelihood.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] general questions regarding divergent transitions after warmup
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] general questions regarding divergent transitions after warmup
messages.body_plain:
I would not advise trusting the posterior.

A divergence indicates that there is some pathological neighborhood in parameter
space that Stan is not able to explore.  That neighborhood might be extremely small,
in which case you could possibly ignore it, or it might be really big, in which case
you absolutely cannot without biasing your fit significantly.

If the pathological neighborhood is small then you should be able to remove the
divergences by decreasing the step size, which is accomplished by increasing
the adapt_depth.  Hence the recommendation in RStan.

But if increasing adapt_delta doesn’t remove the divergences then you have a
large pathological region.  In particular, small increases to adapt_delta let you
explore the neighborhood a bit more, but that just lets you see more pathologies
and hence more divergences pop up.  So the fact that the divergences persist
even as you increase adapt_delta is a sign that there is something seriously
wrong.

If your model is hierarchical then you’ll definitely need the non-centered
parameterization if you’re seeing divergences.

I'd recommend upgrading to 2.11 and using our new syntax!
I'd declare mu to be the type you want rather than trying
to convert a vector to array.

This

> log1m_exp(neg_binomial_2_log_log(0,mu[n],phi)))

is just the log of 1 minus the neg binomial evaluated
at 0, which gives you truncation below at 1 inclusive.

The bigger point is that negative binomial goes above
12, but your data doesn't.  Could it have?  If not, negative
binomial is probably the wrong model here.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] how to constrain the sum of variables to stay positive
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] how to constrain the sum of variables to stay positive
messages.body_plain:
No, it'll be a while before that's implemented.

We'd never code a regression like this:

> y_vector - a_parameter * x_parameter  ~ lognormal(mu, sigma)

It's saying, modulo Jacobian, that we have

  (y_vector - a_parameter * x_parameter - log(mu)) ~ normal(0, sigma);

We'd instead want to roll a_parameter * x_parameter in with log(mu).

If we do regressions that are constrained to be positive,
we typically use a link function like log, so we deal
with an exp() inverse transform to constrain to positive.  That
does change the scales.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the suggestions. I tried rescaling by standardizing the numerical predictor variables (dividing by their standard deviation as they were already centred) and this made the sampling go a lot faster. It took almost 27 hours to run 4 chains in parallel with 1000 warm-up iterations and 3000 post-warmup iterations. However, the model did not converge, all group-level effects had Rhats larger than 1.1. Specifying tighter priors gave convergency problems as well (also when specifying a prior for all population-level effects).

I did discover an alternative that runs faster and converges perfectly. Simply multiplying the 1/Y values with a large constant (1 000 000 in my case) did the trick. This time, it took nearly 12 hours to complete and gave no convergency problems.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] general questions regarding divergent transitions after warmup
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] general questions regarding divergent transitions after warmup
messages.body_plain:
Again, the concern here is that the divergences persist even for very small step sizes,
which suggests that the pathological neighborhoods are relevant.  Note also that once
you get past adapt_delta = 0.999 or so it becomes harder and harder to get smaller
step sizes by increasing adapt_delta, so there’s not much else you can do with tuning.

Why would these pathologies be relevant even if you don’t always see divergences?
Intuitively, the number of divergences are proportional to the _boundary_ of the pathological
neighborhood, not it’s volume or probability, which determine how strongly ignoring those
neighborhoods might bias your MCMC estimators.

If you see lots of divergences then you have a pathological neighborhood with a large
boundary that suggests large volume/probability and large biases.  This is clearly bad.

If you see occasional divergences then the pathological neighborhood has a small boundary,
and this could mean two things.  First, the neighborhood could just be small and ignoring
it might be okay.  But it could also just be that the neighborhood is elongated and exposes
just a small surface to the sampler even though it has appreciable probability and could
be important for accurate estimators.

The fact that the divergences persist even for small step sizes would suggest the latter
case, which is why I would still be suspicious and continue to try to improve your model
implementation.  In particular, try to identify where in parameter space the divergences
arise to see if you can figure out what correlations might be causing them.

messages.body_plain:
> Is there a way to figure out where the divergences happen?   I only
> see displays in RStan of where the initial point is, but the diverging
> neighborhood is only indirectly related to these locations.

It’s not the initial point that is shown, but the point sampled from the
trajectory prior to proposing the new subtree with the divergence.
It’s still not exactly where the divergence occurred, but it can be closer
than the initial point.  Also, a divergence is technically a property of
the trajectory and not a single point, so it can be difficult to track back
and blame a single point even if the entire trajectory was saved.

> Can running adaptation longer help?  The reason I ask is that if step
> sizes / mass matrix is too big, it'll also cause divergences.

Yes, but it would cause constant divergences, not spurious ones.
Riemannian could help, but in general the mass matrix would have
to be especially poor to cause serious divergence problems.
