messages.body_plain:
You need to think in terms of inference for unknowns.
When you predict new y-tilde given new x-tilde, you
are using the model in its forward (generative) direction.
In order to infer the x from y, you need to invert everything
Bayesian style.  In Stan terms, this means defining a joint
distribution p(y, x, alpha, beta), which you've done if you've
given x a distribution, then you need to do inference on
x-tilde given y-tilde and alpha and beta.  To do that in Stan,
you need to declare the x-tilde as parameters unless you
can analytically figure out p(x | y, alpha, beta) [which is
sometimes possible for joint models such as Gaussian
processes].

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Unless you are trying to build in a measurement error
model, you want to replace this:

>   x_dist ~ normal(x, sigma_x);
>   y ~ normal(alpha + beta * x_dist, sigma);
>
>   // Replicate the model, so we can sample x_tilde, given y_tilde.
>   y_tilde ~ normal(alpha + beta * x_tilde, sigma);

with

parameters {
  real mu;
  ...

model {
  x ~ normal(mu, sigma_x);        // need a new parameter mu for this and a new
  x_tilde ~ normal(mu, sigma_x);  // new x's distributed same way

  y ~ normal(alpha + beta * x, sigma);                // y's given by regression
  y_tilde ~ normal(alpha + beta * x_tilde, sigma);    // new y's done same way

If you're building measurement error to x, then you need to add another
level.

In this model, I don't think x_tilde and y_tilde will affect
estimates of alpha, beta, or sigma (but x_tilde will affect
mu and sigma_x).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
If you map a -> log(mu + a * x), and mu is not a parameter (?)
then the log Jacobian you need is just

  log abs(d/d.a log(mu + a * x))

We try to follow Gelman's convention that Greek letters are parameters
and Roman letters are data, so having a data variable mu is confusing.
If in fact, you are really mapping (a, mu) -> (log(mu + a * x), mu)
where mu is a parameter, that's a different Jacobian.

- Bob

But I've noticed that users often don't know about this.  I've been told that for some reason we can't make those two lines automatic, but could we at least make them easier to do?  Maybe some option in the stan() call or something, or a function stan_fast() or something like that?  I really hate to think about all those users who are (a) recompiling their model every time, and (b) running in serial, when they could be running in parallel 4 times as fast!

A

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Problems with reproducibility/setting seed for random number generator
messages.body_plain:
> On Aug 4, 2016, at 12:44 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Wednesday, August 3, 2016 at 5:58:07 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I have no idea how that interacts with R
>
> Not at all, except for memory consumed
>
> or what users want for reproduciblity within an R session
>
> I can't imagine anything other than it be reproducible, which it is currently.

It's reproducible, but you can't reset that reproducibility within
a session.  Not sure exactly why you'd want to compute the same
thing twice, but presumably that's what they're asking.  Same reason
R lets you call set.seed() as many times as you want.

> The OP believes it is a bug that
>
> foo_rng(seed = 42L) != foo_rng(seed = 42L)
>
> which is because the first call to foo_rng constructs the Boost PRNG with the static keyword and seed 42 and then updates the state of the PRNG after generating some random number. Thus, the second call to foo_rng skips constructing the Boost PRNG and does not reset the seed to 42.

I agree with the OP here, because it sure looks like those should
return the same thing.  If the second call doesn't do anything
with the seed argument, it should alert the user by throwing an
exception or at the very least printing some kind of warning.

>
> If the Boost PRNG were not declared with the static keyword, then
>
> foo_rng() == foo_rng() # default seed in both cases is 0L
>
> because it would be constructed with seed 0 by the first call to foo_rng and destroyed and then reconstructed with seed 0 by the second call to foo_rng and redestroyed. This behavior would be atypical for R users since
>
> rnorm(n = 1) != rnorm(n = 1)
>
> and, if not recognized, would lead to disastrous results because all the realizations of foo_rng() would be the same.

I agree that would be bad news.

But presumably an R user would expect a and b to get the same value in:

> set.seed(42)
> a = rnorm(n = 1);
> set.seed(42)
> b = rnorm(n = 1);

> To avoid this, the user would have to pass a seed explicitly each time foo_rng was called, so that
>
> foo_rng(seed = 0L) != foo_rng(seed = 1L)
>
> which is also atypical for R.
>
> An alternative would be to introduce some additional functions like
>
> construct_PRNG(seed = 0L)
> destroy_PRNG()
>
> that the user would have to call explicitly before / after calling foo_rng(). That seemed difficult for me (to pass the reference to the PRNG to all _rng functions) and for users (who do not have to do that before / after calling functions like rnorm).

That would be most natural for the R users, I'd
think, with a default construction on entry.

> The way it works now is the way it has always worked, it is reproducible, and no one has mentioned it until today. And I don't know why anyone would want to call a _rng function multiple times with the same PRNG state within the same R session.

Agreed.  And no point doing work on spec without a good motivation.

- Bob

interfaces.  The declaration is just that --- a declaration

HMC is the restriction---it only handles continuous
parameters.  Systems like PyMC3 that do HMC and discrete
parameters alternate discrete sampling and HMC.

messages.subject: Re: Complex ODE based Models
messages.subject_clean: Complex ODE based Models
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the great news.

Few comments:

PBPK (physiologically based PK) models - which are extension of multi-compartmental PK models - are described both with ODE and algebraic equations or by DAE (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_algebraic_equation) in general. It might be worthwhile including this aspect.

Also, I have tried stan's ODE solver and it chokes when PBPK model is fed. There are techniques to solve ODE's in an approximate way - see orthogonal collocation "Numerical Solution of Differential Equations with Orthogonal Collocation" - but I saw some other techniques that are being used by stan users.

Linas

I have a simple three level hierarchical model to estimate variability: analytical, intra- and inter-lot.

-I wonder if there are ways to speed up the model.
-Is there any regular way to impose priors? For example it is natural to assume that analytical variability is the same for different products so once I have estimated analytical variability for product A I would like to use it as a prior for product B instead of using uninformative prior.

Thanks,
Linas

stan model is attached. It is from pharma domain but I assume similar approach could be used in any manufacturing domain.

The problem is very simple. We have bunch of tablets from different lots and we need to estimate analytical variability, intra- and inter-lot variability. Each tablet is grinded and 3 HPLC injections are run. Assuming that three HPLC injections per tablet are enough to estimate analytical variability the code tries to estimate all three variabilities. Of course I assume that analyst is the same and there is no analyst introduced variability as well as there is no standard variability.

Thanks,
Linas

If a user wants to automate that, he/she can add the following to their .Rprofile file ($HOME/.Rprofile):

setHook(packageEvent("rstan", "onLoad"), function(...) {

  rstan::rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)

  options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

})

I have no real opinion on this, but the changes are visible by the time RStan's .onAttach is run so that startup messages can be modified, perhaps to check if the options are already set and/or spit out instructions about modifying one's profile. E.g., running:

profileFile <- file.path(Sys.getenv("HOME"), ".Rprofile")

if (!file.exists(profileFile)) file.create(profileFile)

cat("\nsetHook(packageEvent(\"rstan\", \"onLoad\"), function(...) {",

    "  rstan::rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)",

    "  options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())",

    "})\n", sep = "\n", file = profileFile, append = TRUE)

On Thursday, August 11, 2016 at 2:03:44 PM UTC-4, Linas Mockus wrote:
> The problem is very simple. We have bunch of tablets from different lots and we need to estimate analytical variability, intra- and inter-lot variability. Each tablet is grinded and 3 HPLC injections are run. Assuming that three HPLC injections per tablet are enough to estimate analytical variability the code tries to estimate all three variabilities. Of course I assume that analyst is the same and there is no analyst introduced variability as well as there is no standard variability.

As soon as you say HPLC I don't think you can claim "simple" any more! :)   So it looks like your model is working with concentrations as data rather than the actual response from the HPLC.  In that case I think what you're doing is the best you can do.  Three injections is better than one but you'll still need to assume the analytical variability doesn't change to get enough data to estimate it.  If you were interested in testing that assumption my first guess at an improved model would be to model variability as changing with time as one of the issues with chromatographic instruments is that the response drifts over time (both noise and mean) which is why if you really want to trust your numbers you would run standards, sample, sample, sample, standard, sample, samples, standard, etc... and the model would work with two types of data: a) standards where both the concentration and response are known; and b) samples where only repeated measurements of response are known.  There was a model like that on the list a while back based on one of Andrew's papers but it was challenging IIRC.

Krzysztof

Ok, that worked pretty well!
I'm still a bit confused, so I'll explain my thoughts...

Now, x and x_tilde come from the same distribution N(mu, sigma_x). This is what fixed the problem.
y and y_tilde also come from a common distribution, which makes sense.

For (x, y), we are providing data for both x and y, and the "free" parameters are alpha, beta and sigma. I'm using the default uniform priors for these, so they are free to fall where they may.
However, for (x_tilde, y_tilde), we are only providing y_tilde. Since there is one less constraint (no x_tilde data), there will be minimal effect on alpha, beta and sigma.
So, alpha, beta and sigma are more influenced by (x, y) than (x_tilde, y_tilde).
And, x_tilde falls out as desired.

Is this correct?

My next step is to perform some conditional posterior predictions.
For example, if I now have two predictors, x1 and x2, and at some point I learn the true value of x1, what is the subsequent posterior of x2?
I think I can figure this out, but any tips would be appreciated.

Thanks!
Paul

messages.subject: little story of the Folk Theorem of Statistical Computing
messages.subject_clean: little story of the Folk Theorem of Statistical Computing
messages.body_plain:
A colleague and I were working on a data analysis problem, had a very simple overdispersed Poisson regression with a hierarchical, varying-intercept component.  Ran it and it was super slow and not close to converging after 2000 iterations.  Took a look and we found the problem:  The predictor matrix of our regression lacked a constant term.  The constant term comes in by default if you do glmer or rstanarm, but if you write it as X*beta in a Stan model, you have to remember to put in a column of 1's in the X matrix (or to add a "mu" to the regression model), and we'd forgotten to do that.

Once we added in that const term, the model (a) ran much faster (cos adaptation was smoother) and (b) converged just fine after just 100 iterations.

Yet another instance of the folk theorem.

A

messages.subject_clean: Re[2]: [stan-users] Re: Complex ODE based Models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Linas!

Have you tried the recent "bdf" integrator in Stan? That uses CVODES which is a very robust integrator specifically tailored for large ODE systems.

If you have a large ODE system and only want to estimate a few parameters, then make sure that all parameters which are held fixed are passed into the integrate function via the x_r argument. This is really important to keep things manageable.

Also: Do you have the Jacobians of your ODE RHS function available? If not consider using a package like dMod (on CRAN). Using dMod you will be able to generate automatically the Jacobian of the ODE RHS wrt to the parameters and the states. Once you have those, it is possible to supply these to Stan - if you are willing to put together a bit of C++. This is completely unsupported and an experimental use of Stan, but it can give massive speedups - I have done this approach myself and got about 3x speedup for a small 3 state system; for these large systems I expect even larger speedups. However, this all depends on getting the Jacobians right for which a tool like dMod is the only feasible way of doing it, I think. In case you want to try this approach I can share an example of a 2-cmt oral dosing situation where I use dMod to generate the code I needed.

Sebastian

Thanks.  We should definitely make those consistent.

As Michael just wrote to our users list, it's tricky because we
only plot one point and it's the entire trajectory that diverges.
The divergence in question is when the Hamiltonian, which is supposed
to remain constant, gets far away from its initial value during
leapfrog integration (due to numerical issues of not having a small
enough step size and the gradient with small step sizes not being
very good in highly curved volumes of the posterior).

from Michael Betancourt:

> It’s not the initial point that is shown, but the point sampled from the
> trajectory prior to proposing the new subtree with the divergence.
> It’s still not exactly where the divergence occurred, but it can be closer
> than the initial point.  Also, a divergence is technically a property of
> the trajectory and not a single point, so it can be difficult to track back
> and blame a single point even if the entire trajectory was saved.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Sample independent variable given dependent variable values
messages.body_plain:
> On Aug 12, 2016, at 12:15 AM, Paul <pwmor...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Ok, that worked pretty well!

Glad to hear it.

> I'm still a bit confused, so I'll explain my thoughts...

This stuff's all very confusing the first time around until you
get the hang of thinking in terms of the marginal distributions
of the things you're interested in and can work all the algebra
out in your head (I'm still counting on my fingers;  Michael
and Andrew do this stuff at the snap of a finger).

>
> Now, x and x_tilde come from the same distribution N(mu, sigma_x). This is what fixed the problem.

Not just that.  It's that

> y and y_tilde also come from a common distribution, which makes sense.

They come from a common distribution only conditioned on alpha, beta,
sigma and x and x_tilde.

> For (x, y), we are providing data for both x and y, and the "free" parameters are alpha, beta and sigma. I'm using the default uniform priors for these, so they are free to fall where they may.

That's not the right way to think about it.  The right
way to think about uniform priors is that they put a ton of
probability mass out in the tails --- they're not uniform in
the way most people think.  That is, they put a million times
more weight on a value being between 1 million and 2 million
than they put on the value being between 0 and 1.  Andrew's
written extensively on this [see the manual for citations to papers,
or check out BDA].  This is why we don't even like those hacked
"flat(tish)" priors from BUGS, such as gamma(0.001, 0.001)
or normal(0, 1000).  We almost always have some notion of the
scale of the results before we start.

> However, for (x_tilde, y_tilde), we are only providing y_tilde. Since there is one less constraint (no x_tilde data), there will be minimal effect on alpha, beta and sigma.

The reason is just that if you look at the posterior

  p(alpha, beta, sigma | y, x)

without x_tilde involved at all, and compare it to the marginal
posterior

  p(alpha, beta, sigma | y, x, x_tilde)

you get from

  p(alpha, beta, sigma, y_tilde | y, x, x_tilde)

then they are the same.  Warning:  this isn't the case for
every "missing data" model (though that term is vague, so you
have to be careful with definitions).

> So, alpha, beta and sigma are more influenced by (x, y) than (x_tilde, y_tilde).
> And, x_tilde falls out as desired.
>
> Is this correct?
>
> My next step is to perform some conditional posterior predictions.
> For example, if I now have two predictors, x1 and x2, and at some point I learn the true value of x1, what is the subsequent posterior of x2?
> I think I can figure this out, but any tips would be appreciated.

You just need to fix x1, then you can do inference on x2.  In general,
in Bayesian models, you set up a joint distribution and you can
then do inference on whichever variables you want given observations
of the others.

The manual chapter on missing data is what you want to look at for
how to code this up in Stan.  It's easier in BUGS/JAGS as they just
let you pass in the equivalent of R's NA wherever you want and figure
out all the coding internally (the benefit of restricting your attention
to acyclic directed graphical models).

- Bob

messages.subject: Let's add a mixture distribution to Stan
messages.subject_clean: Let's add a mixture distribution to Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  What with all this discussion of the mixture model and whether or not it involves "contrivances," I was thinking we should revive the idea of including a generic mixture distribution in the Stan language.  Something like this:

y ~ normal_mixture(lambda, mu, sigma);
which would be shorthand for the mixture of normal distributions with lambda being an array of weights, mu being an array of means, and tau being an array of sigmas

Or maybe this:  y ~ mixture(lambda, normal, mu, sigma); and, more generally, y ~ mixture(lambda, distribution_name, argument_1, argument_2, . . .);

Bob and I discussed this a few years ago and, as I recall, he had some other ideas for the syntax too.  It depends how general one wants it to be.  But we could always start with normal_mixture and multi_normal_mixture, which would cover most of the uses, I think.

Anyway, my suggestion is that, given the popularity of mixture models, it could be useful to have such a syntax directly in Stan so that users don't have to do the log_prob_sum think by hand.

A

--

In terms of speed, rather than:

	for (i in 1 : N) {
		mu [i] <- MU + sigma_intra * ii [lot_samples [i]] + sigma_inter * iii [lots [i]];
		log_lik [i] <- normal_log (injections [i], mu [i], sigma);
	}
  ...
  increment_log_prob (sum (log_lik));

you can just drop the transformed parameters block altogether and use

  injections ~ normal(MU + sigma_intra * ii[lot_samples] + sigma_inter * iii[lots],
                      sigma);

You'll have to redefine ii and iii as vector[N_LOTS] and vector[N_LOT_SAMPLES]
respectively to allow the vector algebra.

We've also updated the syntax with Stan 2.9, so it's

   target += foo;

rather than

   increment_log_prob(foo)

and = instead of <- in assignments.  We still support the old syntax,
but you'll get deprecation warnings.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Let's add a mixture distribution to Stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Let's add a mixture distribution to Stan
messages.body_plain:
What Rob actually implemented was this:

  target += log_mix(lambda, normal_lpdf(y | mu[1], sigma[1]),
                            normal_lpdf(y | mu[2], sigma[2]));

Works for arbitrary binary mixtures with lambda in (0, 1)
and any densities on the log scale.  It lets you, for instance,
use the same sigma in each case without having to artificially
create vectors of repeated values.

We could try some fancier things that get unfolded in
code.  The problems with log_mix are that

  * it only works for binary mixtures (we'd need log_mix(simplex, vector),
    but we never got around to that one)

  * no vectorization (this is tricky because we don't have the probability
    functions that return vectors yet, as Aki has been asking for for Loo
    and xvalidation).

  * no logit-scale mixture proportion (not sure this is important, but
    it has come up)

I could pretty easily build the syntaxes you suggest below (as in a week
of coding and testing time given everything else I do), but those haven't
been a high priority compared to the gazillion other things I have to do
to the language, like adding ragged arrays (big project I want to do next
after taking care of a bunch of little bugs).

If we support y ~ mixture(...), then we probably also want
mixture(y | ...) for flexiblity and consistency.  And we probably want the
usual kind of vectorization in case some parameters are shared.

The hurdle to implementing this and why I'll probably have to do it is
that it's not a usual function in that it works on other function names.
It'll have to go into the parser directly (at least until I figure out
higher-order functions, an even bigger project).

We could write it as a Stan function, though that wouldn't give
us the analytical derivatives that would speed it up (neither would
the mixture(...) form).

So like everything else, it's easy to look at one case and think it's
sufficient, but when you dig a little deeper, what everyone wants is
much more complex.  Not impossible, just a week long project rather than
one I could knock off in an afternoon.

- Bob

The good part that not all parameters are of interest. The characteristics of organ, tissues and drug are described by physiological and compound-specific parameters. Physiological Parameters include arterial and venous blood flows, tissue volumes, tissue blood flow rates and tissue composition (lipid, phospholipids, and water).
Compound-specific Parameters include physicochemical properties (e.g. logP, pKa, dissolution rate) and biochemical/ biophysical properties (e.g. Vmax, Km, and permeability, fraction unbound in plasma or tissues, blood to plasma ratio). PK-derived Parameters are computed by combining compound-specific and physiological parameters, such as tissue-to-plasma partition coefficients (Kpu) estimated from logP, pKa and tissue composition and intrinsic clearance (CLint) derived from Vmax, Km and amount of liver microsomal protein. We are interested in PK parameters which may be estimated even from scarce data.

I will try to conquer my model using the outlined procedure. Hopefully I will be able to cite stan... Just for the heck of it the model is attached. Originally it was in C++ and was automatically translated directly to stan so there are lots of formatting issues.

The posterior mean is printed by the VarCorr() function, which is called by the print method. The draws of that standard deviation are not stored. You can pretty much recreate its posterior distribution by taking the standard deviation of that parameter across groups at each iteration. Something like

mat <- as.matrix(post)
b <- mat[,grepl("^b\\[")]
summary(apply(b, MARGIN = 1, sd))

messages.body_plain:
On Friday, August 12, 2016 at 10:30:35 AM UTC-4, Linas Mockus wrote:
> Should I use a more complicated model for measurement error of peak area than just normal? What about the model between concentration and peak area? Should it be linear or some other shape?

I'd start with normal and go from there---it's going to be instrument dependent (in the case
of HPLC it'll be detector-dependent). Peak area is going to (usually) be positive so log-normal
would be a fine choice.

tl;dr: logistic curve, maybe linear for qc

Long version: Most analytical instruments produce a low signal whether the analyte is
present or not but there's typically a baseline subtraction resulting in an
arbitrary quantity measured with noise when the analyte is below a minimum
detectable level.  Since you are dealing with peak area rather than signal itself
this gets subtracted out so zero means the quantitiy is less than the minimum
detectable level (assuming the pre-processing is working well).
Then there's typically a non-linear region with increasing slope, a linear region
which is where people usually expect the instrument to be reliable for quanitfying
the analyte.  Really if you do a decent job of modeling the shape of this
curve and the uncertainty it's fine to use the non-linear region too, you'll just see
the measurement uncertainty go up as you near zero.  Finally at really
high concentrations the detector can get saturated and the response
is nonlinear again but with a decreasing slope.  With HPLC when the analyst
sees that a sample is saturating the detector (or just when they know the
concentration is high before running it) they will just dilute the sample and scale
afterwards so you may never see this issue in reported data.  If you're lucky a logistic
curve would follow this curve fine but I'm not sure if it would do a decent job
in the non-linear regions.

In a qc situation like yours hopefully all the measurements will be right in the
middle of the linear range of the instrument (since they should know concentrations
ahead of time) and you can just use a linear relationship.

Krzysztof

>
> Linas

messages.body_plain:
Because MCMC works only when all chains are exploring the same neighborhoods.  If any are exceptional chains then there are subtle pathologies in the interaction of the Markov transition and target distribution that affect the Markov transition itself and hence all of the chains.  This is why running multiple chains is so useful.

Yeah, I'm struggling a little. I've read John Kruschke's book, which was a great introduction, but I probably need to look further. Do you recommend BDA as the next step?

>

> > Now, x and x_tilde come from the same distribution N(mu, sigma_x). This is what fixed the problem.

> way to think about uniform priors is that they put a ton of
> probability mass out in the tails --- they're not uniform in

> more weight on a value being between 1 million and 2 million
> than they put on the value being between 0 and 1.  Andrew's
> written extensively on this [see the manual for citations to papers,

That makes sense. Is a uniform prior considered appropriate when it's given bounds?

I'm thinking of my x and x_tilde distributions, which are currently normally distributed. The x and x_tilde data I'm creating is randomly distributed over the range [-5, 5], so a normal distribution doesn't seem appropriate. Should I specify a uniform distribution with these bounds?

>
> without x_tilde involved at all, and compare it to the marginal
> posterior
>

>
> you get from
>

>
> then they are the same.  Warning:  this isn't the case for
> every "missing data" model (though that term is vague, so you

> On Aug 13, 2016, at 6:45 AM, Paul <pwmor...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
>
> This stuff's all very confusing the first time around until you
> get the hang of thinking in terms of the marginal distributions
> of the things you're interested in and can work all the algebra
> out in your head (I'm still counting on my fingers;  Michael
> and Andrew do this stuff at the snap of a finger).
>
> Yeah, I'm struggling a little. I've read John Kruschke's book,
> which was a great introduction, but I probably need to look further.
> Do you recommend BDA as the next step?

I would recommend Gelman and Hill's regression book as the
next step.  I found it very hard to jump into BDA myself because
it presupposes you have a very good grasp of math stats before
you start.  But once you're ready to read it, it's awesome.
Peter Hoff's book is nice, too, if you're comfortable with calc
and linear algebra, but not with math stats.

> >
> > Now, x and x_tilde come from the same distribution N(mu, sigma_x). This is what fixed the problem.
>
> Not just that.  It's that
>
> > y and y_tilde also come from a common distribution, which makes sense.
>
> They come from a common distribution only conditioned on alpha, beta,
> sigma and x and x_tilde.
>
> > For (x, y), we are providing data for both x and y, and the "free" parameters are alpha, beta and sigma. I'm using the default uniform priors for these, so they are free to fall where they may.
>
> That's not the right way to think about it.  The right
> way to think about uniform priors is that they put a ton of
> probability mass out in the tails --- they're not uniform in
> the way most people think.  That is, they put a million times
> more weight on a value being between 1 million and 2 million
> than they put on the value being between 0 and 1.  Andrew's
> written extensively on this [see the manual for citations to papers,
> or check out BDA].  This is why we don't even like those hacked
> "flat(tish)" priors from BUGS, such as gamma(0.001, 0.001)
> or normal(0, 1000).  We almost always have some notion of the
> scale of the results before we start.
>
> That makes sense. Is a uniform prior considered appropriate when it's given bounds?

We have recommendations on our wiki for priors

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations

and also in the manual regression chapter.  In particular, we do *not*
recommend hard upper and lower bounds other than for parameters
that are physically constrained (like for bernoulli or binomial
parameters which must be in (0, 1), or scale parameters which
must be in (0, inf)).

> I'm thinking of my x and x_tilde distributions, which are currently normally distributed. The x and x_tilde data I'm creating is randomly distributed over the range [-5, 5], so a normal distribution doesn't seem appropriate. Should I specify a uniform distribution with these bounds?

This is a case where it would be appropriate because it's the
true model.  But you probalby just want to simulate with normal(0, 2)
or something rather than uniform(-5, 5).

> > However, for (x_tilde, y_tilde), we are only providing y_tilde. Since there is one less constraint (no x_tilde data), there will be minimal effect on alpha, beta and sigma.
>
> The reason is just that if you look at the posterior
>
>   p(alpha, beta, sigma | y, x)
>
> without x_tilde involved at all, and compare it to the marginal
> posterior
>
>   p(alpha, beta, sigma | y, x, x_tilde)
>
> you get from
>
>   p(alpha, beta, sigma, y_tilde | y, x, x_tilde)
>
> then they are the same.  Warning:  this isn't the case for
> every "missing data" model (though that term is vague, so you
> have to be careful with definitions).
>
> Ok, I'll need to think about this.

This is the kind of thing that BDA assumes you're going to
be comfortable doing.

> > So, alpha, beta and sigma are more influenced by (x, y) than (x_tilde, y_tilde).
> > And, x_tilde falls out as desired.
> >
> > Is this correct?
> >
> > My next step is to perform some conditional posterior predictions.
> > For example, if I now have two predictors, x1 and x2, and at some point I learn the true value of x1, what is the subsequent posterior of x2?
> > I think I can figure this out, but any tips would be appreciated.
>
> You just need to fix x1, then you can do inference on x2.  In general,
> in Bayesian models, you set up a joint distribution and you can
> then do inference on whichever variables you want given observations
> of the others.
>
> That worked ok, when I fix x1_tilde.
>
> If I don't fix x1_tilde (both x1_tilde and x2_tilde are parameters), I'm not sure what to expect.
> Will I get the joint distribution of x1_tilde and x2_tilde, given y_tilde (and the other parameters)?

Exactly.  That's always what you get given a joint distribution.

> Then, the modes of the x1_tilde and x2_tilde posterior marginals would indicate the values most likely to have generated the given y_tilde?

"Most likely" is not a Bayesian concept because it has zero measure
(no probability mass).  The marginal posterior means give you the
Bayesian point estimate that minimizes expected square error.  The
posterior mode doesn't have an interpretation in and of itself because
it depends on parameterization.  I wrote a case study for this:

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/mle-params.html

- Bob

I'm afraid we don't have better examples of usage of the C++ library.
We're in the middle of refactoring all this code, so the way
optimization is accessed in the C++ API will change very soon
to become much easier to use on the outside.

The classes we use assume that you have a Stan model instance,
but that's also not well documented---it's defined as a C++
concept, so there's not an object-oriented base class anywhere.
This may also get refactored soon.  So far, we haven't been too
concerned about API stability in stan-dev/stan.  We expect
stan-dev/math to be stable at this point, and we expect the
stan-dev/stan algorithms to become much more stable in a few
months after a couple more refactors (change the C++ API, but
they won't change the external behavior of any of the Stan
interfaces---that's coming in Stan 3 after the refactor, but at
that point, the API will be stable).

Like most projects, it took us three tries or so to figure out
what we really needed at the API level.

- Bob

First, we tend to think like Bayesians and treat X as a random variable
all the time.  The question I think you have is whether it's measured
with noise or not.  You can check out the manual chapter on measurement
error models.

You might want to check out our manual chapter on priors, too.  You
won't need that lower=0.001 business in Stan and we don't recommend
hard upper-bound constraints on positive-constrained parameters as they
don't do what people expect them to do.  I need to get a case study on
this written because I'm writing it too frequently in the mailing list
(second time in the last ten messages or so), because people copy
the practices of BUGS.

I don't quite understand what you're asking w.r.t. kernel density
estimation, but maybe somebody else will.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
It works in Stan even with MCMC, it's just slow.

Here's the model for a single hidden layer neural
network that I came up with;  it includes the evaluation
on held-out data.  As you can see, the model's very
simple.

- Bob

functions {

  /**
   * Return the application of tanh() elementwise to the specified
   * matrix.  // FIXME(carpenter): remove when tanh vectorized
   *
   * @param u Input matrix.
   * @return
   */
  matrix tanh_eltwise(matrix u) {
    matrix[rows(u), cols(u)] tanh_u;
    for (j in 1:cols(u))
      for (i in 1:rows(u))
        tanh_u[i, j] = tanh(u[i, j]);
    return tanh_u;
  }

  /**
   * Returns linear predictor for restricted Boltzman machine (RBM).
   * Assumes one-hidden layer with logistic sigmoid activation.
   *
   * @param x Predictors (N x M)
   * @param alpha First-layer weights (M x J)
   * @param beta Second-layer weights (J x (K - 1))
   * @return Linear predictor for output layer of RBM.
   */
  matrix rbm(matrix x, matrix alpha, matrix beta) {
    return tanh_eltwise(x * alpha) * beta;
  }

}
data {
  int<lower=0> N;               // num train instances
  int<lower=0> M;               // num train predictors
  matrix[N, M] x;               // train predictors
  int<lower=2> K;               // num categories
  int<lower=1, upper=K> y[N];   // train category

  int<lower=1> J;               // num hidden units

  int<lower=0> Nt;              // num test instances
  matrix[Nt, M] xt;             // test predictors
  int<lower=1, upper=K> yt[N];  // test category
}
parameters {
  matrix[M, J] alpha;
  matrix[J, K] beta;
}
model {
  matrix[K, N] v;

  // priors
  to_vector(alpha) ~ normal(0, 2);
  to_vector(beta) ~ normal(0, 2);

  // likelihood
  v = rbm(x, alpha, beta)';
  for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ categorical_logit(col(v, n));
}
generated quantities {
  int<lower=1, upper=K> yt_sim[Nt];  // test observations
  real log_p_yt;
  real accuracy;
  matrix[K, Nt] v;
  v = rbm(xt, alpha, beta)';
  log_p_yt = 0;
  accuracy = 0;
  for (n in 1:Nt) {
    vector[K] theta;
    theta = softmax(col(v, n));
    log_p_yt = log_p_yt + categorical_lpmf(yt_sim | theta);
    yt_sim[n] = categorical_rng(theta);
    if (yt_sim[n] == yt[n])
      accuracy = accuracy + 1;
  }
  accuracy = accuracy / Nt;
}

messages.body_plain:
I'm definitely interested in this effort.  I've used MCSim in the past, mostly for system dynamics <http://www.systemdynamics.org/what-is-s/> models of the sort one might create with Vensim <http://www.vensim.com/>.  Perhaps the key special feature that requires is so-called tabular nonlinearities.  In MCSim, I'd use the GSL (not available here, I know) to interpolate between points.  You can see an example at https://www.gnu.org/software/mcsim/mcsimqrc.pdf.  Often, these models are simply used to generate simulation output, but they are also used to estimate parameters.  It would be nice to be able to do such modeling easily in Stan.

Not long ago, I got called upon to do some hydrological modeling, and I came across conceptual hydrological models (PBPK for rivers?).  One important challenge is defining initial conditions--in this case, often moisture content in the layers of soil.  Those are, in general, unknown, but it's really handy to know boundary conditions when solving a system of ODEs. :-)  The way I think they get around this is through optimization--varying, for example, the initial soil moisture content until they get an output that matches real data.  Conceptually, that's easy to think of for a stream that runs dry in the summer: after some number of days with no precipitation and no flow, there is also probably no stored water, at least in the upper soil layers.  I'm obviously no expert here, but it would be nice to be able to handle such models, as well.

There are apparently other problems with conceptual hydrological models involving accuracy.  Some authors point out that it's low, partially because a river is a complex distributed system, and partially because they're often trying to calibrate a model with lots (for them--perhaps 50 or so) parameters with little real data--mostly precipitation, temperature, and river flow measured on a daily basis, but those are hard things to measure over a distributed area in the wild.

Bill

On Fri, Aug 12, 2016 at 5:30 AM, Linas Mockus <linasm...@gmail.com> wrote:

> The good part that not all parameters are of interest. The characteristics of organ, tissues and drug are described by physiological and compound-specific parameters. Physiological Parameters include arterial and venous blood flows, tissue volumes, tissue blood flow rates and tissue composition (lipid, phospholipids, and water).
> Compound-specific Parameters include physicochemical properties (e.g. logP, pKa, dissolution rate) and biochemical/ biophysical properties (e.g. Vmax, Km, and permeability, fraction unbound in plasma or tissues, blood to plasma ratio). PK-derived Parameters are computed by combining compound-specific and physiological parameters, such as tissue-to-plasma partition coefficients (Kpu) estimated from logP, pKa and tissue composition and intrinsic clearance (CLint) derived from Vmax, Km and amount of liver microsomal protein. We are interested in PK parameters which may be estimated even from scarce data.

Bob,

That nonlinearity isn't used as a spline basis function.  In an ODE, the derivative is some function of the state of the system and any inputs, right?  The behavior of the system gets interesting, if that relationship between a state variable and a derivative is nonlinear.  A physicist might use a quadratic or some other analytic function to describe that relationship, while a system dynamicist would draw a function and then digitize key (x,y) points for the system to interpolate (I often have used Stineman interpolation).  You're at Columbia, right?  Check out a copy of Sterman's /Business Dynamics/; there's a whole chapter on nonlinearities.

Does that help?

As for the SIR model, you can find a chapter on the SIR model and its variants in Sterman, used there to model diseases, the diffusion of ideas, and the like.

Do you have any pointers to using Stan with unknown initial conditions?  That's what I was trying to get out in https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/ode$20initial$20conditions%7Csort:relevance/stan-users/mPIxQvGFZBM/46fRB2AmBQAJ, and I came away with the impression that it couldn't be done.

If you look at the feature/issue-1751-service-methods branch there are some pretty complete tests for the upcoming interfaces.
That's the branch with the upcoming refactor.  I've spent a little time adding tests for the sampling functions so I can vouch
for the tests there being straightforward to follow (at least for me after working on Stan for a while).  Happy to answer specific
questions here if you get stuck.

If you are writing C++ code rather than expecting an interface (rstan) to work you could just take that branch and follow the
tests in src/test/stan/services/optimize/*_test.cpp  to see how to run the optimizer with a model.  If you want a skeleton for what
the "model" object needs to look like you can take a simple Stan model and compile it to a .hpp file to see the methods you
need to implement.  Ultimately you  would just be replacing the lob_prob calculation with your own and then it's all just
arranging the plumbing with the var_context for data.

Krzysztof

Stan is a generic tool for Bayesian inference and maximum
likelihood estimation for custom, parametric statistical
models (or non-parametrics like Gaussian processes).
For more info and comparisons to other similar systems,
see:

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/stan-paper-revision-feb2015.pdf

Or you can check out our manual to get a feel for the kind of
problems Stan solves.

If you want to do deep belief nets, as discussed in the link,
you're better off with other systems such as Google's TensorFlow.

- Bob

Bob,

Directly to your question about the model: there are no "inputs" to this model, at least in the MCSim sense.  sir.model defines the dynamics of the system: states, outputs (to expose them), and initial values of parameters and states. It then defines the dynamics, akin to the ODE function call, and it defines calculated outputs, akin to generate quantities in Stan.  The system starts in an initial state that's not in equilibrium, and it progresses towards equilibrium.

sir.test01.in <http://sir.test01.in> should be obvious except perhaps for two aspects.  Each Simulation{} section defines a new run of the model, and each PrintStep defines when it will produce output (variable name plus the arguments to something like R's seq()).  (There's also a Print statement that lets you define specific times.)

Bill

Thanks for the pointers.  I still don't get why you're using
splines, but I'm not very fluent in any of these examples or
in non-parametric methods, so I'm sure that's my fault.

ll try to find the time to check out Sterman's book and
maybe create my own example of a SIR model (I wouldn't
have expected a SIR model in a book with "business" in
the title, though if I had to guess, it'd be for product
introduction and dissemination applications).

There's an example where the initial conditions are a mixture
that's unknown in this case study on soil-carbon compartment
models:

  http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/soil-knit.html

Here's the relevant part of the code:

    C_t0[1] <- gamma * totalC_t0;
    C_t0[2] <- (1 - gamma) * totalC_t0;

    ...

    C_hat <- integrate_ode(two_pool_feedback,
                           C_t0, t0, ts, theta, x_r, x_i);

In this case, gamma is a parameter and totalC_t0 is known,
so it makes the initial conditions C_t0 parameters and hence
unknown.  Anyway, Stan supports any combination of known and
unknown parameters and initial conditions.  We don't support
unknown initial times (yet, though we've gotten requests).

- Bob

> That nonlinearity isn't used as a spline basis function.  In an ODE, the derivative is some function of the state of the system and any inputs, right? >
> Does that help?
>

> >
> > Not long ago, I got called upon to do some hydrological modeling, and I came across conceptual hydrological models (PBPK for rivers?). I actually don't know that chains will affect each other in Stan. And I am not sure how it works. Is the actual algorithm explained in Stan reference book or something else?

As for the problem I am having now, shall I simply run one chain at a time so that a bad chain would not affect the others, and then repeatedly run a few dozens of chains and select the best one?

Thanks,
Jingjing

2016-08-12 16:21 GMT-04:00 Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu>:

> Stan is, umm, kinda sampling through neighborhoods that are, y'know, adaptive.

> > On Aug 12, 2016, at 1:36 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >

> > Because MCMC works only when all chains are exploring the same neighborhoods.  If any are exceptional chains then there are subtle pathologies in the interaction of the Markov transition and target distribution that affect the Markov transition itself and hence all of the chains.  This is why running multiple chains is so useful.
> >
> > On Aug 12, 2016, at 10:31, Jingjing Chen <chen...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >

> > > Why should I suspect the other chains when one of them is misbehaving? I thought that the chains don't affect each other in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. Is that true?
> > >
> > > 在 2016年8月12日星期五 UTC-4下午1:23:18，Michael Betancourt写道：
> > > > Never ever ever do this.  If even one chain is misbehaving then it indicates that all of the chains are biased and should be suspect.  I'd also be surprised if all of our other diagnostics are not going crazy.
> > > >
> > > > On Aug 12, 2016, at 07:38, Jingjing Chen <chen...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > >

Bob,

Look at the example on p. 2 of the two-pager I linked to.  Pretend "Balance" is what you have in a savings account, and "desiredOutflow" is what you intend to spend a month on, say food at restaurants.  You add nothing to that Balance ever.

The model as show continuously draws 100 per unit time from that balance, but that can't go on forever; the bank will shut it off at 0.  In order to approach 0 smoothly, as you might do in practice, we have an "EffectOfLowBalance" that is 1 when the balance is high (so it doesn't affect desiredOutflow), and it declines smoothly to a constant fraction of Balance when Balance gets low.  That is, at high Balance, outflow is constant; at low Balance, outflow is a constant times the remaining Balance.  The transition is smooth, thanks to the GSL interpolation.

Yes, that's a spline.  No, that's not a basis function AFAICT.  It's part of the likelihood, if you will, if I were only doing estimation, but I'm doing forward simulation.

Does that help?

Bill

messages.subject: Gaussian predictive process models for large-ish data
messages.subject_clean: Gaussian predictive process models for large-ish data
messages.body_plain:
First, big thanks to the stan-dev team for creating and continuing to improve Stan.

In trying to fit some spatial Gaussian process models with hundreds/thousands of spatial locations, I was running into prohibitively long run times, and ran across Gaussian predictive process models as described in the following:

Finley, Andrew O., et al. 2009. "Improving the performance of predictive process modeling for large datasets." (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2743161/)

Banerjee, Sudipto, et al. 2008. "Gaussian predictive process models for large spatial data sets." (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2741335/)

For certain spatial models, these reduced rank predictive process models should scale much better to large n datasets. In case this is useful for others running into similar problems with spatial models or other Gaussian process models, here's a little write up: http://mbjoseph.github.io/2016/08/14/gpp.html, and here's the source code for a speed test experiment testing run times and efficiency between the full and reduced rank GP models: https://github.com/mbjoseph/gpp-speed-test. For an example of this approach in action, also see the following paper from Cameron Bracken that uses a reduced rank GP representation to model spatial dependence in the parameters of the generalized extreme value distribution with over 2000 point locations: http://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.08560

Looking forward, many approaches for modeling large spatial data that have emerged in recent years rely heavily on sparse covariance matrix representations. When more sparse matrix functionality (particularly Cholesky decomposition) is added to Stan, that will be exciting for spatial applications.

messages.subject: Very large, sparse covariance matrix in multilevel GP
messages.subject_clean: Very large, sparse covariance matrix in multilevel GP
messages.body_plain:
Hi all -

Let's say I have a data generating process for some observation i in group j:

y(i, j) ~ GP(mean process (X(i, j)), covariance function(X(i, j) | group level parameters (j) ) )

where group level parameters in the covariance function come from some hyperdistribution.
This parameter distribution _is_ the research question. Each group has a different number of
observations.

I'm currently implementing this by building up each group's covariance matrix with its own
group-level parameters, and then using a very large block-diagonal covariance matrix to store
all the group-specific covariance matrices. I am doing this in the transformed parameters block.

My estimation model is then

y ~ GP(mean process, enormous block-diagonal covariance matrix)

This works well for a small number of groups (10), but obviously doesn't scale well to the full
dataset.

In the full dataset, there are 65 groups with group sizes of around 15, so the resulting large
covariance matrix would be around 99% 0 entries. I'm not using any sparse structures.

How should I go about using the sparse data structures to help with the scaling? In particular, given
I'm generating the giant covariance matrix in the transformed parameters, is there a way to
call `csr_extract_v` and `csr_extract_u` in that block, so I can reassemble the dense covariance
matrix in the model block? Or should I be constructing the enormous matrix as a local variable
(to my mind, this will be very slow, it being evaluated every leapfrog step)? Or something else?

Thoughts?

Jim

messages.body_plain:
You are misunderstanding the problem here.  The chains do not interact
and hence do not affect each other.  Rather the fundamental issue is that
a Markov transition will yield a good Markov chain with respect to a given
target distribution only when _all chains achieve the same behavior
independently of each other_.  If any chain behaves differently than the
others then there is some pathological neighborhood of parameter space
that the other chains just haven’t encountered yet.

messages.body_plain:
> On Aug 15, 2016, at 5:01 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> B
> I'm not sure.  I'd been thinking simplex, vector, vector, but I wonder if maybe simplex, array, array would be more logical.  I say this because if we want
> multi_normal_mixture, it would make sense to be multi_normal_mixture(vector | simplex, array of vectors, array of matrices).  So there's a certain logic to use arrays of length K for any variables that are repeated in the K-component mixture.
> Or am I overthinking this?

Not at all.  We'll get you thinking like a programmer in no time.
It's all about the generalizations and edge cases.

I think we should use arrays (of real or vector)
for things that aren't going to be used as vectors (matrices)
and vectors/matrices for things that are.

Of course, this confuses our users, hence our allowing both
alternatives in lots of cases (as in vectorized densities).

> I do think that having a normal_mixture and multi_normal_mixture will alleviate many users' concerns about the apparent complexity of the Stan code for mixtures.

That will cover some cases.  But as an example, the model leading
to this discussion was a beta mixture for priors on a Bernoulli
parameter (not saying it's a good idea, just that it was in
Kruschke's book).

> To us, the use of "target +=" is super-clean, but I can see that for users who are familiar with Bugs, "target +=" can look like a hack.

What is a hack and what is natural is in the eye of the beholder.
On the other hand, I don't know how anyone could call

  target += u;

a hack compared to the BUGS/JAGS zeros trick:

  0 ~ dpois(u);

- Bob

messages.subject: When does it aid performance to put computations in the transformed parameters section?
messages.subject_clean: When does it aid performance to put computations in the transformed parameters section?
messages.body_plain:
Sometimes models have intermediary/derived quantities that could be computed in either be the model section or the transformed parameters section. An example would be the non-centered parameterization of a hierarchical regression (aka Matt trick). I thought I'd read in the manual that the declarations & computations in the transformed parameters section were computed less frequently than those in the model section, but now I see that Figure 29.1 (pg. 318 of manual v2.11.0) lists them both as being computed on each leapfrog step. On the other hand, if only the model block is used, one can put all the intermediary/derived quantities in a local block and avoid memory overhead of storing them across steps, right? So, are there cases that achieve performance speed ups by using the transformed parameters section?

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

messages.body_plain:
No, the only difference is that the transformed parameters
are saved and local variables in the model block are not.
Otherwise, they execute exactly the same code in C++.

We've been considering two competing changes:

* removing the transformed parameters block altogether (deprecating,
  but still supporting for backward compatibility), and

* allowing increments to the log density in the transformed parameter
  block that go into the Jacobian (and hence will be ignored for
  maximum likelihood estimates)

- Bob

messages.subject: Vectorizing Mixtures
messages.subject_clean: Vectorizing Mixtures
messages.body_plain:
Section 10.5 (pg 117 in v2.11.0) of the manual asserts that it's not possible to vectorize a mixture model. It presents the valid, non-vectorized model:

    for (n in 1:N) {
      target += log_sum_exp(log(lambda)
        + normal_lpdf(y[n] | mu[1], sigma[1]),
        log1m(lambda)
        + normal_lpdf(y[n] | mu[2], sigma[2]));
    }

where presumably lambda is a real, so it would be erroneous to try:

    target += log_sum_exp(log(lambda)
      + normal_lpdf(y | mu[1], sigma[1]),
      log1m(lambda)
      + normal_lpdf(y | mu[2], sigma[2]));

However, what if one builds up a vector of mixture proportions, one for each observation y, as in:

    vector[N] lambda_vec ;
    lambda_vec = rep_vector(lambdaN) ;
    target += log_sum_exp(log(lambda_vec)
      + normal_lpdf(y | mu[1], sigma[1]),
      log1m(lambda_vec)
      + normal_lpdf(y | mu[2], sigma[2])) ;

Shouldn't this work? Or would the overhead of creating/filling the new vector eliminate any benefit of vectorization?

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Vectorizing Mixtures
messages.body_plain:
> On Aug 15, 2016, at 4:51 PM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Oh, I see that log1m() only works on reals, so one would need to do:
>
>     vector[N] lambda_vec ;
>     lambda_vec = rep_vector(lambdaN) ;
>     target += log_sum_exp(log(lambda_vec)
>       + normal_lpdf(y | mu[1], sigma[1]),
>       log(1-lambda_vec)
>       + normal_lpdf(y | mu[2], sigma[2])) ;

No, that won't work, because normal_lpdf() returns a single value
that is the sum of the log densities of the entry.  We need to
write a vectorized form of log_mix, but it's not going to save much
because there's very little in the way of shared computation to reuse.

For another efficiency tip, you wouldn't want to do

> lambda_vec = rep_vector(lambdaN) ;

and then call log(lambda_vec), because it'd compute that log N times.
Instead, you'd want to do

  lambda_vec = rep_vector(log(lambda), N);

so it only gets computed once.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I don't think we'll be deprecating ~ any time soon.  And
nothing else is scheduled to be deprecated.

The next big change for 2.12 will be allowing compound
declare/define, e.g.

  real a = 5.7;

and vectorizing most of the unary functions.  No other
big deprecations on the way.

We'll also be allowing ways for users to control whether
the ~ statements and _lpdf, _lpmf functions include
constant terms, but the default behavior won't change (not
included with ~, included with functions).

We're probably going to allow incrementing the Jacobian
in the transformed parameter block with the behavior that
the density increments won't be included for maximum likelihood.

Other than allowing some new data types (sparse matrices
and ragged arrays, no projected time of arrival), I don't anticipate
many changes.  I tried to get all the deprecating changes in
one go.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Default priors vs. Uniformly distribution
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Default priors vs. Uniformly distribution
messages.body_plain:
I believe the issue is that the support of the priors needs to match
the constraints on the parameters.

Oversimplifying a bit, when you put the uniform priors in, you're
saying that values of sigma > 100 have zero probability, but are still
valid (similarly for beta) and should be explored by HMC. This causes
problems for sampling since it tries to explore the whole distribution
and hits the zero probability regions. If you do mode finding
(optimization), there isn't an issue since it focuses Stan's attention
on a fairly small region near the mode (which, under your
construction, is in the support of the priors).

If you really want to use those uniform priors, you also need to
constrain beta and sigma to match the support. It would, of course, be
better to use better priors (see [1] for some guidance) but I can
understand using these sort of priors as a teaching example /
robustness check.

The default "uniform priors" [2] are uniform over the entire range of
the parameters so they avoid this issue.

When you say:

> MLE is equivalent to Bayesian + Uniformly distributed priors

That's only half true.

MLE is equivalent to _finding the posterior mode_ with a uniform prior
(Stan's "optimizing" mode). Bayesian inference explores the entire
posterior (typically with MCMC - Stan's "sampling" mode) and typically
reports 'whole distribution' summaries (posterior means, medians, or
credible intervals) - not just the mode.

Cheers,
Michael

[1] https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations
[2] In theory, there are other issues because "Uniform on R" isn't a
valid distribution, but with enough data, those problems vanish in
this example. I'd counsel against depending on this phenomenon and
just use weak priors.

messages.body_plain:
> On Aug 15, 2016, at 7:41 PM, 'lizzy2016' via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
>
>
> I was wondering if someone could help me understand why applied uniformly distributed priors vs. default priors outputting drastic different results. Aren't default priors actually uniform distributions?

Stan's default priors are uniform on the declared constraint.
So if you declare a variable with <lower=0>, then the prior
is uniform on (0, infinity).

> Basically, i ran a linear regression via a simple Stan code as below. If commenting out the following two priors
> beta ~ uniform(-5000, 5000);
> sigma ~ uniform(0, 100);
>
> The result is similar as lm, as expected because MLE is equivalent to Bayesian + Uniformly distributed priors.

I don't know what you mean by "Bayesian" here.  If you're
talking about posterior modes, then yes, if there are no
reparameterizations involved, then the posterior mode (often
called the max a posterior or "MAP" estimate) will be the
same as the maximum likelihood estimate (MLE).

But the MLE isn't a Bayesian estimate.  We usually use the
posterior mean, not the posterior mode, because it minimizes
expected square error of the estimated parameters.

>
> However, if including them, the result from Stan is terrible; the chains don't even converge. By running lm, i know the coefficients are bounded by [-5000, 5000] and that's why i set the priors as beta ~ uniform(-5000, 5000);

Even if you know the MLE for the parameters falls in (-5000, 5000),
that doesn't mean putting a (-5000, 5000) prior won't affect the
posterior mean.  You didn't show us how you're fitting here.

What was the MLE for the parameters?  If it's near the boundaries
of (-5000, 5000), these uniform priors are going to have a big effect.

If you're just using Stan's MLE, then uniform priors won't have
much effect if the priors are away from the boundaries.

And yes, you want to constrain the parameters to <lower=-5000, upper=5000>
if you have a uniform(-5000, 5000) distribution, because Stan requires
the model to have support (non-zero density, finite log density) for
every value of the parameters meeting the constraints.  If the parameters
are near the boundaries of (-5000, 5000), then you can run into
computational issues due to transforms.

But as Andrew says, this is probably not what you want to be doing anyway.

- Bob

>
> Can someone help? Thanks a lot.
>
> stanmodelcode = "
> data {
> int <lower=1> N;
> int <lower=1> K;
> matrix[N, K] X;
> vector[N] y;
> }
>
>
> parameters {
> vector[K] beta;
> real<lower=0> sigma;
> }
>
>
> model {
> vector[N] mu;
> mu <- X * beta;
>
> // beta ~ uniform(-5000, 5000);
> // sigma ~ uniform(0, 100);
>
>
> y~ normal(mu, sigma);
>
> }
>
> "
>

messages.body_plain:
Andrew was just making a joke.  See:

  http://andrewgelman.com/2016/03/15/stan-backronym-just-a-joke/

If you want to understand how Stan adapts during warmup,
it's explained in the manual.  We have to adapt the mass matrix
(basically scale of each parameter by default) and step size (HMC
uses an iterative algorithm for integrating the Hamiltonian)
for HMC, but it's done independently in each chain.

The chains *do not* communicate with each other during warmup.
As Andrew said (joking aside), they could, but they don't in
the current (2.11) version of Stan.

- Bob

> On Aug 16, 2016, at 12:36 AM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> Hi, yes I meant "adaptive," but the way that this is currently implemented in Stan is separately for each chain. It would be possible to have adaptation that would use chains together--such algorithms exist--but this is not how we are doing things in Stan right now.
> A
>
>> On Aug 15, 2016, at 1:15 AM, Chen Jingjing <chen...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> Thanks for your thorough explanation! Actually that is my impression when I read your previous response. However when I read Andrew's comment, "kinda sampling through neighborhoods that are, y'know, adaptive", I thought it meant that the chains interact with each other, otherwise what does "adaptive" mean here? Please correct me if I am wrong. I only have very basic understanding of Hamiltonian MC and Stan.
>>
>> Thanks,
>> Jingjing
>>
>> 2016-08-14 23:30 GMT-04:00 Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com>:
>> You are misunderstanding the problem here.  The chains do not interact
>> and hence do not affect each other.  Rather the fundamental issue is that
>> a Markov transition will yield a good Markov chain with respect to a given
>> target distribution only when _all chains achieve the same behavior
>> independently of each other_.  If any chain behaves differently than the
>> others then there is some pathological neighborhood of parameter space
>> that the other chains just haven’t encountered yet.
>>
>>
>> On Aug 14, 2016, at 9:46 AM, Chen Jingjing <chen...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>>> I actually don't know that chains will affect each other in Stan. And I am not sure how it works. Is the actual algorithm explained in Stan reference book or something else?
>>>
>>> As for the problem I am having now, shall I simply run one chain at a time so that a bad chain would not affect the others, and then repeatedly run a few dozens of chains and select the best one?
>>>
>>> Thanks,
>>> Jingjing
>>>
>>> 2016-08-12 16:21 GMT-04:00 Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu>:
>>> Stan is, umm, kinda sampling through neighborhoods that are, y'know, adaptive.
>>>
>>>> On Aug 12, 2016, at 1:36 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>> Because MCMC works only when all chains are exploring the same neighborhoods.  If any are exceptional chains then there are subtle pathologies in the interaction of the Markov transition and target distribution that affect the Markov transition itself and hence all of the chains.  This is why running multiple chains is so useful.
>>>>
>>>> On Aug 12, 2016, at 10:31, Jingjing Chen <chen...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>>> Why should I suspect the other chains when one of them is misbehaving? I thought that the chains don't affect each other in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. Is that true?
>>>>>
>>>>> 在 2016年8月12日星期五 UTC-4下午1:23:18，Michael Betancourt写道：
>>>>> Never ever ever do this.  If even one chain is misbehaving then it indicates that all of the chains are biased and should be suspect.  I'd also be surprised if all of our other diagnostics are not going crazy.
>>>>>
>>>>> On Aug 12, 2016, at 07:38, Jingjing Chen <chen...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>>
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Dear Stan Users,
>>>>>>
>>>>>> I finished running a chain and found that its so stuck in the same place that some of the parameters literally never change during the second half of the chain (and the first half is thrown away and not recorded),  with a standard deviation of 10^-13. It happened once with my model. Other chains seems fine. I am wondering if there is a way I can diagnose the useless chains and abort them. It would be even better if that chain can be restarted with a different initialization.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Thanks,
>>>>>> Jingjing
>>>>>>
>>>>>>
