messages.body_plain:
Thanks for following up.  Indeed, you need to simulate
properly from the model if you want to recover parameters
properly.

The LKJ distribution was developed by Ben from
Lewandowski, Kurowicka and Joe's paper on generating
random correlation matrices.  There's a duality between
generating random variates and defining a distribution.

I don't know what you mean by building up the Cholesky.
My guess is that you missed the rather involved Jacobian
that we explain in the manual following the LKJ paper.
That's the tricky bit of both random generation and
writing the prior.

You can actually use Stan's generated quantities block
to generate random correlation matrices using
lkj_corr_rng or lkj_cholesky_corr_rng depending on whether
you want the full matrix or the Chokesky factor.

If you use eta = 1, you get uniformly distributed random
correlation matrices.  You'll get the same distribution of
random variates using lkj_corr_rng and taking the Cholesky
factor as using lkj_cholesky_corr_rng.

If code's open source, reposting it is legal if it's
accompanied by the license.  Usually in these kinds of
situations, people don't mind.  You'd need a lawyer and
a court case to sort out fair use in these situations.

- Bob

> On Aug 15, 2016, at 11:58 PM, Roy Martin <royw...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi again,
>
> I thought I'd update this thread, as I believe I recently stumbled upon another potential variation of the "Folk Theorem" in this MVP model sim. After much consternation surrounding recovery of Omega (the correlation of D responses) from fake data with larger D (more response vectors), I came to the conclusion that generating Omega by building up the Cholesky, as shown above, perhaps doesn't work that well when D is larger than say, 10 or so. Sorry, I haven't yet fully gathered why that might be and maybe someone could fill me in or just tell me I'm wrong. Maybe it has something to do with this interesting description Ben Goodrich posted way back when: (https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/YlwuJgCmLxk/2VoGOKkfRkIJ), which I haven't yet had the time to contemplate.
>
> Nevertheless, I was fairly frustrated by this behavior with fake data because the results I've gotten using real ecological data have seemed highly reasonable. So, recently I ran across a script on Richard McElreath's Rethinking Github for generating random correlations from the LKJ distribution. It turned out that using that script to generate the fake Omega for this MVP model produced much nicer results, though lp__ is still shaky in some cases as expected. Yet, in every case I've tried so far (with D up to 30), all parameters fall within credible intervals at roughly the rates expected, with neff > 10%, etc etc. By comparison, with the previous approach to simulating Omega, the modeled 95% intervals would include the simulated Omega values no more than 70% of the time, typically due to drastic underestimates of the absolute magnitude of larger correlations.
>
> So, I thought I'd follow up on this thread with this tidbit above and tack on the code from Rethinking for simulating the correlations, which I believe follows code from Ben Goodrich (according to the Github comments). I'm hoping it is OK to repost that code here. I felt it might be helpful for anyone else fiddling with this model in the future. I actually just purchased Richard's book today if that counts for anything ;)
>
> #Code to generate Omega from the LKJ distribution (from Richard McElreath's Rethinking package)
> rlkjcorr <- function ( n , K , eta = 1 ) {
>
>   stopifnot(is.numeric(K), K >= 2, K == as.integer(K))
>   stopifnot(eta > 0)
>   #if (K == 1) return(matrix(1, 1, 1))
>
>   f <- function() {
>     alpha <- eta + (K - 2)/2
>     r12 <- 2 * rbeta(1, alpha, alpha) - 1
>     R <- matrix(0, K, K) # upper triangular Cholesky factor until return()
>     R[1,1] <- 1
>     R[1,2] <- r12
>     R[2,2] <- sqrt(1 - r12^2)
>     if(K > 2) for (m in 2:(K - 1)) {
>       alpha <- alpha - 0.5
>       y <- rbeta(1, m / 2, alpha)
>
>       # Draw uniformally on a hypersphere
>       z <- rnorm(m, 0, 1)
>       z <- z / sqrt(crossprod(z)[1])
>
>       R[1:m,m+1] <- sqrt(y) * z
>       R[m+1,m+1] <- sqrt(1 - y)
>     }
>     return(crossprod(R))
>   }
>   R <- replicate( n , f() )
>   if ( dim(R)[3]==1 ) {
>     R <- R[,,1]
>   } else {
>     # need to move 3rd dimension to front, so conforms to array structure that Stan uses
>     R <- aperm(R,c(3,1,2))
>   }
>   return(R)
> }
>
> #Generate random correlation matrix for D responses
> Omega <- rlkjcorr(1, D, eta=1)
>
>
>
>
>
>
> On Wednesday, June 8, 2016 at 11:43:45 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Thanks for following up and sharing the working code.  It
> is a hard model to fit, even when the data scales are
> reasonable.
>
> What you're citing is an an application of what Andrew calls
> the folk theorem:
>
> http://andrewgelman.com/2008/05/13/the_folk_theore/
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Jun 8, 2016, at 11:36 AM, Roy Martin <royw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hey Bob (and Andrew),
> >
> > Many thanks for taking the time again. And sorry for the delayed response. I spent some time head scratching and thinking about your helpful comments and believe I came to a resolution.
> >
> > Essentially, I believe I just wasn't considering the scales correctly here. I went back to thinking about Andrew's 2006 paper on weakly informative priors for logistic regression and realized that the betas I was simulating for this probit-based model probably just didn't make any sense! I was thinking about logit scale, when I should have been considering that the scale for probit coefficients should be smaller; about 1.6 times smaller, I gathered from a little googling.
> >
> > So, going back to Gelman et al. (2006), I took the recommended weakly informative priors for logit parameters and used that idea to roughly divide everything I was thinking before by 1.6 for the simulation of fake data. I changed the prior in the Stan (not STAN!) model for the betas to Cauchy, following the paper, with scale = 2.5/1.6. As a result, everything is running quite well (and fast!) and parameter recovery, post-checks, etc are all pretty nice. Well, lp_  can still be a little troublesome, but for the most part it converges with relatively low neff (around 10% to 15% of total posterior samples). Varying N also has the expected behavior. Great!
> >
> > Though it isn't much different from your original sim and model, Bob, I'll post my fake data simulation and Stan model below in case anyone runs across this and finds it useful.
> >
> > Many thanks again,
> >
> > -Roy
> >
> > Fake data simulation
> > set.seed(6)
> > N <- 1000
> > D <- 2
> > x <- cbind(
> >   x1=as.numeric(rnorm(N)>0),
> >   x2=rnorm(N,0,0.5),
> >   x3=rnorm(N,0,0.5),
> >   x4=rnorm(N,0,0.5),
> >   x5=rnorm(N,0,0.5))
> >
> > K <- ncol(x)
> > beta <- matrix(rnorm(D * K, 0, 0.9), D, K)
> >
> > set.seed(6)
> > # stick breaking construction to generate a random correlation matrix
> > L_Omega <- matrix(0,D,D);
> > L_Omega[1,1] <- 1;
> > for (i in 2:D) {
> >   bound <- 1;
> >   for (j in 1:(i-1)) {
> >     L_Omega[i,j] <- runif(1, -sqrt(bound), sqrt(bound));
> >     bound <- bound - L_Omega[i,j]^2;
> >   }
> >   L_Omega[i,i] <- sqrt(bound);
> > }
> >
> > Omega <- L_Omega %*% t(L_Omega);
> >
> > yMatLin <- (x %*% t(beta))
> > z <- yMatLin + rmvnorm(N, sigma=Omega)
> > y <- ifelse(z > 0,1,0)
> >
> >
> >
> > data {
> >  int<lower=1> K;
> >  int<lower=1> D;
> >  int<lower=1> N;
> >  matrix<lower=-1,upper=1>[N,D] y;
> >  matrix[N,K] x;
> >  }
> > parameters {
> >  matrix[K,D] beta;
> >  cholesky_factor_corr[D] L_Omega;
> >  matrix<lower=0>[N,D] abs_ystar; //latent variable
> >  }
> > transformed parameters {
> >  matrix[N,D] z;
> >  z <- (y .* abs_ystar);
> >  }
> > model {
> >  L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(1);
> >  to_vector(beta) ~ cauchy(0, 1.5625);
> >  {
> >   matrix[N,D] beta_x;
> >   beta_x <- x * beta;
> >   for (n in 1:N)
> >    z[n,] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(beta_x[n,], L_Omega);
> >   }
> >  }
> > generated quantities {
> >  matrix[D,N] z_new;
> >  matrix[D,D] Omega;
> >  Omega <- multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L_Omega);
> >  {
> >   matrix[D,N] beta_x;
> >   beta_x <- (x * beta)';
> >   for (n in 1:N)
> >    z_new[,n] <- multi_normal_cholesky_rng(beta_x[,n], L_Omega);
> >   }
> >  }
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > On Saturday, June 4, 2016 at 1:45:30 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > When you say the parameters don't fit, the question is
> > whether 50% of them are in the 50% posterior intervals.
> > Not whether they're all exactly right.  You won't
> > typically be able to recover fake data exactly perfectly
> > except in the asymptotic limit of infinite data.
> >
> > Are the R-hats near 1?  Are the effective sample sizes
> > reasonable?
> >
> > I take it in those figures that the red circles are
> > simulated values and the dots are posterior means or
> > medians and the intervals are some kind of posterior
> > interval?  And what was the eta in the LKJ prior you were
> > using and how much data was there?
> >
> > Are you sure JAGS is getting into the tails of this model?
> > Assuming the intervals are the same quantiles, the posteiror
> > uncertainty looks larger in the Stna model.
> >
> > You may want to try writing exactly the same model in
> > Stan.  It's hard to compare apples and oranges.
> >
> > As to the simulations with higher variance, it will be harder
> > to fit for the same reason it's always harder to fit if you
> > simulate with higher variance --- there's more sampling
> > variation with higher variance, so you need more data to
> > recover the true values of the other parameters.  (Just
> > think of generating 10 draws with normal(0, 0.1) vs. normal(0, 10).
> > You'll get averages much closer to 0 with the former than the
> > latter.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > P.S.  "Stan" isn't an acronym.
> >
> > > On Jun 2, 2016, at 4:53 PM, Roy Martin <royw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hi,
> > >
> > > I apologize to keep asking questions on this particular model, as from reading old posts on the MVP, it seems like maybe the MVP is just generally a tough fit for STAN. However, I thought I'd try one last request to see if anyone out there has come across any tricks for improvement. Like others, I have had trouble getting neff up for lp__ in this model. I have gathered from old posts that it has to do with high correlation in the posterior between the parameters and latent variable.
> > >
> > > The alternative I have is a JAGS version. Aside from a different prior on the correlations, you estimate the covariance, Sigma, using the wishart, and then rescale all of the betas based on the diagonal. Compared to Bob's version in STAN with the LKJ prior on Omega_L, which is the cholesky of the correlation matrix with diagonal 1. Of course, the JAGS version takes at least an order of magnitude longer to run, and neff can also be a little troublesome, though it typically will converge well after enough iterations. Generally, for 5 or less responses, the JAGS thing takes about 20-30 min to do what the STAN version does in 20 seconds to a couple of minutes. So naturally, I want to use STAN! And I generally like the LKJ prior, because it is just more intuitive for me.
> > >
> > > However, aside from the general problem with convergence of lp__, which I could live with, the STAN model doesn't seem to do well at recovering Omega, in particular, compared to the JAGS version. I'm not sure if it has to do with the lkj prior (I've tried eta=4, 2, 1.5, and 1 to no avail) or is a symptom of something else, but Omega is very nearly always underestimated, particularly for larger correlations, of course. Basically, it seems harder to pull the correlations away from unit correlation than it should be. The JAGS version seems to do a better job with this. I attached a couple of pictures showing an example comparing a run with JAGS vs STAN with 4 responses and N=100. The fake data was generated with Bob C's sim for mvp. This is just one example, but is representative, though maybe not as bad as many others I've done with larger and smaller D with pretty much the same issues.
> > >
> > > Finally, I have also noticed that the STAN version tends to maybe systematically over-/underestimate some betas for some D. Too negative for truly negative betas and too positive to true positive ones. I didn't test this formally, but it seems that placing a strong prior (e.g., normal(0,1) vs. normal(0,5)) on the betas in STAN maybe helps a little with this, which helps maybe a little with Omega. I attached figures for comparison.
> > >
> > > So, I guess I'm just throwing out some symptoms in a last ditch effort with hopes someone with more expertise (I'm an ecologist and relatively new bayesian/STAN user) might be able to diagnose a problem for which there is a solution in STAN. I've also attached the two models. Please let me know if there is anything else I could provide that might help.
> > >
> > > Thanks for reading.
> > >
> > > -Roy
> > >
> > >
> > > Omega figures: Top figure is STAN, bottom is JAGS
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Beta figures (STAN top, JAGS bottom):
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > STAN model:
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >  data {
> > >   int<lower=1> K;
> > >  int<lower=1> D;
> > >  int<lower=1> N;
> > >  matrix<lower=-1,upper=1>[N,D] y;
> > >  matrix[N,K] x;
> > >  }
> > > parameters {
> > >  matrix[K,D] beta;
> > >  cholesky_factor_corr[D] L_Omega;
> > >  matrix<lower=0>[N,D] abs_ystar; //latent variable
> > >  }
> > > transformed parameters {
> > >  matrix[N,D] z;
> > >  z <- (y .* abs_ystar);

On Monday, August 15, 2016 at 5:58:14 PM UTC-4, Roy Martin wrote:
> I thought I'd update this thread, as I believe I recently stumbled upon another potential variation of the "Folk Theorem" in this MVP model sim. After much consternation surrounding recovery of Omega (the correlation of D responses) from fake data with larger D (more response vectors), I came to the conclusion that generating Omega by building up the Cholesky, as shown above, perhaps doesn't work that well when D is larger than say, 10 or so. Sorry, I haven't yet fully gathered why that might be and maybe someone could fill me in or just tell me I'm wrong. Maybe it has something to do with this interesting description Ben Goodrich posted way back when: (https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/YlwuJgCmLxk/2VoGOKkfRkIJ), which I haven't yet had the time to contemplate.

The onion method is probably more numerically stable than the transformation of canonical partial correlations that is used in Stan, but they yield the same density for correlation matrix. If your problem is lack of numerical stability, then maybe the onion transformation will help. But in a model, you wouldn't use the _rng function; you need to declare the primitives as parameters, do the onion transformation to get the (Cholesky factor of the) correlation matrix, evaluate the likelihood of the data given the (Cholesky factor of the) correlation matrix, and put the corresponding priors on the primitives such that the resulting correlation matrix is distributed LKJ a priori.

Ben

 sigma ~ uniform(0, 100000);

On Monday, August 15, 2016 at 4:03:10 PM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On Aug 15, 2016, at 7:41 PM, 'lizzy2016' via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> >
> >
> > I was wondering if someone could help me understand why applied uniformly distributed priors vs. default priors outputting drastic different results. Aren't default priors actually uniform distributions?
>
> Stan's default priors are uniform on the declared constraint.
> So if you declare a variable with <lower=0>, then the prior
> is uniform on (0, infinity).
>
> > Basically, i ran a linear regression via a simple Stan code as below. If commenting out the following two priors
> > beta ~ uniform(-5000, 5000);
> > sigma ~ uniform(0, 100);
> >
> > The result is similar as lm, as expected because MLE is equivalent to Bayesian + Uniformly distributed priors.
>
> I don't know what you mean by "Bayesian" here.  If you're
> talking about posterior modes, then yes, if there are no
> reparameterizations involved, then the posterior mode (often
> called the max a posterior or "MAP" estimate) will be the
> same as the maximum likelihood estimate (MLE).
>
> But the MLE isn't a Bayesian estimate.  We usually use the
> posterior mean, not the posterior mode, because it minimizes
> expected square error of the estimated parameters.
>
> >
> > However, if including them, the result from Stan is terrible; the chains don't even converge. By running lm, i know the coefficients are bounded by [-5000, 5000] and that's why i set the priors as beta ~ uniform(-5000, 5000);
>
> Even if you know the MLE for the parameters falls in (-5000, 5000),
> that doesn't mean putting a (-5000, 5000) prior won't affect the
> posterior mean.  You didn't show us how you're fitting here.
>
> What was the MLE for the parameters?  If it's near the boundaries
> of (-5000, 5000), these uniform priors are going to have a big effect.
>
> If you're just using Stan's MLE, then uniform priors won't have
> much effect if the priors are away from the boundaries.
>
> And yes, you want to constrain the parameters to <lower=-5000, upper=5000>
> if you have a uniform(-5000, 5000) distribution, because Stan requires
> the model to have support (non-zero density, finite log density) for
> every value of the parameters meeting the constraints.  If the parameters
> are near the boundaries of (-5000, 5000), then you can run into
> computational issues due to transforms.
>
> But as Andrew says, this is probably not what you want to be doing anyway.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> >
> > Can someone help? Thanks a lot.
> >
> > stanmodelcode = "
> > data {
> > int <lower=1> N;
> > int <lower=1> K;
> > matrix[N, K] X;
> > vector[N] y;
> > }
> >
> >
> > parameters {
> > vector[K] beta;
> > real<lower=0> sigma;
> > }
> >
> >
> > model {
> > vector[N] mu;
> > mu <- X * beta;
> >
> > // beta ~ uniform(-5000, 5000);
> > // sigma ~ uniform(0, 100);
> >
> >
> > y~ normal(mu, sigma);
> >
> > }
> >
> > "

messages.body_plain:
It depends what the variance is.  That shouldn't stop
Stan's no-U-turn sampler from converging, but it
may require more warmup than the default to find the
scale when the parameters are on the order of 4000.

But what you'll find is that if the posterior standard deviation is
more than 500 for the parameter with marginal mode of 4000,
then putting a uniform(-5000,5000) prior will skew the posterior
mean to the low side compared to wider priors.

So as Andrew keeps saying, we really don't recommend these
hard boundaries in priors for just this reason---they don't
do what people think they're going to do.  And as I keep
saying, I need to write some case studies to show this.

- Bob

> > posterior mean, not the posterior mode, because it minimizes
> > expected square error of the estimated parameters.

messages.body_plain:
It varies by member.  But all the usual advice about
debugging any computer program holds.  I usually debug
everything (including models) by printing.  The first
step is always to get a minimal reproducible example that
isolates the bug.  We almost always then turn that into
a unit test.  The first suspect's always the math library
(stan-dev/math), then if I can verify the problem's not there
(because the unit test passes), I work up to the Stan library
(stan-dev/stan), and then up to CmdStan (stan-dev/cmdstan).

I work in emacs and a unix shell and almost always debug
by printing.  Even when I can get something like gdb
working, I've never been good at getting the checkpointing
and stepping working, so I almost always use a divide-and-conquer
approach with print statements and tests within the code that
verify things do what I think they're going to do.

It's a pain that our templated C++ code takes so long to
rebuild, but it's better at the math library level than
trying to compile and run a Stan program.  The unit tests
are set up so they can be run individually.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm experimenting with a hierarchical model which includes a Exponentially Modified Normal Distribution and I want to implement a parameter estimation on µ (and later extending this maybe on sigma and lambda).
The problem is that I have initialization errors, if the loop over the sampling statement for the exp_mod_normal is longer than 54 (variable "number" in the stan-code) - and I can't explain this. If the loop is 54 or less everything works fine and I get the print output with changing values. The number 54 has no relationship with the data. The error:

[298] "Rejecting initial value:"
[299] "  Log probability evaluates to log(0), i.e. negative infinity."
[300] "  Stan can't start sampling from this initial value."
[301] "Initialization between (-2, 2) failed after 100 attempts. "
[302] " Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model."

All parameters are initialized by stan and I use Rstan 2.10.1 on Ubuntu 16.04. I wrote example data ranges in the comments.

messages.body_plain:
It's much more robust to parameterize in terms of Cholesky
factors.  We prefer the LKJ priors on correlation matrices
scaled by a vector of scales---there's a description of how to
do this in the manual chapter on regression.  And a paper
by Ben Goodrich showing why the LKJ priors make a lot more
sense than Wisharts (degrees of freedom parameter controls
prior concentration around unit matrix).

Also, you want to vectorize all those sampling statements for
efficiency.

To eliminate the divergences, you want to switch to a non-centered
parameterization (more efficient in both HMC and Gibbs).  There's
a description in the manual.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
So... the issue is that there's an issue with the Eigen C++ library for that particular K. In C++ (on a Mac, using clang++ 703.0.29), this matrix will get through the cholesky decomposition just fine:

  Eigen::MatrixXd K(3, 3);
   K <<
      5.006077533027154,   23.39404564220951,   0.1089147679987995,
     23.39404564220951,   146.8106822579209,   4.484612487682218,
     0.1089147679987995,  4.484612487682218,   0.4239981299549255;

and this won't:

  Eigen::MatrixXd K(3, 3);
  K <<
    5.0060775330271543,  23.394045642209505, 0.10891476799879951,
    23.394045642209505,  146.81068225792086,  4.4846124876822184,
    0.10891476799879951,  4.4846124876822184, 0.42399812995492547;

I don't know why it fails, but now that I have a reproducible example, I'm going to add an issue to the math library, add a test case, and hopefully we'll have a fix soon at the math library.

For the time being, we should try to find you a workaround. Is there a way to slightly perturb your starting point for now and see if that moves things forward?

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Arya,

The matrix you're printing out is rounded, and not precisely the matrix that's getting decomposed while the model is running. The matrix that is printed above is poorly conditioned (i.e. abs(max(eigen(K)$values))/abs(min(eigen(K)$values)) is quite large, on the order 1e7). It's not a problem with cholesky_decompose, but rather the fact that the matrices you're decomposing are close to singular.

Rob

messages.subject: Limited density variations: general question
messages.subject_clean: Limited density variations: general question
messages.body_plain:
I'm wondering if there is any general advice for fixing models that have really limited density variations and are demonstrating random walk behavior. Michael lays out the problem really well in this paper <https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.0906.pdf>, but RMHMC isn't available yet.

I ask because I have a GLMM with ~500 random effects, where both the centered and noncentered form have really low Neff/N for one hypervariance in particular. The NUTS criteria look good -- no divergences at 0.8 and reasonably low tree depths. The issue appears to be that a trajectory can only traverse a really small portion of the marginal distribution for the hypervariance.

Is there any general advice for dealing with a situation like this? Or maybe something else is going on in the model that I'm missing (see attached if interested).

Thanks,
Cole

On Wednesday, August 17, 2016 at 2:29:45 PM UTC-4, Cole Monnahan wrote:
> Is there any general advice for dealing with a situation like this? Or maybe something else is going on in the model that I'm missing (see attached if interested).

We have had really good success with reparameterizing the X matrix of a GL{M}M in terms of its QR factors; i.e. if X = Q * R run the model with Q in place of X and then multiply the coefficients on Q by the inverse of R after-the-fact. This is semi-automatic in rstanarm, just change

fit <- glmer(toF ~ State + Pods + (1 | PlantID) + (1 | Year) + (Pods-1 | PlantID),
             family = binomial, data = flowers)

to

library(rstanarm)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
fit <- stan_glmer(toF ~ State + Pods + (1 | PlantID) + (1 | Year) + (Pods-1 | PlantID), family = binomial,
                  data = flowers, QR = TRUE, prior = NULL)

or do it yourself with rstan.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Rob, that's an astute point about the rounding. That's why the Cholesky solve works in R, but not Stan. You're absolutely right, the non-rounded version should NOT work because it's a 3x3 matrix with rank only equal to 2.

The reason the rank is only 2 is because it's a linear kernel. So if X is a data matrix with N rows, and D columns, the linear kernel would be X*X^T, which is NxN and has rank at most D. So if D < N the matrix would not be invertible, as was the case with me because I had D=2, N=3. If on the other hand I had a different kernel such as the RBF then D would be uncountably infinite and hence much larger than N, making my kernel invertible.

This sort of illustrates a hand-wavy way to see why GP's have identifiability issues, as Michael Betancourt has mentioned on here in the past. The "feature-space" is of much higher dimension than the amount of data you have.

Thank you Daniel and Bob for the debugging tips! I think using the RBF kernel instead of the linear kernel should fix things. I'm going to try that next.

messages.body_plain:
I'm very confused by your intentions here.  Why would you use a normal
truncated at (0, 1) rather than, say, a beta distribution?  When
you say "atom", you just mean constants?

I also don't understand your graphical notation.  Can you write
out the joint density p(param1, ..., paramM, data1, ..., dataN)?
Usually that's of the form of a prior p(param1, ..., paramM)
times a likelihood p(data1, ..., dataN | param1, ..., paramM).
As soon as we understand that, we can help, but it's hard to
infer from a pile of models with questions scattered throughout.

If you only want to sample from the prior, you just need to
code p(param1, ..., paramM) rather than trying to hack around
a likelihood.

As to the Stan syntax error, you can only truncate sampling notation,
not arbitrary statements.

I have no idea about the R questions, but you may want to post those
in a separate message to get the R devs attention.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I am trying to implement somebody else's model and they want a truncated normal.

With the likelihood P(data1, ..., dataN | param1, ..., paramM ) set to 1,

P(param1, ..., paramM, data1, ..., dataN) = P(data1, ..., dataN | param1, ..., paramM )P(param1, ..., paramM ) = P(param1, ..., paramM ) = Product of densities of (Alpha[i,j] | Cjj, pi_i)'s, i.e. \Prod_{i =1}^L \Prod_{j =1}^J P(Alpha[i,j] | Cjj, pi_i),

where (Alpha[i,j] | Cjj, pi_i) is distributed the same as a normal random variable with mean pi_i and variance (C_jj)(pi_i)(1 - pi_i) before truncation, but then move all the mass below 0 to be at 0 and all the mass above 1 to be at 1.

More detail is given on page 2 of the attached pdf under "Factoring the Posterior."

I just found your thread

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/reparameterizing$20truncated$20distributions|sort:relevance/stan-users/LsO6DAk0w58/IaN-itZhZK0J <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/reparameterizing$20truncated$20distributions%7Csort:relevance/stan-users/LsO6DAk0w58/IaN-itZhZK0J>

on reparameterizing when you have a parameter of interest that is truncated. I'll read that while I wait on your response.

because the notation is completely unfamiliar and it's a
massive definition.

I think the assumptions about dtnorm in there are wrong (or
the package implementing dtnorm is broken), because
truncation does change means and variances.  It also sounds
like you're defining censoring, not truncation, which results
in a mixed density/mass function, but as I said, this is very
hard for me to follow.

If you could ask a simpler question, or actually define
a density in standard statistical notation, we might be
able to help.

Or maybe someone else might be able to help.

Our general advice is to start with a small model that works
and gradually add features to it.  Starting with these massive
definitions is a recipe for failure, even for us.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Account for country-level predictors and individual-level predictors in a mixed model?
messages.body_plain:
> On Aug 17, 2016, at 8:41 PM, Allard van Mossel <a.van....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear list,
>
> I'm having a bit of trouble with building a relatively simple mixed model in Stan. I'm using a binomial logit model, to explain what basically comes down to the number of heads resulting from a known number of coin tosses, where coins are tossed in different countries, with a fixed number of sessions of coin tosses within each country (i.e. a few sessions that each have a known number of coin tosses).

We prefer the general term "binary trial" to "coin toss" as these
aren't coin tosses.

> I have two types of predictors; the first set varies within countries, while the second set only varies between countries (i.e. they capture a characteristic of the country).
>

> I'm using the model below to capture these differences and this produces reasonable estimates and fairly accurate predictions. Nevertheless, I wonder if I correctly account for the different types of predictors when I allows the country-level predictors to affect the overall intercept that is used as the mean for the country-level random intercepts. Are there any alternatives?

>
> Thanks in advance!
>
> data {
>     int<lower = 0> Ntotal; // total number of sessions
>     int<lower = 0> tosses[Ntotal]; // number of tosses for this session
>     int<lower = 0> heads[Ntotal]; // number of heads in this session

I'd strongly suggest more meaningful variable names
than "tosses" and "heads".

>     int<lower = 1> Ncountries;
>     int<lower = 1, upper = Ncountries> country[Ntotal];
>     int<lower = 0> Npredictors_i; // number of within-country predictors
>     matrix[Ntotal, Npredictors_i] X_i; // within-country predictors

>     int<lower = 0> Npredictors_c; // number of country-level predictors
>     matrix[Ntotal, Npredictors_c] X_c; // country-level predictors

You just want Npredictors_c here and to make it a vector.  See
below for why this is most likely wrong.

> }
>
> parameters {
>     real mu0; // overall intercept
>     real<lower = 0> sigma; // variability of country-level random intercepts
>     vector[Ncountries] beta0_c; // country-level random intercepts, after accounting for between-country effects
>     vector[Npredictors_c] country beta; //country-level effects

I think this is supposed to be countrybeta.  It helps immensely
if you send us models that compile.

>     vector[Npredictors_i] beta; // within-country effects
> }
>
> model {
>     mu0 ~ normal(0, 1);
>     sigma ~ cauchy(0, 1);
>     beta ~ normal(0, 1);
>     countrybeta ~ normal(0, 1);
>
>     beta0_c[country] ~ normal(mu0 + X_c * countrybeta, sigma);

This last line is almost certainly wrong.  It's not guaranteed to
put a distribution on each instance of beta0_c and may put more
than one on some.

I think you want something like the following:

  data {
    vector[Npredictors_c] X_c;  // predictors for countries

and then the parameters will look like:

  parameters {
    real beta_c;  // country slope
    real mu_c;    // country intercept

and the delaration for beta0_c is as you have it, with the model
for them being:

  model {
    beta0_c ~ normal(beta_c * X_c + mu_c, sigma);

>     heads ~ binomial_logit(tosses, beta0_c[country] + X_i * beta);

Aside from naming, the likeihood here looks like what you want.

You will probably find it more efficient (and much better converging)
to use the non-centered parameterization, but lets take one
step at a time.

There's a good discussion of these kinds of models in Andrew's
papers on red-state/blue-state (recreated in the Gelman and Hill
regression book, which I'd strongly recommend if you're working
on these kinds of problems).

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: Marginalizing imputed sample size (yea...): Am I doing it right?
messages.body_plain:
I'm working on a meta analysis problem examining the effects of temperature on the decay rate of pathogens by incorporating reported time series of concentration and decimal reduction times from numerous studies in the literature. We're modeling the concentrations (C), including those associated with decimal reduction times, as mean estimates derived from samples of size S, with sample standard deviations sigma_C. Within the overall model, then, we account for the standard error of the mean concentrations using a normal distribution with scale parameter sigma_C/sqrt(S).

Many studies do not report either or both sigma_C or S, and so we have imputation models for these missing values. In the case of S, we use a negative binomial distribution fitted to the mean sample size of each study for which sample sizes were reported, with a multivariate normal prior on the mean and dispersion parameters. Since S is discrete, it must be marginalized to run the models in Stan (Since S essentially weights the influence of each observed concentration, I think we could also reasonably use a gamma distribution to calculate it, but I will need to learn to marginalize for a mixture model later on, so want to do this treating S as a discrete parameter).

The general model for observation i in experiment j in study L is

Ci ~ Normal ( μC0_j – Kj * ti  , σC_i / √SL )

μC0_j­­ ~ Normal ( C0_j , σC_i / √SL )

Kj ~ Normal ( K25 * eλ(T_j – 25) , σK )

K25 ~ HalfNormal ( μK25 , σK25 )

λ ~ Normal ( μλ , σλ )

μK25 ~ HalfNormal ( M2030 , Kscale )

μλ ~ Normal ( 0 ,  max( 1, ln( Kscale ) ) )

σK,σK25 ~ t ( 3 , 0 , Kscale )

σλ ~ t( 3 , 0 , max( 1, ln( Kscale ) ) )

Imputation Block

ln ( σC_i ) ~ Normal ( XT * β + μRes , σRes )

C, t ( time ), T_j, C0_j (initial concentration) , M2030, Kscale, XT (linear predictors for the standard deviation) and all the multivariate normal means and covariance matrices are provided as data.

Would that be more or less correct?

messages.body_plain:
What msm means by the truncated normal density is given in blue on page 4 of the attached pdf. It is also the same as the pdf given here: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truncated_normal_distribution.

Basically, if X ~ Truncated Normal(mu, sigma^2, a, b), then the pdf of X is f_X(x) = f_N(mu,sigma^2)(x) / [F_N(mu,sigma^2)(b) - F_N(mu,sigma^2)(a)], where f_N(mu,sigma^2) and F_N(mu,sigma^2) are the pdf and cdf of a normal random variable with mean mu and variance sigma^2.

The parameters (Alpha[i,j] | Cjj, pi_i) are distributed truncated normal(mu = pi_i, sigma = sqrt(Cjj * pi_i * (1 - pi_i)), lower bound a = 0, upper bound b = 1).

Basically, I want to know how to perform Fit 12 of my original post (i.e. sample from my posterior, which is a product of these (Alpha[i,j] | Cjj, pi_i) densities) without getting divergent transitions.

Divergent transitions concern me because I know they're an indication that the leapfrog algorithm isn't approximating Hamiltonian dynamics "well" in some sense, and when I print the object coming out of stan() in Fit 12, the posterior means for C11 and C22 appear a bit off:

             mean se_mean   sd   2.5%    25%    50%    75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat

pi_vec[1]    0.50    0.00 0.28   0.03   0.26   0.50   0.74  0.97  7842    1

pi_vec[2]    0.50    0.00 0.29   0.03   0.25   0.50   0.74  0.97  7796    1

pi_vec[3]    0.50    0.00 0.28   0.03   0.26   0.50   0.74  0.97  8435    1

C_vec[1]     0.51    0.00 0.28   0.03   0.26   0.51   0.75  0.97  7722    1

C_vec[2]     0.51    0.00 0.28   0.04   0.26   0.51   0.74  0.97  7504    1

Alpha[1,1]   0.50    0.00 0.29   0.02   0.25   0.50   0.75  0.97  8189    1

Alpha[1,2]   0.50    0.00 0.29   0.02   0.24   0.50   0.75  0.97  8677    1

Alpha[3,2]   0.50    0.00 0.29   0.03   0.25   0.50   0.75  0.97  8917    1

lp__       -13.48    0.04 2.71 -19.54 -15.09 -13.16 -11.55 -9.03  4513    1

The posterior is the prior, and in the prior, C_vec[1] i.e. C11 ~ U(0,1) and C_vec[2] i.e. C22 ~ U(0,1), so E(C_vec[1]) = E(C_vec[2]) = 0.5, but STAN returns C_vec[1] and C_vec[2] posterior means of 0.51 and 0.51 respectively. Maybe that's close enough to 0.5, but 0.51 -/+ 2*se_mean is narrower than 0.51 -/+ 2*(0.005) = (0.5, 0.52), which doesn't quite cover 0.5.

Also I don't care about samples from the prior per se. My only interest in the prior is to check that I was getting STAN to sample correctly, because when I sample from the prior, I have a "right answer" (i.e. I know that E(C_jj) = 0.5) to compare a posterior mean to, but when I sample from a real posterior that isn't the same as the prior because the likelihood isn't set to 1, I don't have a right answer to compare to (which is why I'm doing MCMC).

Based on your thread (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/reparameterizing$20truncated$20distributions|sort:relevance/stan-users/LsO6DAk0w58/IaN-itZhZK0J <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/reparameterizing$20truncated$20distributions%7Csort:relevance/stan-users/LsO6DAk0w58/IaN-itZhZK0J>) I have an idea for how to do this Matt Trick for my truncated normal on the Alpha[i,j]'s, but I need to specify different bounds on different elements of the matrix Alpha. I will think about this tomorrow.

messages.body_plain:
My guess is that the erfc evaluation is underflowing to 0,
and hence the entire exp_mod_normal density is underflowing to 0
and hence the total density to 0, which causes HMC to reject.
The problem we have with HMC is that we also need derivatives,
so even if the log erfc(x) might not underflow, it's derivative
will be 1 / erfc() d/dx erfc(x) and that will be prone to instability
because the erfc is not on the log scale.

It may be possible to make exp_mod_normal more stable with something
like a Taylor series expansion, but we don't really have the
resources to concentrate on that.

We're always happy to take pull requests for more stable
arithmetic functions!

I don't know if you cold scale the values in the model somehow.
If not, you'll either need a different sampler or to change the
model.

- Bob

Nice formulation!  You could also code this in one go as:

  beta[5:6] = alpha / (1 - sum(x));

I'm still getting used to this slicing magic myself.

The transform of alpha to beta[5:6] is linear in the data,
so no need for a Jacobian.

> On Aug 18, 2016, at 4:34 AM, Qian Zhang <qian.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> What msm means by the truncated normal density is given in blue on page 4 of the attached pdf. It is also the same as the pdf given here: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truncated_normal_distribution.

That's the same distirbution as you'd get from Stan.  It
does *not* put all the mass for observations outside of
the bounds at the bounds.

> The parameters (Alpha[i,j] | Cjj, pi_i) are distributed truncated normal(mu = pi_i, sigma = sqrt(Cjj * pi_i * (1 - pi_i)), lower bound a = 0, upper bound b = 1).

This doesn't make sense, but you probably just mean that Alpha[i, j]
has the truncated normal distribution given C[j, j], p[i, i]?, and
a and b.  That can be coded directly in Stan using truncation, but
if the Alpha[i, j] are near the 0, 1 boundaries, it's going to
be very unstable numerically.

> Basically, I want to know how to perform Fit 12 of my original post (i.e. sample from my posterior, which is a product of these (Alpha[i,j] | Cjj, pi_i) densities) without getting divergent transitions.

I didn't understand the model, so it's hard to suggest
fixes.  Assuming it's coded correctly, that usually requires
a reparameterization if simply reducing the step size doesn't
help.  Some of these models have nasty curvatures that Euclidean
HMC has a hard time with.

To test if it's coded correctly, you want to simulate data
from the model and see if you can recover the parameters.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Ben,
  This is using STAN as installed from CRAN.   The obvious thing for me to do is to toss in a print statement or two, which is of course hard to do with namespaces, square or cube that difficulty as soon as S4 enters the picture.  (Is there an analog to assignInNamespace?)  Perhaps I'll have to download the source, but that may be a few weeks given some deadlines.

   I did execute getMethod("sampling", "stanmodel"), and the line you point to is in the local code, so we don't have a version issue.

   Yes, I would be interested in survival problems.  One reason is an open issue in coxme.  Assume a random intercept per group in a Cox model, and now move towards the limit case of only a few subjects per institution.  (This is common in multi-center trials of uncommon diseases.)  If some of the groups have no deaths, the unconstrained intercept for that group is -infinity.   The overall impact of this is to pull var(intercept) towards too large a value.  If the variance gets too large the Laplace approx begins to fail.  I have one nasty data set that breaks coxme and every other package I know, in that the final variance estimate is silly: it predicts some to be nearly immortal.  (It's a terrible model for said data set, but that won't stop users.)   The obvious solution is a strong prior on the variance, e.g. I find a group intercept of -3 = relative risk of 1/20 very had to swallow, no matter how much that hospital's CEO wants to brag.  This of course fits naturally into the MCMC framework.   This has been a practical problem for UNOS (United Network for Organ Sharing), as they are required by law to publish outcome information from all centers.  Without some shrinkage small centers, e.g., any pediatric transplant program, will see extreme highs and lows in the hazard ratio.  On the other hand they don't want to shrink much, so as to respond quickly to any center with a problem in post-transplant care.

Terry

On Thursday, August 18, 2016 at 10:02:52 AM UTC-4, Terry Therneau wrote:
> Yes, I would be interested in survival problems.  One reason is an open issue in coxme.  Assume a random intercept per group in a Cox model, and now move towards the limit case of only a few subjects per institution.  (This is common in multi-center trials of uncommon diseases.)  If some of the groups have no deaths, the unconstrained intercept for that group is -infinity.   The overall impact of this is to pull var(intercept) towards too large a value.

We have had success overcoming similar issues with lme4::[g]lmer and gamm4::gamm4 by using stan_glmer and stan_gamm4. A stan_coxme function would be very similar. Just need to support a few more likelihood functions and handle censored observations. Jacki B has been doing some of these things using PyStan.

https://github.com/hammerlab/survivalstan

Ben

>
> I'm working on a meta analysis problem examining the effects of temperature on the decay rate of pathogens by incorporating reported time series of concentration and decimal reduction times from numerous studies in the literature. We're modeling the concentrations (C), including those associated with decimal reduction times, as mean estimates derived from samples of size S, with sample standard deviations sigma_C. Within the overall model, then, we account for the standard error of the mean concentrations using a normal distribution with scale parameter sigma_C/sqrt(S).
>
> Many studies do not report either or both sigma_C or S, and so we have imputation models for these missing values. In the case of S, we use a negative binomial distribution fitted to the mean sample size of each study for which sample sizes were reported, with a multivariate normal prior on the mean and dispersion parameters. Since S is discrete, it must be marginalized to run the models in Stan (Since S essentially weights the influence of each observed concentration, I think we could also reasonably use a gamma distribution to calculate it, but I will need to learn to marginalize for a mixture model later on, so want to do this treating S as a discrete parameter).
>
> The general model for observation i in experiment j in study L is
>
>
>
> Ci ~ Normal ( μC0_j – Kj * ti  , σC_i / √SL )
>
> μC0_j­­ ~ Normal ( C0_j , σC_i / √SL )
>
> Kj ~ Normal ( K25 * eλ(T_j – 25) , σK )
>
> K25 ~ HalfNormal ( μK25 , σK25 )
>
> λ ~ Normal ( μλ , σλ )
>
> μK25 ~ HalfNormal ( M2030 , Kscale )
>
> μλ ~ Normal ( 0 ,  max( 1, ln( Kscale ) ) )
>
> σK,σK25 ~ t ( 3 , 0 , Kscale )

>
>

> SL ~ Neg Binom ( μS , φS )

messages.body_plain:
This is really interesting. I fixed a bug in my noncentered application and it is mixing MUCH better now.

I ran a quick comparison against the rstanarm code you posted and got this:

model minESS time ESS.per.time
noncentered 70.1 135 0.52
rstanarm 92.2 455 0.202

 So it's mixing better but taking much longer. Is this what you'd expect? I had to switch prior=NULL with prior=normal() due to an error.

I haven't looked any deeper and would be willing to if you think it's worth it. The code used to make table is below.

Thanks,
Cole

noncentered.fit <-
  stan(file='wildflower_nc.stan', data=data, init=inits, pars=pars, chains=1)
noncentered.sims <- extract(noncentered.fit, permuted=FALSE)
noncentered.ess <- monitor(noncentered.sims, print=FALSE)[, 'n_eff']
noncentered.time <- sum(get_elapsed_time(noncentered.fit))
noncentered.df <- data.frame(model='noncentered', minESS=min(noncentered.ess),
           time=noncentered.time,
           ESS.per.time= min(noncentered.ess)/noncentered.time)

## rstanarm code from Ben Goodrich; modified slightly
## https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/LRnibbozy_w/mVE64492AAAJ
flowers <- as.data.frame(data[c('year', 'plant', 'stage', 'Pods', 'toF')])
rstanarm.fit <- stan_glmer(toF ~ stage + Pods + (1 | plant) + (1 | year) + (Pods-1 | plant), family = binomial,
                  data = flowers, QR = TRUE, prior = NULL, chains=1)
rstanarm.fit2 <- rstanarm.fit$stanfit
rstanarm.sims <- extract(rstanarm.fit2, permuted=FALSE)
rstanarm.ess <- monitor(rstanarm.sims, print=FALSE)[, 'n_eff']
rstanarm.time <- sum(get_elapsed_time(rstanarm.fit2))
rstanarm.eff <- min(rstanarm.ess)/rstanarm.time
rstanarm.df <- data.frame(model='rstanarm', minESS=min(rstanarm.ess),
           time=rstanarm.time,
           ESS.per.time= min(rstanarm.ess)/rstanarm.time)
print(rbind(noncentered.df, rstanarm.df), digits=3)

messages.subject_clean: NIPS Workshop "Practical Bayesian Nonparametrics"
messages.body_plain:
----------- Forwarded message ----------

CALL FOR PAPERS

NIPS 2016 Workshop:
Practical Bayesian Nonparametrics
December 9 or 10, 2016 (date to be confirmed)
Barcelona, Spain
https://sites.google.com/site/nipsbnp2016/

Because of the NIPS early registration deadline this year, we will
have two rounds of submission. Papers submitted to the first round
will receive a decision before the early registration deadline.
Authors may submit any number of papers to both rounds.

Important Dates:
 Round 1 & ISBA@NIPS Travel Award Submission Deadline:  September 22, 2016
 Round 1 Acceptance Notification: October 3, 2016
 NIPS Early Registration Deadline:  October 6, 2016
 Round 2 Submission Deadline: October 9, 2016
 Round 2 Acceptance Notification: October 20, 2016
 Presentation Type (Poster/Oral) and Travel Award Notification: October 20, 2016
 Final Paper Due:  December 1, 2016

=======================================================

In theory, Bayesian nonparametric (BNP) methods are well suited to the
large data sets that arise in the sciences, technology, politics, and other
applied fields. By making use of infinite-dimensional mathematical structures,
BNP methods allow the complexity of a learned model to grow as the size
of a data set grows, exhibiting desirable Bayesian regularization properties
for small data sets and allowing the practitioner to learn ever more from larger
data sets. These properties have resulted in the adoption of BNP methods
across a diverse set of application areas---including, but not limited
to, biology,
neuroscience, the humanities, social sciences, economics, and finance.

In practice, BNP methods present a number of computational and modeling
challenges. Recent work has brought a wide range of models to bear on
applied problems, going beyond the Dirichlet process and Gaussian process.
Meanwhile, advances in accelerated inference are making these models
tractable in big data problems.

In this workshop, we focus on the practical aspects of BNP.
We will explore new BNP methods for diverse applied problems, including
cutting-edge models and inference algorithms being developed
by application domain experts. We invite paper submissions that will be
presented in either oral or poster form. We welcome submissions from
the following list of areas:

* The application of Bayesian nonparametric methods to new application domains.
* Inference algorithms for BNP, including MCMC, SMC, variational
methods, and others.
* Novel Bayesian nonparametric models for new or existing problems.
* Software packages that allow the widespread use of BNP methods,
including probabilistic programming languages and implementations of
general-purpose inference algorithms.

A major focus of the workshop will be to expose participants to
practical software
tools for performing Bayesian nonparametric analyses. In particular,
we will host
hands-on tutorials to introduce workshop participants to some of the
software packages that can be used to easily perform posterior inference
for BNP models: Stan, BNPy, and BNP.jl. There will also be two panel
discussions---one each on applications and software---focused on practical
issues underlying applying BNP methods to real-world problems.

We will bring together participants from a variety of fields, including machine
learning, statistics, engineering, political science, and various biological
sciences. The workshop will be relevant both to BNP experts as well as
those interested in learning how to apply BNP models. There will be a special
emphasis on work that makes BNP methods easy-to-use in practice and
computationally efficient. Participants will leave the workshop with
(i) exposure
to recent advances in the field, (ii) hands-on experience with software
implementing BNP methods, and (iii) an idea of the current challenges that
need to be overcome in order to make BNP methods more widespread in practice.

Invited Speakers:

Tamara Broderick (MIT)
Bailey Fosdick (Colorado State University)
Maria DeYoreo (Duke University)
Marc Deisenroth (Imperial College London)
Jennifer Hill (New York University)

Invited Panelists (Applications):

Bailey Fosdick (Colorado State University)
Maria DeYoreo (Duke University)
Suchi Saria (Johns Hopkins University)
Jim Griffin (University of Kent)
Marc Deisenroth (Imperial College London)
Jennifer Hill (New York University)

Invited Panelists (Software):

Mike Hughes, Harvard University, lead dev on BNPy
Martin Trapp, Austrian Research Institute for Artificial Intelligence,
lead dev on BNP.jl
Dustin Tran, Columbia University, lead dev on Edward and Stan contributor
Stan Representative

Submissions:

Submissions are solicited in the form of an extended abstract of 2–4
pages in PDF format using the NIPS style (author names do
not need to be anonymized and references may extend as far as
needed beyond the 4 page upper limit). If authors' research has
previously appeared in a journal, workshop, or conference (including
the NIPS 2016 conference), their workshop submission should extend
that previous work. Submissions may include a supplement/appendix, but
reviewers are not responsible for reading any supplementary material.

Submissions will be accepted either as contributed talks or poster
presentations.  There will be no published proceedings for this
workshop; we hope that authors will find discussion and feedback at
the workshop beneficial for developing the research they present, and
we encourage authors to submit their resulting work for publication in
other venues after the workshop.

Extended abstracts will be submitted in two rounds due to the
NIPS early registration deadline this year. The deadline for the first round
is September 22, 2016 for authors that wish to receive a response
before the early registration deadline. The deadline for the second round
Is October 9, 2016. Travel awards for students and young researchers
will be awarded for the best contributed work in the form of free workshop
registration. Authors may also apply for a competitive ISBA@NIPS Travel
Award. See the workshop website for details on how to apply:
https://sites.google.com/site/nipsbnp2016/

messages.body_plain:
thanks for all the answers:

@Ben: I would like to avoid for now installing a new version, I'm running the models in a server, and there are other people using Stan right now. Do you think that "target += likelihood_contributions;" will be critical?

@Krzysztof: what do you mean by look at model vs. data comparisons? And the thing is that I don't want to start modifying the model, I don't  mind if the the model has a terrible fit to the data (in fact I'll be even happy if this is the case). But I guess I can't argue that the model doesn't fit the data well just by the lack of convergence, right?

@Bob: I  parametrized everything as best I could do following the advice of the stan-list, and I put everything that I could in unit scale.

And another general question is, can I use the 3 estimates of the parameters that I have from the 3 subsets of the data as initial values for fitting the complete dataset? Is this a good idea?

Or can I use the average of the 3 estimates for the priors of the model that I'll fit to the whole dataset?

> With more data, the posterior can be more highly curved
> (same phenomenon as narrowing posterior intervals) and
> harder to move through with the Hamiltonian simulation.
>
> The usual advice applies, which is to try a higher adapt_delta,
> and if that doesn't work, reparameterize.
>
> It can help immensely to put everything on a unit scale.
>
> - Bob

>
>

> > Your model is a bit too complicated to immediately recognize why it is not working well. You can improve the speed a bit by not calling sampling statements within a loop over the observations; just collect the likelihood contributions in a vector inside the loop and do

> > outside the loop. But that won't change the shape of your posterior distribution, which is where the real problem lies somewhere.

> On Aug 18, 2016, at 10:32 PM, Bruno Nicenboim <bruno.n...@gmail.com> wrote:

> thanks for all the answers:
>
> @Ben: I would like to avoid for now installing a new version, I'm running the models in a server, and there are other people using Stan right now. Do you think that "target += likelihood_contributions;" will be critical?

That's just new syntax for "increment_log_prob(likelihood contributions)".

>
>
> @Krzysztof: what do you mean by look at model vs. data comparisons? And the thing is that I don't want to start modifying the model, I don't  mind if the the model has a terrible fit to the data (in fact I'll be even happy if this is the case). But I guess I can't argue that the model doesn't fit the data well just by the lack of convergence, right?
>
> @Bob: I  parametrized everything as best I could do following the advice of the stan-list, and I put everything that I could in unit scale.
>
>
> And another general question is, can I use the 3 estimates of the parameters that I have from the 3 subsets of the data as initial values for fitting the complete dataset? Is this a good idea?

Maybe.  Are the chains all getting to roughly the same place
and converging to the same adaptation parameters (mass matrix
and step size)?  If so, starting near or in the typical set will
help speed up adaptation because it won't have to find the typical set.

Or are they getting stuck in weird places?  That's a sign of
bigger trouble as Michael keeps pointing out on our lists.

Have you already increased adapt_delta and decreased stepsize?

You just want to be careful to add some noise so that you can
measure convergence.

> Or can I use the average of the 3 estimates for the priors of the model that I'll fit to the whole dataset?

This is the focus of a lot of work on parallelizing MCMC.  The
problem is that the effect of the prior is going to change.  But
it should be OK for inits.

- Bob

We're modeling the concentrations (C), including those associated with decimal reduction times, as mean estimates derived from samples of size S, with sample standard deviations sigma_C. Within the overall model, then, we account for the standard error of the mean concentrations using a normal distribution with scale parameter sigma_C/sqrt(S).
> > >
> > > Many studies do not report either or both sigma_C or S, and so we have imputation models for these missing values. In the case of S, we use a negative binomial distribution fitted to the mean sample size of each study for which sample sizes were reported, with a multivariate normal prior on the mean and dispersion parameters. Since S is discrete, it must be marginalized to run the models in Stan (Since S essentially weights the influence of each observed concentration, I think we could also reasonably use a gamma distribution to calculate it, but I will need to learn to marginalize for a mixture model later on, so want to do this treating S as a discrete parameter).

> > > SL ~ Neg Binom ( μS , φS )
> > > Β ~ MVNormal ( Meansβ , Σβ )
> > > ( μRes , σRes ) ~ MVNormal ( MeansRes , ΣRes )
> > > ( μS , φS ) ~ MVNormal ( MeansS , ΣS )
> > >
> > > C, t ( time ), T_j, C0_j (initial concentration) , M2030, Kscale, XT (linear predictors for the standard deviation) and all the multivariate normal means and covariance matrices are provided as data.
> > >
> > > In order to marginalize S, I was thinking that I could basically ignore everything (leave it as sampling statements in the model block) except for the normal density assigned to C, which drives the likelihood, μC0_j,and the binomial distribution on S itself. Is this correct? In which case, ignoring for the moment the different articulations of the variables at the level of experiment j and study L:

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Account for country-level predictors and individual-level predictors in a mixed model?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Account for country-level predictors and individual-level predictors in a mixed model?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Bob,

Thank you for your time and the quick response!

> >     matrix[Ntotal, Npredictors_c] X_c; // country-level predictors
>
> You just want Npredictors_c here and to make it a vector.  See
> below for why this is most likely wrong.

> >     beta0_c[country] ~ normal(mu0 + X_c * countrybeta, sigma);
>
> This last line is almost certainly wrong.  It's not guaranteed to
> put a distribution on each instance of beta0_c and may put more
> than one on some.
>
> I think you want something like the following:
>
>   data {
>     vector[Npredictors_c] X_c;  // predictors for countries
>
> and then the parameters will look like:
>
>   parameters {
>     real beta_c;  // country slope
>     real mu_c;    // country intercept
>
> and the delaration for beta0_c is as you have it, with the model
> for them being:
>
>   model {
>     beta0_c ~ normal(beta_c * X_c + mu_c, sigma);

Thanks for pointing this out, that line is indeed wrong. However, I have either misunderstood how Stan uses the specification of a model, or my ambiguous naming (sorry about that, I will be more clear in the future) might have lead to a bit of confusion.
If I follow the suggestion above, my understanding is that I will have one parameter for a country slope (`beta_c`), that is the same for every country. I do indeed want the same slopes for each country predictor variable, but since I have multiple country-level predictor variables (`Npredictors_c` predictor variables, such as GDP, and other socio-economic factors) I think I should adapt the model slightly to fit a separate country slope for each of them. I would also have the change the format of the `X_c` data to reflect that I have one observation for each predictor variable, for each country.

The model would then be as follows:

data {
    int<lower = 0> Ntotal;                              // total number of sessions
    int<lower = 0> tosses[Ntotal];                      // number of tosses for this session
    int<lower = 0> heads[Ntotal];                       // number of heads in this session

    int<lower = 1> Ncountries;                          // number of countries
    int<lower = 1, upper = Ncountries> country[Ntotal]; // indicates the country of the session
    int<lower = 0> Npredictors_i;                       // number of regular predictor variables
    matrix[Ntotal, Npredictors_i] X_i;                  // regular predictors
    int<lower = 0> Npredictors_c;                       // number of country-level predictor variables
//OLD:    matrix[Ntotal, Npredictors_c] X_c;
    matrix[Ncountries, Npredictors_c] X_c;              // country-level predictors (one entry for each predictor, for each country)

}

parameters {
    real mu0;                           // overall intercept
    real<lower = 0> sigma;              // variability of country-level random intercepts

    vector[Ncountries] beta0_c;         // country-level intercepts, after accounting for country-level predictors
    vector[Npredictors_c] countrybeta;  // effect of country-level predictor variables
    vector[Npredictors_i] beta;         // effect of regular predictor variables

}

model {
    mu0 ~ normal(0, 1);
    sigma ~ cauchy(0, 1);
    beta ~ normal(0, 1);
    countrybeta ~ normal(0, 1);

//OLD:    beta0_c[country] ~ normal(mu0 + X_c * countrybeta, sigma);
    beta0_c ~ normal(mu0 + X_c * countrybeta, sigma);

    heads ~ binomial_logit(tosses, beta0_c[country] + X_i * beta);
}

Your variable naming (`mu_c` and `beta_c`) is much more clear than mine and I will adopt this in my model—I'm just using the old naming here to ease the comparison with the old version of the model. The same goes for the non-centered parameterization (which turned out to be about twice as efficient, although Stan already does a great job). Gelman and Hill's book is very helpful, and this has gotten me to also buy Gelman's Bayesian book. I remember seeing those red-state/blue-state models featured on his blog a while ago. I looked them up and they're quite similar, although I couldn't find the Stan code, probably because this dates from before Stan?

- Allard

Op donderdag 18 augustus 2016 02:50:12 UTC+2 schreef Bob Carpenter:

>
> > On Aug 17, 2016, at 8:41 PM, Allard van Mossel <a.van....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Dear list,
> >
> > I'm having a bit of trouble with building a relatively simple mixed model in Stan. I'm using a binomial logit model, to explain what basically comes down to the number of heads resulting from a known number of coin tosses, where coins are tossed in different countries, with a fixed number of sessions of coin tosses within each country (i.e. a few sessions that each have a known number of coin tosses).
>
> We prefer the general term "binary trial" to "coin toss" as these
> aren't coin tosses.
>
> > I have two types of predictors; the first set varies within countries, while the second set only varies between countries (i.e. they capture a characteristic of the country).
> >
> > I'm using the model below to capture these differences and this produces reasonable estimates and fairly accurate predictions. Nevertheless, I wonder if I correctly account for the different types of predictors when I allows the country-level predictors to affect the overall intercept that is used as the mean for the country-level random intercepts. Are there any alternatives?
> >
> > Thanks in advance!
> >
> > data {
> >     int<lower = 0> Ntotal; // total number of sessions
> >     int<lower = 0> tosses[Ntotal]; // number of tosses for this session
> >     int<lower = 0> heads[Ntotal]; // number of heads in this session
>
> I'd strongly suggest more meaningful variable names
> than "tosses" and "heads".
>
> >     int<lower = 1> Ncountries;
> >     int<lower = 1, upper = Ncountries> country[Ntotal];
> >     int<lower = 0> Npredictors_i; // number of within-country predictors
> >     matrix[Ntotal, Npredictors_i] X_i; // within-country predictors
>
> >     int<lower = 0> Npredictors_c; // number of country-level predictors
> >     matrix[Ntotal, Npredictors_c] X_c; // country-level predictors
>
> You just want Npredictors_c here and to make it a vector.  See
> below for why this is most likely wrong.
>
> > }
> >
> > parameters {
> >     real mu0; // overall intercept
> >     real<lower = 0> sigma; // variability of country-level random intercepts
> >     vector[Ncountries] beta0_c; // country-level random intercepts, after accounting for between-country effects
> >     vector[Npredictors_c] country beta; //country-level effects
>
> I think this is supposed to be countrybeta.  It helps immensely
> if you send us models that compile.
>
> >     vector[Npredictors_i] beta; // within-country effects
> > }
> >
> > model {
> >     mu0 ~ normal(0, 1);
> >     sigma ~ cauchy(0, 1);
> >     beta ~ normal(0, 1);
> >     countrybeta ~ normal(0, 1);
> >
> >     beta0_c[country] ~ normal(mu0 + X_c * countrybeta, sigma);
>
> This last line is almost certainly wrong.  It's not guaranteed to
> put a distribution on each instance of beta0_c and may put more
> than one on some.
>
> I think you want something like the following:
>
>   data {
>     vector[Npredictors_c] X_c;  // predictors for countries
>
> and then the parameters will look like:
>
>   parameters {
>     real beta_c;  // country slope
>     real mu_c;    // country intercept
>
> and the delaration for beta0_c is as you have it, with the model
> for them being:
>
>   model {
>     beta0_c ~ normal(beta_c * X_c + mu_c, sigma);
>
>
> >     heads ~ binomial_logit(tosses, beta0_c[country] + X_i * beta);
>
> Aside from naming, the likeihood here looks like what you want.
>
> You will probably find it more efficient (and much better converging)
> to use the non-centered parameterization, but lets take one
> step at a time.
>
> There's a good discussion of these kinds of models in Andrew's
> papers on red-state/blue-state (recreated in the Gelman and Hill
> regression book, which I'd strongly recommend if you're working
> on these kinds of problems).
>
> - Bob
>

messages.body_plain:
I didn't write that BUGS example.  Not sure I wrote that part of
the manual either --- it's a group effort.  Also, I'm not the
WAIC or model comparison expert, so hopefully someone else will
jump in.

- Bob

> On Aug 19, 2016, at 4:07 PM, Burak Gunhan <burak...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
>
> As you described in the Chaper 11.2 of the Stan manual, meta-analyses based on binomial data can be modelled using normal model (using log-odds ratio transformation) or using binomial model (using binomial structure of data directly). I took the binomial stan code from one of your BUGS-translation: https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/blob/master/bugs_examples/vol1/blocker/blocker.stan.
>
> I am interested in sparse datasets. And since normal modeling approach using approximation, I want to show that binomial modelling give better results compared to normal modeling. This is done by here  http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20827667
>
> I dont think it is becuse of WAIC, but maybe because they are not comparable models. But still I want to compare them?
>
>
> On Friday, August 19, 2016 at 3:51:18 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I don't understand the transforms you're doing here or why the
> normal model has only one parameter whereas the binomial model has
> N + 1 parameters.  Or why you model rc and rt in the binomial
> model and not in the normal model.  I may be missing something,
> but the models don't look comparable.  Also, you have an inverse logit
> transform in the binomial model and I don't see anything similar in
> the normal model (but may be missing it).
>
> I'm not an expert on WAIC, but it's not the gold standard in model
> comparison.  If the models are correct, you might want to try more
> robust predictive evaluations (like predictive p-values or simple
> cross-validation or held-out evaluation).
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Aug 19, 2016, at 3:43 PM, Burak Gunhan <burak...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> >
> > Dear Stan experts,
> >
> > I am using Stan to fit a fixed effect meta-analysis model. I took Stan code for the non-hierarchical model from Chapter 11.2 of the Stan manual. And I also want to use binomial non-hierarchical model. I attached my two Stan codes (NM.stan and BM.stan).
> >
> > To compare those two models, I simulated data based on the binomial non-hierarchical model (I attached the Stan code, BM_sim.stan). Then I analyzed the simulated data using normal non-hierarchical model and binomial non-hierarchical model. And then I compared them using loo package based on WAIC results. WAIC says that normal model is preferable, but I dont understand, how come true model is not preferable?
> >
> > Maybe it is not a Stan-related question but a simple statistical question, but how come normal model performs better than binomial model when I simulate data from binomial model? At what point I am doing wrong?
> >
> > I also simulated 1000 dataset. As a result, bias that I obtained from Normal model is smaller than binomial model.
> >
> > Here is my Sessioninfo()

messages.subject_clean: Windows10 compiling error?
messages.body_plain:
I ran into something similar. I think it has to do with interactions between the upgrade to RTOOLS34 and a recent upgrade of the devtools package.

The key is making sure that the correct RTOOLS is on your path and that the BINPREF environment variable is set correctly.

If you run `devtools::dr_devtools()`,  `devtools:::scan_path_for_rtools()`, and `devtools:::scan_registry_for_rtools()` these functions give you good diagnostic information about what R thinks your build configuration is and may help you figure out how to get properly configured.

For me, the answer was to install RTOOLS33, put that on my path and put `BINPREF = g:/Rtools/mingw_$(WIN)/bin/` in ~/.R/Makevars

Yes, vectorization.  We will take any of the
arguments as vectors/arrays or scalars as long as
all the arguments either have the same size container
or are scalars.  I don't know how to warn users about
this, but this isn't the only time it's come up.  Reminds
me of the some of the "clever" things R does that can lead
to errors, like broadcasting up (repeating entries) to fill
arrays.

> //OLD:    matrix[Ntotal, Npredictors_c] X_c;

> }
>
> parameters {

>     vector[Ncountries] beta0_c;         // country-level intercepts, after accounting for country-level predictors
>     vector[Npredictors_c] countrybeta;  // effect of country-level predictor variables
>     vector[Npredictors_i] beta;         // effect of regular predictor variables
> }

>     sigma ~ cauchy(0, 1);
>     beta ~ normal(0, 1);
>     countrybeta ~ normal(0, 1);

red-state/blue-state example in it.  The extra you get
there is a multivariate prior in that it's varying slope
and varying intercept (we now prefer different priors than
the hack of scaling a covariance matrix---we can put an
LKJ prior on a correlation matrix and scale that).

harder in that it assumes much more mathematical skill and
background (I had to read Gelman and Hill first and I was
a math major who'd done analysis as an undergrad, but no stats).

messages.subject: Jacobian implementation in hierarchical GLMM
messages.subject_clean: Jacobian implementation in hierarchical GLMM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Folks,

I'm attempting to implement a hierarchical model and suspect I need a Jacobian adjustment to allow for proper sampling, but I'm having some difficulty incorporating the necessary changes. For context, I'm using a mixed logistic model to predict coyote (relative) probability of use which is fed as a parameter into a coyote 'removal' risk model (another mixed logistic). Independently, deer (relative) probability of use is estimated using yet another mixed logistic model. Study area extrapolations for the removal (x_RemPred) and deer (y_DeerPred) models are then incorporated into a GAM (as x and y respectively) using penalized regression splines. Although a GAM is likely overkill, my goal is to compare the non-linear spatial relationship between coyote management (removal risk) and deer space use (relative probability of use and surrogate for the management objective), while accounting for the uncertainty at all levels in the overall model.

I don't really care about retaining x_RemPred and y_DeerPred and have thus declared them locally and estimated each using inv_logit(alphas + xPred*betas) with respective alphas and betas in the model block. So, to my main question, I'm assuming I do in fact need a Jacobian adjustment after the sampling statement on line 183 because of the local transforms. If this is correct, how would I do so?  I've tried a few options, but none result in proper mixing...just flat-lined traceplots at init values.  Although I suspect this could be due to other reasons than the absence of a Jacobian adjustment, if I break apart the GLMMs from the GAM (by feeding the x_RemPred and y_DeerPred as data), each converges quite rapidly.

A tremendous thanks in advance!!

Peter

I have no idea what a "GAM" is, but when you have a transform
like

  y_DeerPred[nd] = inv_logit(mu_alphaDeerYear + xDeerPred[nd]*betaDeer);

with mu_alphaDeerYear and betaDeer parameters, you want to think
about

and then do this:

  mu_alphaDeerYear ~ normal(0, 10);

  betaDeer ~ normal(0, 5);

then doing this doesn't make much sense

  y_DeerPred ~ normal(alphaGAM + x_RemPred*betaGAM + Z*u, sigmaEps);

because you've already generated the mu_alphaDeerYear and betaDeer
parameters and y_DeerPred is defined as a function of those (and
predictors).

So I'm not sure what the intent is, because it doesn't correspond to
a generative model (way of generating parameters from priors (and
predictors), then generating the data from priors (and predictors).

- Bob

variables involved, you want to look at the multivariate variable
transform.  But I think here you want to rethink the modeling choices.

@krzysztof: A brief explanation about the model

The idea of the model is that participants take the same time (mu_rt) to make any of the 4 decisions (stored as winner) and this time is independent of the experimental manipulation (but it varies by participant and by item, the so-called random effects). The experimental manipulation affects the decision (winner[i]), also with random effects by participant and by item, but not the time. The complicated thing about the model, is that when a participant makes a wrong decision (!=1) then there's a probability  P_redo of redoing the decision and getting it right, and when that happens the time is increased (in log scale) by mu_add. The final time is log-normal distributed but shifted by participants. Maybe I'm skipping some details, but it seems to be identified and I can recover roughly the parameters.

I'm attaching a simplified version which is non-hierarchical and with a non-shifted distribution, and the code in R that generates data.

@Bob: I couldn't check if chains converged to the same adaptation parameters (I only saved the printed output), so I'll check it with the next model that finishes. And I want to try another model with init values anyway in the meanwhile, what does it mean to add some noise to measure convergence?, is something like 1 SD enough? too much? too little?

@Ben: I tried to do the increment_log_prob(likelihood contributions) with the much simpler non-hierarchical version of my model, and it took slightly longer. Is this something that should have some benefit only in very complex models? Should I try it anyway?

> And I want to try another model with init values anyway in the meanwhile, what does it mean to add some noise to measure convergence?, is something like 1 SD enough? too much? too little?

By default, Stan initializes all parameters uniformly in (-2, 2) on
the unconstrained scale (then, e.g, positive parameters are exp
transformed, bounded parameters are inv_logit transformed, etc.).

We want to start in different parts of the posterior to find different
modes and make sure each chain is able to move to the same posterior
volume and mix there.  You can see the description of R-hat in
the manual or in Gelman's books or papers.  So we'd recommend initializing
around a single point, even if you start there.

- Bob

messages.subject: Exact sparse CAR with cheap determinant calculations
messages.subject_clean: Exact sparse CAR with cheap determinant calculations
messages.body_plain:
Here's a fast and exact sparse conditional autoregressive (CAR) model that extends the sparse approximate approaches provided by Kyle Foreman and others in previous threads.

Source code is here: https://github.com/mbjoseph/CARstan and I've also attached pdf summary of what's going on. The main trick is that the determinant for the multivariate normal prior on the spatial random effects can be computed efficiently following a trick described in Jin, Xiaoping, Bradley P. Carlin, and Sudipto Banerjee. "Generalized hierarchical multivariate CAR models for areal data." Biometrics 61.4 (2005): 950-961.

This determinant trick with the sparse matrix operations that Kyle Foreman developed provides 1-2 order of magnitude speedups with the Scottish lip cancer example. I developed this in the context of a univariate proper CAR model, but the determinant trick also applies to multivariate CAR models.

Here are some previous relevant threads for context:

I apologize for my variable naming scheme here as I realize it's atrocious. Peter
