messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: hanging ODE solver with 2.11
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: hanging ODE solver with 2.11
messages.body_plain:
> On Aug 22, 2016, at 10:26 AM, Bram Thijssen <brams...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hey Bob & Sebastian,
>
> Did you have a chance to look at this?
>
> I've noticed now that if I put limits on the parameters with the pointy bracket notation (e.g. real<lower=0.0015, upper=0.15> theta1 in the parameters block), instead of with a prior (e.g. theta1 ~ uniform(0.0015, 0.15) in the model block), then it does work normally.

If you have theta1 ~ uniform(0.0015, 0.15) in the model block
then you are required to have the lower- and upper-bound
constraints real<lower=0.0015, upper=0.15>.  The log density should
remain finite for any value of the parameters meeting the constraint.

So what's probably happening is that you're managing to initialize,
but then can't move because of rejections from parameter going
outside of (0.0015, 0.15).

> The sampler still has a lot of difficulty converging, but at least it's starting the sampling then. Does this give any clue what might be going on?

Yes :-)

Is there a natural constraint on theta1, such as theta1 in (0, 1)
or theta1 in (0, infinity)?  If so, you may want to try a stronger
unconstrained prior, like normal(0.075, 0.07).

Another thing that will really help is if you can keep the parameters
on the unit scale---then Stan doesn't have to find the right scale
during warmup.  So that'd be something like

theta_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

theta = 0.07 * theta_raw + 0.075;

It's an ugly hack, but it can be hard for Stan to adapt for complex
models during warmup.

- Bob

I wasn't trying to raise the issue of family so much
as the generative nature of the model.

What you can't do in a generative model is put priors on
all three of a, b, and f(a, b).  It's just not generative.
Because once you generate a and b from their priors, you
get f(a, b) deterministically as a function of a and b.

messages.body_plain:
Absolutely self-inflicted, but also simple pedagogically.
Andrew and I disagree on the same point---he wants to use realistic
examples, whereas I want to use minimal cases.  I'm guessing this
is an applied-stas vs. computer-science vs. math thing.
In compute science, we love our "hello world" programs.

The lack of simple examples in BDA and R docs were a real burden
for me when I was (am in the case of R) trying to learn.  And
what's simple/minimal to a (Bayesian) stats or R expert vs.
a new learner varies wildly, which is why I like to keep it
simple.  The more advanced students will understand (even if
they're annoyed) and so will the beginners.

Of course, the final call here is up to Ben Lambert.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I was thinking of hacking together a modification of the current progress info printed during the operation of rstan::sampling() that, when the sample_file and diagnostic_file options are used (typically for high compute-time scenarios) will pull out useful information from those files as they are updated. For example, once warmup is done, it would show the n_eff & Rhat info (or some summary thereof if there are lots of parameters) as new samples come in.

While I'm at it, is there any other information that might be useful to show as well? I'm not confident enough with my understanding of the warmup procedure to venture a guess at what might be useful from that period, but would certainly welcome any thoughts on this.

Cheers,

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.subject: Re: multiple cores issue
messages.subject_clean: multiple cores issue
messages.body_plain:
I downloaded the dev source from github and was able to make it work with a change to the code.  My prior make failed (I think) due to an out-of-sync version of StanHeaders.
Short answer: the .libPaths() environment needs to be preserved, not just the rstan library or its imports.

The dependencies list is deep:
> library(tools)
> temp <- available.packages()
> package_dependencies("rstan", db=temp, recursive=TRUE)

$rstan
 [1] "ggplot2"      "StanHeaders"  "methods"      "stats4"       "inline"
 [6] "gridExtra"    "Rcpp"         "RcppEigen"    "BH"           "utils"
[11] "Matrix"       "stats"        "digest"       "grid"         "gtable"
[16] "MASS"         "plyr"         "reshape2"     "scales"       "grDevices"
[21] "graphics"     "lattice"      "stringr"      "RColorBrewer" "dichromat"
[26] "munsell"      "labeling"     "colorspace"   "stringi"      "magrittr"
[31] "tools"

Here is the relevant line that needs to be added in the stanmodel-class.R file
    ...
            dependencies <- c("Rcpp", "rstan", "rstanarm")
            .paths <- unique(sapply(dependencies, FUN = function(d) {
                dirname(system.file(package = d))
            }))
            .paths <- .paths[.paths != ""]
            .paths <- unique(c(.paths, .libPaths()))     # add this line
   ...
I will guess that .libPaths() alone isn't enough, e.g., for the user who used library(rstan, lib.loc="my_local_lib").  But the old libPath can't be left out either unless you want to recursively chase down all the dependencies of dependencies.  At our inst  things further down that list are not in the same place as rstan, Rcpp, or rstanarm.    (Over 500 users on multiple shared servers of multiple types -- I'm not going to second guess how or why the sys admins organized things into multiple libraries.  The linux bunch at least are a very bright crew.)

Terry T.

> > Hi Terry,
> >
> > When you have a chance, can you try the development version of rstan which has an attempted fix for this issue? Just call
> >
> > devtools::install_github("stan-dev/rstan", ref = "develop", subdir = "rstan/rstan", dependencies = TRUE)
> >
> > You can make it install faster if you use multiple cores by calling Sys.setenv(MAKEFLAGS = 8) or something beforehand.
> >
> > Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Thoughts on more informative progress info?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Thoughts on more informative progress info?
messages.body_plain:
> On Aug 22, 2016, at 8:18 PM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I was thinking of hacking together a modification of the current progress info printed during the operation of rstan::sampling() that, when the sample_file and diagnostic_file options are used (typically for high compute-time scenarios) will pull out useful information from those files as they are updated. For example, once warmup is done, it would show the n_eff & Rhat info (or some summary thereof if there are lots of parameters) as new samples come in.

All the stats for R-hat can be calculated online as draws come in,
but not for the split-R-hat we use.  If you want to do that, it's
expensive to do on the fly and you wouldn't want to have sampling
block while waiting for diagnostics to compute.

With multiple chains, our algorithms require all the chains to
be the same length which you could do by simply ignoring the tails
of some.

Just  counter of which chain is at which iteration would be useful
along with projected time to completion (that can be based on a rolling
average of time taken).

> While I'm at it, is there any other information that might be useful to show as well? I'm not confident enough with my understanding of the warmup procedure to venture a guess at what might be useful from that period, but would certainly welcome any thoughts on this.

>From warmup, there's also the state of where the parameters are at
and also where the stepsize and mass matrix are at (usually diagonal).
When all chains are converging to the same place, stepsize and mass
matrices should be the same across chains.

messages.subject: Lack of trace convergence and low n_eff for poisson models with interaction terms
messages.subject_clean: Lack of trace convergence and low n_eff for poisson models with interaction terms
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am fitting count data to various poisson models using the code and packages that integrate with rstan are outlined in chapter 10 of "Statistical Rethinking" by Richard McElreath,  I have constructed models for my count data, and run them in RStudio using rstan with the ancillary functions from McElreath's github site (see http://xcelab.net/rm/software/).   For the first analysis I constructed models using three main factors.  The full model has eight terms: intercept, three main terms, three two-way interactions, and one three way interaction.  The Widely Applicable Information Criterion (WAIC) was highest for the full model (all interaction terms), and second highest for the model with no three-way interaction.  Interestingly, the next best model was the one with only the intercept and the trap term.  However, when I checked the MCMC diagnostics (Markov chain trace plot convergence and the effective number of samples (n_eff; pages 253-255 in McElreath)), there was no trace convergence and very low n_eff for the full model and the model with all terms except the three-way interaction.  McElreath suggests manipulating priors to be "weakly informative", but I am not sure how to do that.

Here is my model code:

#model with all two-way and three-way interactions
m10.10 <- map(
  alist(
    count ~ dpois( lambda ),
    log(lambda) <- a + bt*trap +
      bd*date + bs*site + btd*trap*date + bts*trap*site +
      bds*date*site + btds*trap*date*site,
    a ~ dnorm(0,100),
    bt ~ dnorm(0,1),
    bd ~ dnorm(0,1),
    bs ~ dnorm(0,1),
    btd ~ dnorm(0,1),
    bts ~ dnorm(0,1),
    bds ~ dnorm(0,1),
    btds ~ dnorm(0,1)
  ),
  data = d)
# Model with no three way interaction
m10.11 <- map(
  alist(
    count ~ dpois( lambda ),
    log(lambda) <- a + bt*trap +
      bd*date + bs*site + btd*trap*date + bts*trap*site +
      bds*date*site,
    a ~ dnorm(0,100),
    bt ~ dnorm(0,1),
    bd ~ dnorm(0,1),
    bs ~ dnorm(0,1),
    btd ~ dnorm(0,1),
    bts ~ dnorm(0,1),
    bds ~ dnorm(0,1)
  ),
  data = d)
# Model with no date*site interaction
m10.12 <- map(
  alist(
    count ~ dpois( lambda ),
    log(lambda) <- a + bt*trap +
      bd*date + bs*site + btd*trap*date + bts*trap*site,
    a ~ dnorm(0,100),
    bt ~ dnorm(0,1),
    bd ~ dnorm(0,1),
    bs ~ dnorm(0,1),
    btd ~ dnorm(0,1),
    bts ~ dnorm(0,1)
  ),
  data = d)
# Model with no bts, bds, and btds interactions
m10.13 <- map(
  alist(
    count ~ dpois( lambda ),
    log(lambda) <- a + bt*trap +
      bd*date + bs*site + btd*trap*date,
    a ~ dnorm(0,100),
    bt ~ dnorm(0,1),
    bd ~ dnorm(0,1),
    bs ~ dnorm(0,1),
    btd ~ dnorm(0,1)
  ),
  data = d)
# Model with no interactions
m10.14 <- map(
  alist(
    count ~ dpois( lambda ),
    log(lambda) <- a + bt*trap +
      bd*date + bs*site,
    a ~ dnorm(0,100),
    bt ~ dnorm(0,1),
    bd ~ dnorm(0,1),
    bs ~ dnorm(0,1)
  ),
  data = d)
#
#submodel 15 (omit location)
m10.15 <- map(
  alist(
    count ~ dpois( lambda ),
    log(lambda) <- a + bt*trap + bd*date,
    a ~ dnorm( 0 , 100 ),
    c(bt,bd) ~ dnorm( 0 , 1 )
  ), data=d)
#submodel 16 (omit date)
m10.16 <- map(
  alist(
    count ~ dpois( lambda ),
    log(lambda) <- a + bt*trap,
    a ~ dnorm( 0 , 100 ),
    bt ~ dnorm( 0 , 1)
  ), data=d )
#submodel 17 (intercept only)
m10.17 <- map(
  alist(
    count ~ dpois( lambda ),
    log(lambda) <- a,
    a ~ dnorm(0,100)
  ), data=d)

### Here is my check for trace convergence and n_eff:
### Verification that the MAP estimates accurately describe the shape of the posterior distribution
## Checking n effective and trace plots for convergence
m10.10stan <- map2stan( m10.10 , iter=3000 , warmup=1000 , chains=4 )
precis(m10.10stan)
pairs(m10.10stan)
plot(m10.10stan)
# neff very small and traces do not converge

m10.11stan <- map2stan( m10.11 , iter=3000 , warmup=1000 , chains=4 )
precis(m10.11stan)
pairs(m10.11stan)
plot(m10.11stan)
#neff very small and traces do not converge

m10.12stan <- map2stan( m10.12 , iter=3000 , warmup=1000 , chains=4 )
precis(m10.12stan)
pairs(m10.12stan)
plot(m10.12stan)
#neff large, traces converge during warmup

m10.13stan <- map2stan( m10.13, iter=3000 , warmup=1000 , chains=4)
precis(m10.13stan)
pairs(m10.13stan)
plot(m10.13stan)
# neff large, traces converge during warmup

m10.14stan <- map2stan( m10.14, iter=3000 , warmup=1000 , chains=4)
precis(m10.14stan)
pairs(m10.14stan)
plot(m10.14stan)
# neff large, traces converge during warmup

m10.15stan <- map2stan( m10.15, iter=3000 , warmup=1000 , chains=4)
precis(m10.15stan)
pairs(m10.15stan)
plot(m10.15stan)
# neff large, traces converge during warmup

m10.16stan <- map2stan( m10.16 , iter=3000 , warmup=1000 , chains=4 )
precis(m10.16stan)
pairs(m10.16stan)
plot(m10.16stan)
# neff large, traces converge during warmup

m10.17stan <- map2stan( m10.17 , iter=3000 , warmup=1000 , chains=4 )
precis(m10.17stan)
pairs(m10.17stan)
plot(m10.17stan)
# neff large, trace converges during warmup

### Here is the code for WAIC computation and graphing
#Model comparisons
#Compare all submodels using "Widely Applicable Information Criterion" or WAIC
#Adding n=le4 for more stable comparison
#Will also plot the comparison
(traps.compare <- compare(m10.10,m10.11,m10.12,m10.13,m10.14,m10.15,m10.16,m10.17 ,n=1e4))
plot(traps.compare)

###  Thank you for the help!!!

George

The priors don't seem too bad, although you might try making dnorm(0,100) into dnorm(0,10).

My hunch is the scale on your predictors. If date, for example, has a large range, then the model will have trouble adapting, given that your priors on all the coefficients imply the same scale for all the predictors. Try standardizing your predictors to the same scale.

I also wonder whether "trap" is meant to be an index variable rather than a continuous predictor. But that's a secondary issue.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Marginalizing imputed sample size (yea...): Am I doing it right?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Marginalizing imputed sample size (yea...): Am I doing it right?
messages.body_plain:
It helps to think generatively---that is,

  * how the parameters arise from the priors (i.e., the prior distribution),
    and then

  * how the data arises from the parameters (i.e., the sampling distribution)

Viewed that way, you don't want to put the prior into the likelihood (which
is just the sampling distribution viewed as a function of the parameters for
fixed data)---the parameters are generated from the priors and then the
data generated from the parameters.  The parameter generation comes first.
Having said that, you can sometimes blend them together with algebra to
get a faster evaluation of the joint density (prior * likelihood).

- Bob

> On Aug 23, 2016, at 3:47 AM, pcoll...@berkeley.edu wrote:
>
> So I've been puzzling about what to do with the dependence of the likelihood on both S and the value of μC0, which is also dependent on S. After some experimentation, it seems like I can incorporate both in the marginalization simply by putting an improper uniform prior (no prior) on μC0 and adding its normal probability density to the baseline negative binomial densities for each value of S. For example, for a single study with 30 observations in a single experiment:
>
> transformed parameters{
> 	vector[15] lps;
> 	for (S in 1:15)

> 		lps[S]=neg_binomial_2_lpmf(S|2,4);//+normal_lpdf(μC0|C0,sd_C0/sqrt(S));

> 	for (S in 1:15)
> 		for (i in 1:30)

> 			lps[S] = lps[S] + normal_lpdf(pts[i]|μC0-k*t[i],SD/sqrt(s));

>
> }
>
>
>
>

messages.subject: Wishlist : a bindable reference manual, a searchable electronic reference manual
messages.subject_clean: Wishlist : a bindable reference manual, a searchable electronic reference manual
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan authors,

The current reference manual is quite nice. But for some knuckledraggers who sometimes use their docs on paper (I happen to be one of them),  it has a quirk :

In the existing PDFs, parts and chapter start immediately after the end of the previous chapter.

Ouch ! This a) slows down searching references by page and b) is ugly as hell...

In common European/American printing usage, odd pages are placed on the right-hand page ("good" page) of a bound document (book). This can be obtained in \LaTeX by using the "twosides" option of the document class (numerous document class support this option, including all classes derived from the "standard classes" of current \LaTeX distributions). This inserts blank pages before the start of a chapter (or a part) when the previous page was an odd page, and fixes the page numbering sequence accordingly.

Since, as far as I know, the source of the reference manual is not accessible, could we have a "boundable" version of the reference manual for this (admittedly retarded) purpose ?

Similarly, for the more enlightened part of the Stan users set, an electronic version of the reference manual could be useful (especially, one could search through the manual with almost any ebook reader, without being constrained by the embedded physical format imposed by the PDF...).

An epub version comes to mind. This also can be produced from a \LaTeX source (with some hooplas for the math code, which is somewhat sparse in the Stan reference manual) : see for example what pandoc <http://pandoc.org/> or calibre <https://calibre-ebook.com/> can accomplish (with a bit of an effort...). Such a document can be read on a lot of supports (computer, tablet, even a phone...), i. e. independently of the computer where Stan is installed...

A much more ambitious alternative would be a cross-referenced hypertext (e. g. an HTML page set locally installed on the user's computer). But that's a lot more effort, and probably not worth it until Stan is more stable, with predictable life duration of a given version more than a couple of months.

HTH,

--
Emmanuel Charpentier

messages.body_plain:
Every part of Stan is open source and the manual comes with
a very liberal CC-BY license.  The manual is on GitHub here:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/tree/develop/src/docs/stan-reference

You could even sell bound copies and Kindle versions on Amazon if you
wanted under the CC-BY as long as the Stan Dev team retains copyright
and is listed as the author.

If you know how to add the blank pages you want (probably just
cleardoublepage and twosided formats somewhere), please
let me know what I need to fix or even better, submit a pull request.
I don't really have time to fiddle with formatting right now.

One issue you're going to have is that the version we distribute
uses the proprietary Lucida fonts.  There's branching logic
in the manual's style to allow it to be generated using
built-in LaTeX fonts, but the formatting of line lengths and
so forth will be off (and the built-in Computer Modern and
Courier are terrible fonts due to too light vertical bars
and mismatched x-heights;  Times Roman is too narrow for
good readability and doesn't match courier in color [typesetting
term]).

If you'd like to figure out how to produce an ePub version
and could send us a pull request, we could include the
script in our distributions.

We're unlikely to ever support versions for more than a couple
months due to lack of resources---we roll rather like R that
way.  But that's not lack of stability---we've maintained
backward compatibility in the major versions (1.x.y and 2.x.y)
throughout and the language all the way back to the beginning.
We just keep adding new features.

We do want to produce an online version, perhaps using the same
system as Hadley Wickham's Advanced R.  It's just too much
trouble given all the LaTeX and the other demands on our time.
We're experimenting with that in the econometrics book we're
writing with James Savage.

Personally, I strongly prefer LaTeX for online reading over Kindle
formats because they're easier to zoom.  In fact, I created that
format to work well on my iPad in GoodReader and to be easily printable
two-up.

- Bob

Unless I'm mistaken, which is very plausible, the expression I wrote above is equivalent to evaluating the joint density of the data and parameter  μC0, the 'true' mean starting concentration / intercept.,for each potential value of the discrete parameter S. It's necessary in order to marginalize S out of both the likelihood of the data and the prior on μC0.

messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

This was discussed back in 2014 (https://groups.google.com/d/topic/stan-users/A52PqqdYNks/discussion), but wondering if there's any updated thinking on resuming chains that have been prematurely terminated (power failure, for example). These days I always run with the sample_file and diagnostic_file arguments to stan::sampling() specified, so presumably I have lots of info on the state of the chain before it was stopped. Thoughts?

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

we're at and what the challenges will be going forward.

updating the language syntax, and squashing longstanding issues,

gradient to follow the posterior in small steps (that's the numerical
integrator to solve the Hamiltonian diff eqs presented by HMC).

We've had a hard time reporting warnings in Stan that users don't
interpret as errors.  Is that because most R programs don't report
any warnings at all?

Yes, standardizing predictors can help, but the usual culprit is
the posterior geometry, as in Neal's funnel example (see the Stan
manual for a description).

messages.body_plain:
Great, sounds like all is well now.

It's not necessarily a problem that parameters are correlated in the posterior. That's normal. It's just that chains with high correlations tend to mix less efficiently.

That one divergent transition is from the final step taken to compute DIC. Scroll up and you'll perhaps see that.

Both divergent transitions and the adapt_delta control parameter are addressed in later chapters, I think in Chapter 13 and Chapter 14, if not already in Chapter 12. It's a Stan setting, so if you search this list, you'll find lots of examples of its use.

And yes, I'd standardize (not just center) all continuous predictors, just so the priors are easy to interpret and on the same conceptual scale (z-score scale).

messages.body_plain:
It's actually the condition of the Hessian (ratio of largest to
smallest eigenvalue of the matrix of second derivatives of the
posterior evaluated at a particular point).  What you see in
the funnel (hierarchical model with no data) is a very flat vertical
and a very sharp horizontal (at least as plotted in the manual)---that is,
a very steep ridge.  That's very badly conditioned and very hard to sample
because you need increasingly small stepsizes to move the in the x direction,
which then won't let you move in the y direction.

The only recourse in these cases is to reparameterize (at least until
we get Riemannian HMC ready for prime time in the interfaces---you can
already use it in C++ directly---it's part of stan-dev/stan now).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Here's a pointer to the root of the MCMC code on GitHub:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/tree/develop/src/stan/mcmc

Stan can handle for loops and Cholesky decompositions---the
gradients are computed automatically by Stan.

And you don't want to use static Euclidean HMC---much better
off using our adaptive NUTS algorithm (see the Hoffman and Gelman
JMLR paper).  The reason HMC wasn't very popular before was
that (a) derivatives are a pain to code and error prone for
complex models, and (b) HMC itself is very sensitive to its
tuning parameters and even when well tuned, usually worse
than NUTS.

Given that you seem capable of some pretty serious coding,
how about contributing to Stan?  We can always use developers
with good C, MCMC, matrix, and calc skills.

- Bob

I don't know how complicated your model is, but Stan isn't
scalable to really complicated densities in high dimensions, which
it sounds like you might be dealing with.

I'd suggest setting the number of iterations low to start (say
100 total), see how things shape up, then extend to more iterations;
you usually need at least 200 to get adaptation working.

Anyway, let us know if you want us to take a look at your Stan
code and provide performance tips.

Also, rather than doing Cholesky decompositions in the code,
we provide Cholesky-factor parameter types for both correlation
and covariance matrices (and don't recommend Wishart priors;
we have an LKJ prior on correlation matrices that can be scaled
with a prior on scales---the LKJ prior has a parameter for degree
of concentration around a unit correlation matrix).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Prof. Carpenter and Prof. Gelman,

    There was a mistake in my code and I fixed it. Stan did an impressive job on my model. It turns out that the resulting samples of two parameters are highly correlated (|rho| > 0.85). I think that's the reason why my vanilla HMC fails to have good performance.

    Actually, I spent a lot of time on coding in this project. In the beginning, R was the only programming language I was familiar with. But its' low speed and poor memory management annoyed me a lot. So I self-studied C, command lines and makefile, and how to use Lapack and Blas in c. My code works pretty well on a simpler model, but things changed a lot after including one more parameter. So I didn't expect that I can finish Stan code within one day! And it gave me a much better performance than my code in C!

    I know the changing of step size and step length does not break the detail balance, but I never came up with any good idea of using that fact until I saw the "adaptive NUTS" paper this Monday. That is delicate and beautiful! I am also trying to understand RMHMC. Now I can't see any reason for not using Stan.

   It would be wonderful if you would provide performance tips for my code. But I want to apply Stan to a higher dimension model, and I also need to polish my code a little bit. So maybe I will contact you later. ^_^

Thank you for everything!

Sincerely,

Lu

> I don't know how complicated your model is, but Stan isn't
> scalable to really complicated densities in high dimensions, which
> it sounds like you might be dealing with.
>
> I'd suggest setting the number of iterations low to start (say
> 100 total), see how things shape up, then extend to more iterations;
> you usually need at least 200 to get adaptation working.
>
> Anyway, let us know if you want us to take a look at your Stan

> Also, rather than doing Cholesky decompositions in the code,
> we provide Cholesky-factor parameter types for both correlation
> and covariance matrices (and don't recommend Wishart priors;
> we have an LKJ prior on correlation matrices that can be scaled
> with a prior on scales---the LKJ prior has a parameter for degree
> of concentration around a unit correlation matrix).
>
> - Bob

That can sometimes be mitigated with a change of parameterization.
See the manual description of Radford Neal's funnel example for
the simple case.

>     Actually, I spent a lot of time on coding in this project. In the beginning, R was the only programming language I was familiar with. But its' low speed and poor memory management annoyed me a lot. So I self-studied C, command lines and makefile, and how to use Lapack and Blas in c. My code works pretty well on a simpler model, but things changed a lot after including one more parameter. So I didn't expect that I can finish Stan code within one day! And it gave me a much better performance than my code in C!

So glad to hear it.   That's pretty much exactly where Andrew
was at with R and why he hired me and Matt in the first place
to do the heavy coding (we both knew C).  Being computer
scientists, we thought we'd try to solve the problem a little
more generally.  Turns out it took a few years and a whole lot
of help from other great programmers and statisticians and
applied mathematicians (see our dev list).

>     I know the changing of step size and step length does not break the detail balance,

You can mess with anything during adaptation before you start
the MCMC chains---that's how we do mass matrix and step size.
The real beauty of NUTS is how it changes the number of steps (i.e.,
integration time divided by step size).

> but I never came up with any good idea of using that fact until I saw the "adaptive NUTS" paper this Monday. That is delicate and beautiful! I am also trying to understand RMHMC. Now I can't see any reason for not using Stan.

Matt's a genius!  It did take him a couple years and a lot
of input from Andrew to come up with the algorithm.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Just make sure that if you have a group of K categorical predictors
that you only have coefficients ("intercepts") for (K - 1) of them.
Because otherwise, if you have a top-level intercept or multiple
such groups of coefficients, the model won't be identifiable.

And if there are more than a couple of group members, you can fit
a hirarchical  prior.

- Bob

Do you mean the point estimates?  Mean or median (50% quantile)?
I was trying to say that this may be the "right" answer given
the skew of positive-only distributions with mass near zero---the
means will inevitably be larger than the modes (if the mode exists).
And as you can see, even the means and medians differ considerably.
The posterior mean is the point estimate that minimizes expected
square error, not the one that is "most likely" in the MLE sense.

I'd try simulating data to see what you get if that's not what
you're doing already.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Try playing around with this:

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  real<lower=0> y[N];
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> beta;      // mean
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> lambda;  // parameter
  lambda = 1 / beta;
}
model {
  y ~ exponential(lambda);
}

with some simulated data (say N = 5; y = runif(N, 0, 1)).

You'll see that the posterior mean won't match the mean
of the data y with MCMC (it's "skewed" in your sense, but the
real skew is coming from the underlying exponential and what
you're calling skew is just a property of the posterior mean
not following the posterior mode).  It will match with an MLE.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, August 25, 2016 at 10:12:48 AM UTC-4, Guido Biele wrote:
> I have problems with divergent iterations in a
> negative binomial regression model.

Negative binomial models are difficult, and there could be many culprits. One general thing pertains to these lines

>   Sigma_beta <- quad_form_diag(L_Omega * L_Omega', tau);
>   beta ~ multi_normal(gamma, Sigma_beta);

By constructing Sigma_beta and passing that to multi_normal (which takes its Cholesky factorization) you can lose a good bit of numerical accuracy. Just pass tau * L_Omega to multi_normal_cholesky() like

target += multi_normal_cholesky_lpdf(beta | gamma, tau * L_Omega);

However, that does not address problems due to differing scales among correlated betas. It is often but not always better to use the stochastic representation of the multivariate normal so that

beta = gamma + tau * (L_Omega * z); // implies: beta ~ multi_normal_cholesky(gamma, tau * L_Omega)

is a transformed parameter, z is a parameter vector, and in the model block

target += normal_lpdf(z | 0, 1);

>From Stan's perspective, working in z-space is frequently easier than working in beta-space.

Ben

I still don't understand what you mean by "skewed" here.  The
term "skew" has a technical meaning in statistics, and I have
a feeling you may be confusing it with the technical term "bias".

>  This isn't true for all the cases where there is a difference however. Treating point estimates with certainty is the mirage---you
want to look at the posterior for the whole model.  Assuming
that population level point estimates (you haven't said which
point estimates you're using---MLE, posterior median, posterior
mean) are representative of the population is also not right.

sarcastic here---it's what I have to do, too.  See, e.g.,

https://lingpipe-blog.com/2014/10/29/beckys-and-my-annotation-paper-in-tacl/

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Always a chance something's wrong with the code or the model
is misspecified.  You can usually find problems in code if
you can't get the right coverage for your posterior intervals for
simulated data.

Could the problem be looking at the posteriors for the parameters
vs. the predictive posterior for new low-level parameters?

For example, if my hierarchical model for low-level parameters
beta[i] is

  for (i in 1:I)
    beta[i] ~ normal(mu, sigma);

then you don't necessarily expect the marginal posterior for mu
to overlap with the marginal posteriors for any of the beta[i].

What you want to look at is the posterior predictive distribution
for the lower-levle parameters, which in Stan looks like this:

generated quantities {
  real beta_tilde;

  beta_tilde = normal_rng(mu, sigma);
}

The posterior on beta_tilde is what you want to look at for
coverage, not the posterior over mu.  The distribution for
beta_tilde draws will be

  p(beta_new | y) = INTEGRAL_{mu, sigma} normal(beta_new | mu, sigma)
                                         * p(mu, sigma | y)
                      d.mu <http://d.mu> d.sigma

where y here is all the original data.  This distribution is
your prediction for the population based on the model and observed
data y.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Great.  We need to get truncated RNGs---it's an issue that
nobody has time to work on.  But the point is that it
doesn't matter if a isn't close if sigma is wide.

Normal priors can be pretty weak, so lots of individual-level
data will overwhelm the population estimates.  If you
have a really spread out population, then you are still going
to get an estimate for a that may have a tight posterior that's
nowhere near the actual values.  But in that case, sigma will
be large, so beta_tilde will be much wider and should still get
the right coverage.

Anyway, glad to see you're doing the right posterior predictive
checks here.

messages.body_plain:
OK I had a crack at doing this based on the scaling properties of the gamma distribution.

I have created two data sets (dat1 and dat2) which are described by N(0, sigma_i) where sigma_1 and sigma_2 have to be learned from a toy data set. sigma_1 and sigma_2 have a hierarchical prior given by gamma(2, 1/hp) where hp is the hyperparameter.

I have created two versions of the model (in one Stan file):
A centered parameterisation based on gamma(2,1/hp)
A non-centered parameterisation based on hp_alt*gamma(2,1) where hp_alt is the hyperprior in this alternative specification.

Code is below for both the R version which calls it, and the Stan code.

I think that these two examples should give the same answer for hp, but they vary slightly. Why is this? Have I implicitly assumed slightly different priors here?

Results from 15 million iterations below. Note that hp and hp_alt (the two different versions of this) differ very slightly, and more than can reasonably be explained by sampling variation.

(sig1 is similar to sig1_alt, and sig2 is similar to sig2_alt, as expected).

Stan code:

data{
  int n;
  vector[n] dat1;
  vector[n] dat2;
}
parameters{
  real<lower=0> hp;
  real<lower=0> hp_alt;
  real<lower=0> sig1;
  real<lower=0> sig2;
  real<lower=0> c1_alt;
  real<lower=0> c2_alt;

}
transformed parameters{
  real sig1_alt;
  real sig2_alt;

  sig1_alt = c1_alt*hp_alt;
  sig2_alt = c2_alt*hp_alt;
}
model{
  // Standard version

  dat1 ~ normal(0, sig1);
  dat2 ~ normal(0, sig2);

  sig1 ~ gamma(2,1/hp);
  sig2 ~ gamma(2,1/hp);

  // Alternate version

  dat1 ~ normal(0, sig1_alt);
  dat2 ~ normal(0, sig2_alt);

  c1_alt ~ gamma(2, 1);
  c2_alt ~ gamma(2, 1);
 }

gendat_1

messages.body_plain:
I don't know why you'd want to add an expression the log
scale to one on the linear scale.   Using Stan's latest notation
(and you don't want to use 2.10 due to a bug, only 2.11), did you
really mean:

  G = G + normal_lpdf(x[i] | mu, sigma) + normal_lcdf(x[i] | mu, sigma)

Assuming n = rows(x) and you intended to add on the log scale, you can replace

   logfunc(n, x, mu, sigma)

with the expression

  normal_lpdf(x | mu, sigma) + normal_lcdf(x | mu, sigma)

And unless you want to be able to call the function with n != rows(x),
you don't want to pass in redundant arguments.

But then I don't see why you'd be adding a CDF term, either, especially
evaluated at the same point x[i] ---are you
trying to do upper-bound truncation by hand by any chance?  If so,
you want to subtract the log CDF evaluated at the truncation point.
That you will need to multiply by n because there's only one truncation
point, unless that also varies by observation.

- Bob

I am building a model for lifetime data that assumes a proportion, p, of units are defective and subject to an additional failure mode. The distribution of X is

Pr(X <= t) = F(t) = 1 - (1 - p * F1(t)) * ( 1 - F2(t))

where X is the failure time for the unit. I assume F1 and F2 are Weibull distributions, and I actually log the data. Y ~ Weibull(shape, scale) implies log(Y) ~ gumbel(-mu, sigma), where mu = log(scale) and sigma = 1/shape.

I simulated data from the model and left-truncated the data at randomly chosen time points. messages.body_plain:
You don't need to assign before returning:

  real sev_logpdf(real y, real mu, real sigma){
    real out;
    out = gumbel_lpdf(-y| -mu, sigma);
    return out;
  }

That can just be return gumbel_lpdf(...).

This prior for p is saying that you expect the
value to be really close to 1 most of the time, but
sometimes very close to 0 and almost never in between:

 p ~ beta(.1, .9);

I'd be inclined to go with a more regularizing prior.
It can really help with computation.

It looks like the divergences (I think that's what's
printed in red?) may all be due to numerical issues in
evaluation.

For efficiency, you don't want to keep taking those logs
and exps of the same values inside the loops --- compute them
on the outside and store in a local variable.

You might want to try coding up the Gumbel directly with
a log scale parameter so you don't need the log to exp to log
transform, which can be unstable.  And then reducing to the point
where you can

And I'd recommend dropping the interval constraints on
log_sigma and just using the prior as is --- normal(0, 1)
should keep it in (-5, 5) unless there's a ton of data
pulling it out, in which case you probably don't want that
constraint anyway.

Also, there's a log1m_exp(u) which is equal to
log_diff_exp(0, u).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Why have a lower=0 bound on the log scale?
And we don't genrally recommend bounds like (-2, 0)
unless the parameter is physically constrained to (-2, 0).
Otherwise, you can bias the posterior means considerably by
truncating non-negligible probability mass.

In general, you just code the generative model directly
in Stan and Stan does the inversion---you shouldn't try
to code the inversion directly unless you have analytical
steps (which can save time and make the statistical mixing
more efficient).

The MLE is not the iteration with the highest log density.
Often the MLE isn't in the typical set at all, so you won't
get anywhere near it (e.g., try sampling from a 20-dimensional
unit normal exactly and see how close you get to zero, the MLE).
What you want to be doing is checking posterior interval
calibration (coverage, say, of the 50% intervals).

Also, just measuring by the log density won't tell you much.

I'm afraid I don't understand this truncated density---maybe
someone else could help?

- Bob

> On Aug 26, 2016, at 5:15 AM, Steven and Jeanette Murray <steven.j...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi there,
>
> I have the following model:
>
> data {
>     int<lower=0> N;                // number of halos
>     vector<lower=0>[N] log_m_meas; // measured halo masses
>     vector<lower=0>[N] sd_dex;     // uncertainty in halo masses (dex)
>     real<lower=0> V;               // Volume of the survey
>
>     // CONTROLS FOR PARAMETER BOUNDS
>     vector<lower=0>[2] hs_bounds;             // Bounds of logHs
>     vector<lower=-2,upper=0>[2] alpha_bounds; // Bounds of alpha
>     vector<lower=0>[2] beta_bounds;           // Bounds of beta
>     vector<lower=0>[2] mmin_bounds;           // Bounds of log_mmin
>     vector<lower=0>[2] mtrue_bounds;          // Bounds of log_mtrue
>     vector[2] lnA_bounds;                     // Bounds of lnA
>
> }
>
> parameters {
>     real<lower=hs_bounds[1],upper=hs_bounds[2]> logHs;               // Characteristic halo mass
>     real<lower=alpha_bounds[1],upper=alpha_bounds[2]> alpha;         // Power-law slope
>     real<lower=beta_bounds[1],upper=beta_bounds[2]> beta;            // Cut-off parameter
>     real<lower=mmin_bounds[1],upper=mmin_bounds[2]> log_mmin;        // Truncation mass
>     vector<lower=log_mmin,upper=mtrue_bounds[2]>[N] log_mtrue;       // True mass estimates
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>     real lnA;
>     real raw_lnA;
>     real gzx;
>
>     gzx <- gammainc((alpha+1)/beta,exp(log10()*(log_mmin-logHs)*beta));
>     raw_lnA <- log(N) - log10()*logHs - log(gzx);
>     lnA <- raw_lnA - log(V);
> }
>
> model {
>     vector[N] y;
>     y <- log_mtrue-logHs;
>     y ~ truncated_logGGD(logHs, alpha, beta, raw_lnA, gzx);
>     for (i in 1:N) log_mtrue[i] ~ normal(log_m_meas[i],sd_dex[i]) T[0,];
> }
>
>
> The code also contains the definition of a function for the truncated_logGGD_log, which I am confident is giving the correct numerical result (from tests outside of Stan). I didn't include it because it distracts from everything else. In short, the truncated_logGGD is the pdf of a generalised-gamma distribution truncated at mmin defined in log10-space. For intuition, this pdf looks like a decreasing power-law up to the value of about logHs, after which it cuts off exponentially. In fact, I can do better than that. Here's a picture of it:
>

> <Auto Generated Inline Image 1.png>

>
> The green and red lines are the truncated GGD (green is the intrinsic parameters of the distribution, red is the estimated).
>
> The input data, log_m_meas, is generated by choosing a value of mmin (in the case above, it is very close to 10^12), generating "intrinsic" data by sampling the truncated_logGGD (the pink region shows this intrinsic distribution), and then applying "measurement uncertainty" by choosing a measured value from a normal distribution with mean given by the intrinsic value, and uncertainty sd_dex[i] (this value is derived from an entirely separate model, and we just take it as "known" in this application).
>
> The above stan model should thus be the inverse generative model (I hope). However, you can see clearly that the parameters are wrong, and not by just a little bit.
>
> So, I had a bit of a deeper look. I calculated the MLE in a simple case using the intrinsic values and no sd_dex (i.e. a simple non-hierarchical model), and then put these parameters back into the full hierarchical model to get an estimate of the log-prob of what I would expect to be very close to the right answer. I also grabbed the MLE (estimated as the iteration with highest log-prob) from the full hierarchical run.
>
> The results were such that (expected - hierarchical) = -94.8. That is, the mode of the hierarchical run was of high probability than the expected answer. That makes sense, because that's where the sampler ended up.
>
> But then I wondered which part of the calculation favours the "wrong" solution, so I printed out the probability before any of the likelihood calculations, after the logGGD call and then after the normal() call. I got the following:
>
>                  |   Hier.    |  Expect.  | Diff.
> -----------------|------------|-----------|--------
> Before anything: |  -4102.91  |  -3036.69 | ~-1070
> After GGD:       |   11040.7  |  11018.7  | ~1100
> After Normal:    |   9947.09  |  10041.9  | ~-100
>
> Basically, if the "before anything" row didn't exist, the model would behave more as I expected -- the expected would be more likely. As far as I can understand, the "before anything" row comes about because of the transformation of parameters to unconstrained space, am I right? I was just wondering why this should mean my model ends up in the "wrong place". As in, if no transformation was applied, and I used the constrained parameters directly, my model would end up in the place I expect it. So why should it change when the transformation is applied? Am I missing something in my model which would account for this?
>
> Thanks for any help!
>
> Regards,
> Steven

p(hp | dat1, dat2) and p(hp_alt | dat1, dat2) and make sure

messages.subject: what is the unit/scale for priors

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

rstanarm is terrific, and my gateway into Bayesian regression. I'm giving a tutorial on rstanarm next month to spread the word. I just would like to clarify one issue. What units are the normal/student priors expressed in? Are they expressed in the raw units of y or in some unit-less transformation of y? I can't find a definitive answer in the package documentation or in the vignettes. It certainly seems like the units are scaled in some way.

In the continuous models vignette <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstanarm/vignettes/continuous.html>, the example uses the default normal(0, 5) but one of the effects has a median effect of 51.8 with a MAD of 15.3. If they units are in the raw units of y, then a prior of normal(0, 5) would regularize a 50 +/- 15 effect.

I also fit two stan_glm models on the iris dataset: `Sepal.Length ~ Sepal.Width * Species`. In one model, I scaled the continuous up measures by 1000 and left the measures unchanged in the other model, but I get comparable effects from both models. For example, the `Speciesversicolor` effect, I get 909.5  +/- 761.4 in the scaled data and 0.9 +/- 0.8 in the unscaled data. Both models have the normal(0, 5) prior, so it seems the prior works in some transformation of y.

Thanks,
Tristan

messages.body_plain:
On Friday, August 26, 2016 at 3:57:38 PM UTC-4, Tristan Mahr wrote:
> rstanarm is terrific, and my gateway into Bayesian regression. I'm giving a tutorial on rstanarm next month to spread the word. I just would like to clarify one issue. What units are the normal/student priors expressed in? Are they expressed in the raw units of y or in some unit-less transformation of y? I can't find a definitive answer in the package documentation or in the vignettes. It certainly seems like the units are scaled in some way.

The details depend on which stan_* function you are using, but rstanarm does not transform y internally ever.

> In the continuous models vignette <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstanarm/vignettes/continuous.html>, the example uses the default normal(0, 5) but one of the effects has a median effect of 51.8 with a MAD of 15.3. If they units are in the raw units of y, then a prior of normal(0, 5) would regularize a 50 +/- 15 effect.

stan_glm() with family = gaussian by default scales the given priors by the reciprocal standard deviations of the x variables.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, August 27, 2016 at 2:06:49 AM UTC-4, ErinC wrote:
> After reading Ben's FAQ on truncated priors, I am still confused about how to apply truncation in multilevel models to avoid having prior probability mass outside of the parameter range.

Truncation is not wrong. Lack of truncation is wrong if you truncate away a non-constant amount of area. Truncation is slow, so we avoid it when truncating away a constant amount of area. Truncation won't help if there is posterior density on the truncation point because that is negative infinity in the unconstrained space. So you are probably better off taking your chances without the constraint and a prior that does not put much density on values that are too low.

>   real mu_c;//IS A CONSTRAINT <lower=0.25> NEEDED because individual c's are constrained > 0.25?

Yes, if you keep that 0.25 constraint on c.

>   mu_c ~ normal( 0 , 1 );//MY Q: IS TRUNCATION NEEDED HERE TOO T[ 0.25, ] because individual c's are bounded below by 0.25?

The area to the left of 0.25 under a standard normal is a constant.

>   c_age ~ normal( 0 , 1 );//prior for effect of age on c. DO I NEED TO WORRY ABOUT THIS TERM BRINGING c_mid < 0.25

Yes.

>   c ~ normal( c_mid , sigma_c ) T[ 0.25, ];//This is what I understood was necessary from the FAQ on truncated priors

because the area to the left of 0.25 is not constant.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Sum-to-zero vector
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to model differences between a set astronomical spectra taken a given number of days apart. My model is that the difference will behave something like:

f2(n, wavelength) = f1(n, wavelength) + delta_t(n) * vector(wavelength)

However, the overall scale of the spectra is not known, and I need to include a constant offset between them:

f2(n, wavelength) = f1(n, wavelength) + delta_t(n) * vector(wavelength) + offset(n)

For my model to be identified, I need to impose some sort of a constraint on the vector. A sum-to-zero constraint makes the most sense.

Kyle

On Saturday, August 27, 2016 at 4:35:21 PM UTC-7, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Kyle:
> Can you explain why you want a set of parameters in your model to sum to 0?
> A
>
> > On Aug 27, 2016, at 7:33 PM, kbo...@berkeley.edu wrote:
> >
> > Hi,
> >
> > I've been trying to implement a sum-to-zero parameter vector in Stan. The manual suggests two ways of doing this: the "K-1" method where the last element is set to the negative sum of the previous ones or the "scaled simplex" method where the mean of a simplex is removed and then scaled. I've been running into issues with both of these:
> >
> > When using the simplex method, my models end up being non-identifiable. Fundamentally, a sum-to-zero vector has only K-1 degrees of freedom while this method has K degrees of freedom. For a two dimensional target vector, the simplex (0.4, 0.6) with scale 10 and the simplex (0.3, 0.7) with scale 5 both give the sum-to-zero vector (-1, 1).
> >
> > With the K-1 method, I find that the last element is privileged relative to the other ones and samples poorly. We've thought about implementing a sum-to-0 vector type in
Stan but haven't gotten around to it.  We would've gone with
the K-1 vector with the last being the negative sum of the
first.  So I'm curious as to why your approach works better,
at least in your problem.

One issue we have with all these parameterizations is how
to put priors on the elements, as we don't really want to
put priors on all K elements with only K-1 degrees of freedom,
but putting them only on K-1 has that asymmetry problem.

We run into similar problems with multilevel models, where
we have K groups, but usually use only (K - 1) non-zero parameters
in order to have identifiability.  Or when we have a multi-logit
regression with K categories in the output and only K-1
coefficient vectors.   We've talked about this one with Andrew,
too, and he's said the same thing about asymmetry, but we've
never come up with a solution that mixes well and has symmetry
for the priors.

For the unit vectors, we actually take K underlying parameters,
but then put a prior on them for identification.  It seems like
we might be able to do something similar here.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for all of your suggestions and replies!

I have been trying out the different variants that you suggested.

If I define a length K vector and put priors on its components constraining them to zero, then it kind of works in lower dimensions (K ~ 3), but breaks in the higher dimensions that I'm working in (K ~ 300). n_eff and Rhat both get significantly worse as the number of dimensions increases, from n_eff ~ 100 and Rhat ~ 1.01 in 3 dimensions to n_eff ~ 4 and Rhat ~ 1.7 in 300 dimensions (with iter=1000, chains=4). It does seem like this should make the model identifiable, so I'm a bit surprised that it doesn't work. Is there a better way to implement the sum-to-zero prior than something like T ~ normal(0, 1)?

I played with the K-1 vector method and it does seem to work reasonably well assuming that I specifically choose initial parameters that give the last vector element a reasonable starting value. With specifically chosen initial parameters, I get n_eff ~ 688 and Rhat=1 for my model with K=300.

I think that the method that I suggested in my first message does have symmetry for the priors assuming that you want the same prior on every element. Putting a normal(0, 1) prior on the T_raw vector seems to be equivalent to putting a normal(0, sqrt((W-1)/W)) prior on each of the elements of the T vector with a sum-to-zero constraint. I don't think that this would work for a prior that is not symmetric around 0.

Kyle

messages.body_plain:
We've had the same problem with trying to identify via the
priors.  It's technically identified for the MLE, but doesn't
do a great job sampling as it's not required to sum to zero.

In our simplex transform, which has the same asymmetry as the sum-to-one
construction, it's set up so that a zero init on the unconstrained space
leads to a uniform init on the constrained space.  But we tend not to
use very high-dimensional simplexes.  Our inits are uniform(-2, 2) by
default.

The sum-to-zero construction where the K-th element is

  alpha[1:(K - 1)] = alpha_raw;
  alpha[K] = sum(alpha_raw[1:(K - 1)])

will also have initial values of alpha = 0 for init alpha_raw = 0.

Thanks for the tip about your prior.  For the sum-to-zero construction
in the manual, putting

  alpha_raw ~ normal(0, 1)

(assuming independent normals per entry),  implies

  alpha[1:(K - 1)] ~ normal(0, 1)

but

  alpha[K] ~ normal(0, sqrt(K - 1))

so it's definitely not symmetric.

- Bob

> > I get better sampling performance with this method compared to either the simplex or K-1 methods. Would it be possible to implement something like this into the Stan language, or have something similar in the manual?
>
> We've thought about implementing a sum-to-0 vector type in
> Stan but haven't gotten around to it.  We would've gone with
> the K-1 vector with the last being the negative sum of the
> first.  So I'm curious as to why your approach works better,
> at least in your problem.
>
> One issue we have with all these parameterizations is how
> to put priors on the elements, as we don't really want to
> put priors on all K elements with only K-1 degrees of freedom,
> but putting them only on K-1 has that asymmetry problem.
>
> We run into similar problems with multilevel models, where
> we have K groups, but usually use only (K - 1) non-zero parameters
> in order to have identifiability.  Or when we have a multi-logit
> regression with K categories in the output and only K-1
> coefficient vectors.   We've talked about this one with Andrew,
> too, and he's said the same thing about asymmetry, but we've
> never come up with a solution that mixes well and has symmetry
> for the priors.
>
> For the unit vectors, we actually take K underlying parameters,
> but then put a prior on them for identification.  It seems like
> we might be able to do something similar here.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] hiararchical modeling in stan
messages.body_plain:
Looking at your generated quantities, I don't think it makes sense to simulate
peak area (peak_area_pred).  You already observe that so if you want to add
the observational noise you could just add it directly to the measurement.  Otherwise
your are ultimately calculating the batch-level average concentration with some noise
whereas you would typically want the sample concentration and uncertainty about
it.

On Thursday, August 25, 2016 at 11:27:46 AM UTC-4, Linas Mockus wrote:
> Krzysztof,
>
> Should I use lognormal for standards? It seems the absolute error gets higher for standards with higher concentration (peak area).

I don't really think I could tell without looking at the data.  The current model assumes
a linear relationship but higher noise for higher standards might just be coming from
the instrument becoming saturated which may be a bigger problem.

>
> I have 10 lots, 10 samples per lot, 1 injections per sample, 3 injections per standard.

I think your model makes it look like the standards are injected once per lot (?) Either that
or something is still off a little.  If so you could either make the model simpler by assuming
that the slope/intercept (c_std) are consistent across lots or get more information out of the
model by adding a hierarchical model for the slope/intercept (replacing this bit):

for (i in 1 : N_LOTS)
        c_std [i] ~ normal (0, 100);

> The example is attached. I am not sure if I handle standards samples standards samples sequence most effectively. Any comments?

Thanks for sharing the example.  If you don't know the sequence I'm not sure that you could do better.  If you do know the sequence you could
use the item's position in the sequence as an effect on the baseline and response (c_std).

Krzysztof

>
> Linas

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sum-to-zero vector
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Sum-to-zero vector
messages.body_plain:
It's up to you, but given your problem description it's pretty clear to me that you should _not_ be defining your parameters to sum to 0.  It's unnecessary and is just slowing you down in various ways.
A

> On Aug 28, 2016, at 12:54 PM, kbo...@berkeley.edu wrote:
>

> Thanks for all of your suggestions and replies!
>
> I have been trying out the different variants that you suggested.
>
> If I define a length K vector and put priors on its components constraining them to zero, then it kind of works in lower dimensions (K ~ 3), but breaks in the higher dimensions that I'm working in (K ~ 300). n_eff and Rhat both get significantly worse as the number of dimensions increases, from n_eff ~ 100 and Rhat ~ 1.01 in 3 dimensions to n_eff ~ 4 and Rhat ~ 1.7 in 300 dimensions (with iter=1000, chains=4). It does seem like this should make the model identifiable, so I'm a bit surprised that it doesn't work. Is there a better way to implement the sum-to-zero prior than something like T ~ normal(0, 1)?
>
> I played with the K-1 vector method and it does seem to work reasonably well assuming that I specifically choose initial parameters that give the last vector element a reasonable starting value. With specifically chosen initial parameters, I get n_eff ~ 688 and Rhat=1 for my model with K=300.
>
> I think that the method that I suggested in my first message does have symmetry for the priors assuming that you want the same prior on every element. Putting a normal(0, 1) prior on the T_raw vector seems to be equivalent to putting a normal(0, sqrt((W-1)/W)) prior on each of the elements of the T vector with a sum-to-zero constraint. I don't think that this would work for a prior that is not symmetric around 0.
>
> Kyle
>
> On Saturday, August 27, 2016 at 6:08:19 PM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> > > On Aug 28, 2016, at 1:33 AM, kbo...@berkeley.edu wrote:
> > >
> > > With the K-1 method, I find that the last element is privileged relative to the other ones and samples poorly.
> >
> > You mean just the K-th component has worse R-hat or
> > lower n_eff?
> >
> > >  A sum-to-zero vector is a point in the K-1 dimensional plane that is orthogonal to the (1, 1, 1, ...) vector, and the "basis vectors" of the K-1 method are complete but not orthogonal in this plane.
> > >
> > > I believe that a better method would be to define an orthogonal basis that maps out this plane. For example, the basis:
> > > [1, -1, 0, 0, 0, ...]
> > > [1/2, 1/2, -1, 0, 0, ...]
> > > [1/3, 1/3, 1/3, -1, 0, ...]
> > > ...
> > > (with normalization of sqrt(1/n + 1)) will work. There might be a better way of generating such a basis that I am not aware of. Here is some example code to implement this transformation:
> > >
> > > parameters {
> > >     vector[W-1] T_raw;
> > > }
> > > transformed parameters {
> > >     vector[W] T;
> > >
> > >     for (w in 1:W-1) {
> > >         T[w] = 0.;
> > >         for (w2 in w:W-1) {
> > >             T[w] = T[w] + T_raw[w2] / w2 / sqrt(1/w2 + 1);
> > >         }
> > >     }
> > >     T[W] = 0.;
> > >
> > >     for (w in 1:W-1) {
> > >         T[w+1] = T[w+1] - T_raw[w] / sqrt(1/w + 1);
> > >     }
> > > }
> >
> > > I get better sampling performance with this method compared to either the simplex or K-1 methods. Would it be possible to implement something like this into the Stan language, or have something similar in the manual?
> >
> > We've thought about implementing a sum-to-0 vector type in
> > Stan but haven't gotten around to it.  We would've gone with
> > the K-1 vector with the last being the negative sum of the
> > first.  So I'm curious as to why your approach works better,
> > at least in your problem.
> >
> > One issue we have with all these parameterizations is how
> > to put priors on the elements, as we don't really want to
> > put priors on all K elements with only K-1 degrees of freedom,
> > but putting them only on K-1 has that asymmetry problem.
> >
> > We run into similar problems with multilevel models, where
> > we have K groups, but usually use only (K - 1) non-zero parameters
> > in order to have identifiability.  Or when we have a multi-logit
> > regression with K categories in the output and only K-1
> > coefficient vectors.   We've talked about this one with Andrew,
> > too, and he's said the same thing about asymmetry, but we've
> > never come up with a solution that mixes well and has symmetry
> > for the priors.
> >
> > For the unit vectors, we actually take K underlying parameters,
> > but then put a prior on them for identification.  It seems like
> > we might be able to do something similar here.
> >
> > - Bob
>

messages.body_plain:
Again, nothing wrong with attacking the technical problem.  But, as with many such problems, I don't think it's real.
A

> On Aug 28, 2016, at 1:27 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> We've had the same problem with trying to identify via the
> priors.  It's technically identified for the MLE, but doesn't
> do a great job sampling as it's not required to sum to zero.
>
> In our simplex transform, which has the same asymmetry as the sum-to-one
> construction, it's set up so that a zero init on the unconstrained space
> leads to a uniform init on the constrained space.  But we tend not to
> use very high-dimensional simplexes.  Our inits are uniform(-2, 2) by
> default.
>
> The sum-to-zero construction where the K-th element is
>
>  alpha[1:(K - 1)] = alpha_raw;
>  alpha[K] = sum(alpha_raw[1:(K - 1)])
>
> will also have initial values of alpha = 0 for init alpha_raw = 0.
>
> Thanks for the tip about your prior.  For the sum-to-zero construction
> in the manual, putting
>
>  alpha_raw ~ normal(0, 1)
>
> (assuming independent normals per entry),  implies

On Sunday, August 28, 2016 at 5:18:29 PM UTC-4, ErinC wrote:
> - What do you mean by truncation 'won't help' if there is posterior density on the truncation point? Should I be getting numerical errors if this happens or will my posterior be wrong without stan error messages?

Probably will get a lot of divergent transitions

>  So you are probably better off taking your chances without the constraint and a prior that does not put much density on values that are too low.
> - Are you suggesting I use more informative priors for mu_c and sigma_c or change the type of prior I use for the population distribution (I'm not sure what a reasonable alternative is to a truncated normal(c_mid, sigma_c))?

If 0.25 is more than 2 or 3 sigma_c units from c_mid, then it will rarely be down to 0.25 but not require a transformation 0.25 + exp(...).

> > >   c_age ~ normal( 0 , 1 );//prior for effect of age on c. DO I NEED TO WORRY ABOUT THIS TERM BRINGING c_mid < 0.25
> >
> > Yes. - What can I do about this? It's not clear to me how to constrain c_age to ensure c_mid stays within [ 0.25, ] since age (age_c for centered) is a continuous variable. I'd like to eventually also add in an additional predictor, which adds challenge.

It is very difficult. You have to store the max and min of age_c in transformed data and then choose bounds on mu_c such that c_age * min_age is small enough when c_age > 0 and c_age * max_age is small enough when c_age > 0.

Ben

constraint will help with mixing.  Having soft identifiability
from priors makes it hard for the model to fit.  That's discussion
we were having with the K-1 coefficient vector vs. K cefficient
vector for multi-logit.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your fast response Bob.

On Saturday, 27 August 2016 03:12:18 UTC+8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Why have a lower=0 bound on the log scale?

You're right, I've removed that now, not that it should make much difference.

> And we don't genrally recommend bounds like (-2, 0)
> unless the parameter is physically constrained to (-2, 0).

What do you suggest then? I wanted to (at least initially) use a uniform prior, but of course it's improper to use an unbounded uniform prior. I know alpha is ~-1.87 and should have a very tight constraint. It will never be greater than -1.5 and there's reason to expect it to be constrained above -2 (though technically it could be lower). Typically I find that it's -1.87 +- 0.02 or so. Given that kind of range, would these bounds still be a source of bias? I've run it again (see below) with more generous bounds to check for myself.

> Otherwise, you can bias the posterior means considerably by
> truncating non-negligible probability mass.
>
> In general, you just code the generative model directly
> in Stan and Stan does the inversion---you shouldn't try
> to code the inversion directly unless you have analytical
> steps (which can save time and make the statistical mixing
> more efficient).
>

Sorry, yes I used the generative model directly. I mean, I generate the data by choosing the parameters, sampling from the truncated_logGGD with those parameters to get log_mtrue, then sampling from a normal to get log_m_meas. That's directly what I have in my model.

> The MLE is not the iteration with the highest log density.
> Often the MLE isn't in the typical set at all, so you won't
> get anywhere near it (e.g., try sampling from a 20-dimensional
> unit normal exactly and see how close you get to zero, the MLE).
> What you want to be doing is checking posterior interval
> calibration (coverage, say, of the 50% intervals).
>

Okay, fair enough. So, are you saying that even though the expected solution had a lower likelihood than another region in my chains, that it's possible that the chain would centre around the expected solution anyway?

> Also, just measuring by the log density won't tell you much.
>

In a couple of re-runs below I show the parameter intervals instead. Is this better?

> I'm afraid I don't understand this truncated density---maybe
> someone else could help?
>

That's fine. I'm confident that the truncated density is doing what it's supposed to.

> - Bob

So, I ran again with the following model (note I just took out some of the bounds on log parameters):

data {
    int<lower=0> N;                // number of halos

    vector[N] log_m_meas; // measured halo masses

    vector<lower=0>[N] sd_dex;     // uncertainty in halo masses (dex)
    real<lower=0> V;               // Volume of the survey

    // CONTROLS FOR PARAMETER BOUNDS

    vector[2] hs_bounds;             // Bounds of logHs
    vector[2] alpha_bounds;          // Bounds of alpha

    vector<lower=0>[2] beta_bounds;  // Bounds of beta

    vector[2] mmin_bounds;           // Bounds of log_mmin
    vector[2] mtrue_bounds;          // Bounds of log_mtrue

    vector[2] lnA_bounds;            // Bounds of lnA
}

parameters {
    real<lower=hs_bounds[1],upper=hs_bounds[2]> logHs;               // Characteristic halo mass
    real<lower=alpha_bounds[1],upper=alpha_bounds[2]> alpha;         // Power-law slope
    real<lower=beta_bounds[1],upper=beta_bounds[2]> beta;            // Cut-off parameter
    real<lower=mmin_bounds[1],upper=mmin_bounds[2]> log_mmin;        // Truncation mass
    vector<lower=log_mmin,upper=mtrue_bounds[2]>[N] log_mtrue;       // True mass estimates
}

transformed parameters {
    real lnA;
    real raw_lnA;
    real gzx;

    gzx <- gammainc((alpha+1)/beta,exp(log10()*(log_mmin-logHs)*beta));
    raw_lnA <- log(N) - log10()*logHs - log(gzx);
    lnA <- raw_lnA - log(V);
}

model {
    vector[N] y;
    y <- log_mtrue-logHs;
    y ~ truncated_logGGD(logHs, alpha, beta, raw_lnA, gzx);

    log_m_meas ~ normal(log_mtrue,sd_dex);
}

I first ran with the following data [this is the same as I used in my results for the last post] (note I constrain alpha, i.e. the power-law slope of the function to (-1.99,-1.7)):

{'N': 5078,
 'V': 1190658.039618655,
 'alpha_bounds': (-1.99, -1.7),
 'beta_bounds': (0.4, 1.2),
 'hs_bounds': (13, 15.5),
 'lnA_bounds': (-48, -37),
 'log_m_meas': array([ 13.35251163, 11.78469724, 12.01253925, ..., 12.72611462, 14.18542692, 12.40310497]),
 'mmin_bounds': (10, 14),
 'mtrue_bounds': (10, 17.0),  # Note: only the upper bound here is actually used.
 'sd_dex': array([ 0.63660784, 0.79483786, 0.79483786, ..., 0.7411142 , 0.7411142 , 0.7411142 ])}

The Stan summary is

                  mean se_mean     sd   2.5%    25%    50%    75%  97.5%  n_eff   Rhat
logHs            14.61    0.02   0.27  14.15  14.42  14.59  14.77  15.21  280.0   1.01
alpha             -1.8  4.7e-3   0.06  -1.92  -1.84   -1.8  -1.75  -1.71  156.0   1.03
beta              0.87  8.4e-3   0.21   0.44   0.71    0.9   1.05   1.19  646.0    1.0
log_mmin         12.03  2.1e-3   0.02  11.98  12.01  12.03  12.04  12.07  126.0   1.03

and the input values were

{'alpha': -1.8682714014860426,  ## outside 50% coverage
 'beta': 0.6999588565297955,    ## outside 50% coverage
 'logHs': 14.312105251983247    ## outside 50% coverage
 'log_mmin': 12.04004004        ## just outside 50% coverage
}

The traceplot looks like:

I then ran it again, with the following data (note the relaxation of several bounds):

{'N': 5046,
 'V': 1190658.039618655,
 'alpha_bounds': (-3, -1),
 'beta_bounds': (0.2, 2.0),
 'hs_bounds': (12, 15.05),
 'lnA_bounds': (-48, -37),
 'log_m_meas': array([ 12.64310298,  11.64157076,  12.23913006, ...,  12.24778487,
         11.71975052,  13.23577041]),
 'mmin_bounds': (10, 14),
 'mtrue_bounds': (10, 17.0),
 'sd_dex': array([ 0.8705571 ,  0.7411142 ,  0.79483786, ...,  0.79483786,
         0.79483786,  0.66539496])}

and get the following results:

                  mean se_mean     sd   2.5%    25%    50%    75%  97.5%  n_eff   Rhat
logHs            14.27    0.03   0.49  12.63  14.23  14.45  14.56  14.64  278.0    1.0
alpha            -1.74  7.1e-3    0.1  -1.88  -1.81  -1.76  -1.69  -1.48  209.0   1.01
beta              1.04    0.02   0.51   0.26   0.58    1.0   1.48   1.95  449.0    1.0
log_mmin         12.02  1.9e-3   0.03  11.97   12.0  12.02  12.03  12.06  190.0   1.01

Now logHs is within range, and so is beta (on account of its range being very large). But alpha is way off.  While running these, I noticed one interesting thing: if logHs is larger than max(log_mtrue), its effect plateau's in terms of its correlation with beta. That is, if the scale where the exponential cut-off happens is outside the range of masses, then it doesn't matter what beta is at all. That's why I've kept logHs bounded to ~15.

I ran the same model but setting the log_mtrue to the actual intrinsic masses (so no hierarchical model) and as a comparison I get the following plot (blue is the constrained model):

You can see the offset of alpha clearly. Do you think I'm doing everything right but perhaps there's just not enough data?

Thanks again,
Steven

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Unexpected rejection of initial values with truncated posterior
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Unexpected rejection of initial values with truncated posterior
messages.body_plain:
What happens when you set the bounds (0, U) on mu is that random
initialization is centered around U / 2;  more specifically, it's
U * inv_logit(uniform(-2, 2)).

When you have the bounds (0, infinity) on sigma, the initialization
is centered around 1;  more specifically, random inits will be
exp(uniform(-2, 2)).

When you put those together, you're trying to evaluate
the gradient of the log density, it underflows due to double-precision
arithmetic.

If you take the same model and provide reasonable inits, such
as mu=1500 and sigma=1500, it will fit OK with that data:

      mean se_mean  sd 2.5%  25%  50%  75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
mu     520      13 310   39  295  486  725  1173   536    1
sigma 1267      17 321  814 1041 1211 1414  2094   363    1

In general, putting things on a more unit-like scale will help immensely
with Stan's adaptation, as well as its ability to get off the ground.

- Bob

>     int<lower=1> N;  // observation count.
>     vector<lower=0, upper=U>[N] X;  // observed values.
> }
> parameters {
>     real mu;
>     real<lower=0> sigma;
> }
> model {
>     // Likelihood.
>     for (n in 1:N) {
>         X[n] ~ normal(mu, sigma) T[0, U];
>     }
>
>     // Prior.
>     mu ~ normal(0, 1000);
>     sigma ~ normal(0, 1000);  // behaves as if T[0,].
> }

> I get a reasonable-looking distribution over mu. However, I wanted to see what the posterior would look like if I restricted mu to the range [0, U]:

What was the behavior?

The 8schools code you sent *is* vectorized in
the densities.  Although 8schools is trivial due
to size, in general

  eta ~ normal(0, 1);

is more efficient than

  target += normal_lpdf(eta | 0, 1);

because it'll drop the constant terms.

The vectorized probability functions are more
efficient because they can share computations and require
fewer virtual function calls for derivative propagation.

- Bob

I don't see how maximum likelihood is relevant here.
But yes, all the intervals are what we're really after,
or even better, the full joint posterior.  That's harder
to measure as you go out into the tails.

Basically, all of our existing convergence diagnostics
are based on expectations.  We just compare multiple MCMC
chains to each other using R-hat.  Our n_eff calculations
for Stan also build-in cross-chain convergence adjustments,
which is why n_eff is the one thing to look at (assuming it's
not too low per iteration that we don't trust the estimates).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi group

Is there any plans for support of lists of vectors of uneven sizes? You can see a matrix as a list of vectors, each of which having the same length, but what if you input data, for example, consists of different cases each having a varying number of observations? The only solution I found so far is to put all the data in a large vector and carry along a second array that indicates the starting position of the different cases. That is error-prone and ugly.

thanks

messages.body_plain:
I want to do a weighted model in Stan - in the very old days, you just duplicated, triplicated etc, the samples that you regarded as more important( like recent samples versus older samples, or samples where the target was known to be less noisy that others ). Now R's lm  lets you provide a weights vector.
For Stan after reading the discussion in the dev-group  - https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-dev/5pJdH72hoM8
I tried this -
      increment_log_prob(wtsnormedLogged[i]*normal_log(sess[i],(  p[i]  + weekly_tv*WEEKLY_TV_SPEND[i] + weekly_rd*WEEKLY_RD_SPEND[i] + tv_coeff*tv_spend_prime[i]
                                   + rd_coeff*rd_spend_prime[i]
                                   + br_coeff*SEM_BRAND_SPEND[i]
                                   + nb_coeff*SEM_NB_SPEND[i] ),sigma_sess));

And for the weights  I provided this via R ( code below is from R ) -  Since stan works in the logged space I thought I shd log the weights vector, in addition to normalising it to 1. I got Rhats of 10**5, 10**7 and so on !

Shdn't I be logging the wts vector then ?

============= R code that creates the weighting vector
wts<-vector(length=(nrow(dms)))
wts<-c(rep(1,N_dates))
wts[as.Date(dms$Date)>as.Date('2014-12-08') & as.Date(dms$Date)<=as.Date('2015-01-05')]<-.0001
wts[as.Date(dms$Date)==as.Date('2015-12-25')]<-.00001
wts[dms$Year>=2016]<-30
total_wt<-sum(wts)
wtsnormed<-wts/total_wt
wtsnormedLogged<-log(wtsnormed)

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] weights to models ?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] weights to models ?
messages.body_plain:
No, definitely not.  Think about what happens when you
have two observations.  You multiply their likelihoods
on the linear scale, so you add them on the log scale,
so that means you multiply the log likelihood by the weight
(which would be 2 in this case).

The new notation is

 target += u;

instead of

  increment_log_prob(u);

and normal_lpdf(y | mu, sigma)  instead of normal_log(y, mu, sigma).

On Tuesday, August 30, 2016 at 1:15:05 PM UTC-4, Shantanu K. Karve wrote:
> Yup I saw that Andrew doesn't like weighting. I'll have to look up the term "generative model" to see what he's getting at

The idea is that the weights don't actually factor in to the data generating process (how the data came to be, so to speak). If you have a sample that you know isn't representative of the population then you can still use a generative model by conditioning on the relevant variables (i.e. the variables that would go into the weights).
