messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] graded irt model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] graded irt model
messages.body_plain:
See inline.

> On Aug 30, 2016, at 4:56 PM, Teddy Groves <groves...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Stan users,
>
> I've been trying to fit a graded item response model and have some questions.
>
> I started with the code that David Furr posted here and made the following changes. First, each of my items has the same number of possible grades, so I put the difficulty parameters in a matrix rather than a vector. Second, I haven't tried to fit any discrimination parameters. Finally, I've attempted to add a subject-level predictor.
>
> My data doesn't quite fit the standard irt paradigm as the 'items' represent types of graded actions rather than exam questions. As a result, many items are attempted multiple times by the same subject. I think this situation still fits within the standard IRT framework but I am no expert.
>
> The STAN code I've been using is as follows:
>
> graded_irt_code_no_discrimination = """
> data {
>     int<lower=1> I;                // number of types of actions
>     int<lower=1> J;                // number of subjects
>     int<lower=1> N;                // number of actions
>     int<lower=1> G;                // number of grades
>     int<lower=1,upper=I> ii[N];    // type of action n
>     int<lower=1,upper=J> jj[N];    // subject for action n
>     vector[J] x;                   // subject-level predictor
>     int<lower=1,upper=G+1> y[N];   // grade for action n, i.e. 1 (max loss), ..., G+1(loss 0)
> }
> parameters {
>     vector[I] kappa_one;                // First difficulties
>     matrix<lower=0>[I, G-1] delta;      // Difficulty step-changes
>     real theta[J];                      // Ability
>     real beta_x;                        // coefficient for x
>     real<lower=0> sigma_x;
>     }
> transformed parameters{
>     ordered[G] kappa[I];    // difficulties
>     for (i in 1:I){
>         kappa[i, 1] <- kappa_one[i];
>         for (g in 2:G){
>             kappa[i, g] <- kappa_one[i] + cumulative_sum(delta[i])[g-1];
>         }
>     }
> }

This is going to be super slow as you're continually recomputing
terms in those cumulative sums.

You can just declare kappa as a parameter directly (as
you've declared it) and put a prior on the differences.

for (i in 1:I)

  kappa[i, 2:G] - kappa[i, 1:(G - 1)] ~ normal(0, 5);

The Jacobian has a constant diagonal, so you don't need
to adjust for it.

It should also be a lot faster.

> model {
>     theta ~ normal(x * beta_x, sigma_x);
>     for (i in 1:I){
>         for (g in 1:G-1){
>             delta[i, g] ~ normal(0, 5);
>         }
>     }
>     kappa_one ~ normal(0, 5);
>     for (n in 1:N) {
>         y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(theta[jj[n]], kappa[ii[n]]);
>     }
> }
> """

The ordered logistic is slow and hasn't been vectorized yet.

The bigger problem for statistical mixing may be that the
ordered logistic isn't identified if you have an intercept,
because it allows all the cutpoints and the intercept to
move together.

>
>
> Unfortunately I can't share the data I used as it's commercially sensitive. There are about 1600 subjects, 11 grades, 40 items and 18176 responses.

It's always good to start with simulated data to make sure
your model's working as intended.

> The model runs as written above, though it seems quite slow to converge. Here are the highlights of the fit summary after 300 iterations in five chains, which took my computer about 1700 seconds:

Was that running in parallel?  How many cores do you have?
We all have four-core CPUs and run four chains in parallel.
Doesn't save compute cycles, but it can be a huge win in
wall time.

> Inference for Stan model: anon_model_e394c55777111f927c5e15a6c0afa0a2.
> 5 chains, each with iter=300; warmup=150; thin=1;
> post-warmup draws per chain=150, total post-warmup draws=750.
>
>                 mean se_mean     sd   2.5%    25%    50%    75%  97.5%  n_eff   Rhat
> kappa_one[0]  -13.86    0.24   2.75 -19.49 -15.78 -13.81 -11.84  -8.84    127   1.01
> kappa_one[1]  -10.79    0.19   2.45 -16.31 -12.39 -10.49  -8.98  -6.73    163    1.0
> ...
> delta[0,0]      1.39    0.08   1.29   0.04   0.39   1.05   1.96   4.66    251    1.0
> delta[1,0]      1.63    0.09   1.43   0.06   0.58   1.29   2.25   5.74    251    1.0
> ...
> theta[0]        0.48    0.02   0.26  -0.03   0.31   0.48   0.64   1.05    251    1.0
> theta[1]        0.26    0.02    0.3  -0.33   0.05   0.25   0.45   0.85    251    1.0
> ...
> beta_x          0.37    0.01   0.04    0.3   0.35   0.37    0.4   0.43      9   1.17
> sigma_x         0.32  6.3e-3   0.03   0.27    0.3   0.32   0.34   0.37     17   1.32
> ...
> kappa[20,8]    -0.25  7.3e-3   0.07  -0.39   -0.3  -0.25   -0.2  -0.12     95   1.04
> kappa[21,8]     0.92  7.9e-3   0.13   0.67   0.84   0.92    1.0   1.19    251   1.02
> ...
> lp__          -2.7e4   27.09 108.34 -2.7e4 -2.7e4 -2.7e4 -2.7e4 -2.7e4     16   1.36

The problem here is thta the model hasn't converged in the beta and sigma parameters.

> I also got quite a few of the following warning message in the first 30 iterations, and a couple more later:
>
> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
>
> validate transformed params: kappa[k0__] is not a valid ordered vector. The element at 2 is -7.65643, but should be greater than the previous element, -7.65643

normal(0, 5) with truncation below at zero isn't a zero-avoiding
prior---there's a non-zero density at zero.  If you really want them
to be non-zero, you should use a lognormal or a gamma of the right shape.

> I'd really like to know:
> 	• Is there a problem with fitting this kind of model to data where the subjects attempt the same item more than once?

Not in principle, but it makes a probably unwarranted independence
assumption across the multiple tries (maybe the later tries will
be more likely to succeed, or maybe the student has the same problem
all the time).

> 	• Why is the warning triggered even though the delta parameter is constrained to be greater than or equal to 0?

See above.  It's the equal that's the problem.

> 	• Is the speed of the model inevitable given the amount of data or is there a way to make it faster?

See above.

> 	• Is there is a neater or more efficient way to obtain the kappa vectors in the transformed parameters block?

See above---just don't do it, or combine terms in
the cumulative sum claculations.

> 	• Have I coded the subject-level predictor correctly? (I'm worried that I might have inadvertently caused scale or identifiability issues.)

I'm not sure why you're sampling here.  I'm not an expert
on these models, though.

> 	• What would be the best way to add item-level predictors?

Just add them like in any other GLM.

> Any help would be greatly appreciated!

Hope that helps.

- Bob

Assuming no saturation linear should be good enough. Right?  I am looking for best practice and based on Andrew's paper thought that linear is oversimplication. For some reason PK folks use lognormal so my impression was that analytical measurements behave lognormal - with higher concentration variability is higher. I am off?

> >
> > "I think your model makes it look like the standards are injected once per lot (?) Either that
> > or something is still off a little.  If so you could either make the model simpler by assuming
> > that the slope/intercept (c_std) are consistent across lots or get more information out of the
> > model by adding a hierarchical model for the slope/intercept (replacing this bit):
> >
> > for (i in 1 : N_LOTS)
> >         c_std [i] ~ normal (0, 100);"

Here I am assuming that standards are injected once per lot. I will update the model based on actual sequence. I have tried hierarchical c_std but don't know if it is a good practice. For me it makes sense to have c_std for every standard injection set (is standards are injected several times per lot then I will have several c_std) or alternatively have hierarchical c_std. The objective of the project is to estimate variability components (intra- inter-lot and analytical). To estimate analytical variability I plan to have several injections per sample.  Maybe I am doing too much and should consider c_std consistent for all lots?
>

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, August 31, 2016 at 5:05:13 AM UTC-4, Paul Viefers wrote:
> Dear all
>
> Starting today, I get some strange behavior in R using stan. In short, I can compile stan models and sample from them, but
> rstan pastes a series of warnings into the console (see below) - no clue what they mean, and

Those are just compiler warnings. Don't worry about them.

> I cannot use a fitted model so sample from it again (see below).

You can't just pass a stanfit object to the first argument of stan() like

> fit2 <- stan(fit, data=c("T",
+                          "y",
+                          "x"),
+              iter=500,
+              chains=1)
Error in path.expand(path) : invalid 'path' argument

The (now outdated) way to do this is to pass it to the argument named fit, like

fit2 <- stan(data = c("T", "y", "x", fit = fit, iter = 500, chains = 1)

but it shouldn't recompile if you just do

fit2 <- stan(model_code = code,, data = c("T", "y", "x"), iter = 500, chains = 1)

which is not to say that only running 1 chain is a good idea.

Ben

messages.subject: Piggypacking Stan's output format and tools
messages.subject_clean: Piggypacking Stan's output format and tools
messages.body_plain:
This may be more relevant for the Stan development team, and if so please forward along or tell me where to resubmit.

I'm interested in adding HMC functionality to an existing piece of software (migrating models to Stan is too time intensive for the moment). My goal is to try and mimic the basic functionality that Stan provides, specifically static HMC & NUTS. If I can get 75% of the functionality and speed that would be a huge step forward.

I don't want to reinvent the wheel so my plan is to model the algorithms (inputs/outputs) to match Stan and then use all the nice features for diagnostics and inference already built in to Rstan.

So I was thinking it would be a good idea to write output to .csv files like cmdstan does, and then coerce them into stanfit objects. Then I'd be able to use the methods for that class, such as monitor, pairs, and even shinystan. I imagine some of the slots wouldn't be relevant, such as @model and @stanmodel, but those could be populated with dummy values. It seems that if I went this approach I could just use read_stan_csv directly.

My question is whether this is an advisable track to take? Or would there be a simpler way to approach this? If it's a reasonable approach, is there an easy way to see the format of the cmdstan csv files? It's not immediately apparent by digging through the cmdstan repo.

Thanks,
Cole

licensed.

Was there anything you needed in RStan that's not in ShinyStan?

Either way, you're better off just reading the data in via
the much simpler Coda format (mcmc.list) and using the monitor()
function and for anything fancier, using ShinyStan, which will
also take simple Coda-formatted input.

We'll be changing the exact format of the CSV files and may even
move to JSON or protocol buffers---no guarantee on stability at
the CSV level in the future.
